GOD'S PROVIDENCE. es, for us, through the long year glowing, Old Winter's face is a beacon fair; Winter comes to our hearts bestowing Feast and frolic and all things rare. _ But what—ah, what of our friends in feather, When whirling round in the gusts that blow, The flakes are falling for days together, And the food of the birds lies hid below? Shall we forget them, not once recalling The thrush's lilt and the linnet's trill? Are there no crumbs from our tables falling, Right welcome alms at the window sill? • 'Nay, but we'll think of our friends in feather.l When the snow lies heaped round the bare tree's stem. And we'll say for the rest, in the iron weather "Our Fattier is theirs, and He feedethlthem." •—FREDERIC% LANGBRIDGE in Tee Quiver.

STREET DOORS. I have no doubt that Bluebeard's chamber door The features of a guiltless portal wore; Its keyhole whispered not; its handle made No sign that all the crime within betrayed; And the smooth panels could their secret keep, As calm pools do that o'er drowned wretches sleep. So smooth, so calm, the city's front doors close On lives laid waste and more than Theban woes; The indifferent wood without grimace shuts in The mother's anguish or the husband's sin. Perhaps the hand, from whose familiar thrill The latch just !fallen scarcely vet is still, lEl' In vain appeases, with beseeching sign. The lawful tyrant, crimson-hot with wine, Or idly strives, beside the fluttering breath, To push away immitigable Death. Who knows or dreams? Men so demurely can Confront their God, much more their fellow-man. But now and then some portal left ajar F- Gives glimpses swift of what our neighbours are, Or, flung back suddenly, lets forth the shriek Of some lone anguish, pent for many a week, Tow'rds which the passers eddy, and incline A moment's ear, then hurry on to dine. • And it so oft hath happened that, whene'er A clink has gaped through which my eye could peer Into one cell of those still murmuring hives, Where we gregarious men lead lonely lives, So much of sin and sorrow have I seen, So many scars yet raw where both have been, So little happiness, but, in its stead, - Abase content, unhopeful, callous, dead, That I have cried, "Fate, show me, then, the home, Where Death or worse hath not this morning come, The one safe sanctuary,whither Sorrow - Came not to- day or will not come to-morrow r And so a line of street doors standing white, Stiff and respectable from morn till night, Is oft as strong to till my mind with glooms As a dumb city of unwindowed tombs, Where my roused fancy, deft in such grim tricks, Strives with a shuddering eagerness to fix In which uncertain one of them may strive Some uncoffined horror dungeoned there alive; Nay, worse than doors of sepulchres are these That close o'er all of Death except his peace! JAMES RUSSELL LOWELL.

Why does a sailor know there is a man in the moon Because he has been to see. A little girl's definition of ice—Water that stayed out in the cold and went to sleep. An editor being challenged, sent word in reply, "When I want to die I can shoot myself." We are asked when a young lady is of age, and we un- hesitatingly- reply not until she is married. " Och," said a love-sick Hibernian, "what a recrea- tion it is to be dying of love! It sets the heart aching so delicately there's no taking a wink of sleep for the . pleasure of the pain!" "Here's the sugar, Angelina—sweet, just like you," he murmured, as he passed her the bowl at the tea table. A moment after she handed him the butter, and whis- pered," Here it is, George—soft, just like you." Many may remember the story of the three aldermen's wives playing at the game, "I love my love with a let- ter.' The first began "I love my love with a G because he is a Grastice;" the second, "I lave my love with an N because he is a Night S' the third, "I love my love with an F because he is a Fisician." It was the " Gustice" himself who gave the toast at a literary dinner, " The three R's, reading, ritine'e rithmetic:" DRUNKENNESS AS AN EXCUSE FOR CRlME.—Perhaps it would be more correct to say dru kenness as a negation of crime, for if there he crime there must needs be re- sponsibility; whereas, if there be no responsibility, there cannot possibly be crime, the criminality lying in the progressive nature of the act, not in the act itself. This being understood, the question arises how far drunken- ness absolves from respensibility. Dr. Savage, of Beth- ,' leheen, discusses this topic in an i teresting paper which appears in the Journal of Mental Science for April. There can he no question as to the responsibility of a person who t nowingly- places himself in a condition to do wrong unconsciously. The criminal act of getting drunk 1 covers all that is done by the self-intsxicator ; but ques- tions arising in connection with accidental drunkenness, pr the permanent effects of drunkenness and hereditary demoralisation by drink, render the general issue ex- tremely complicated. Practically we think it should be ' understood and laid down as a principle that self-intoxi- cation does not negative responsibility, and that the only .question of extenuating conditions must take the farm of an inquiry whether inheritance or disease rendered self-intoxication co abnormally facile as to justify the belief that the act of intoxication was unwittingly ac- complished. The paper by Dr. Savage will repay per- eusaL —The Zancet. MOTISER AND Sme—A boy is not like a girl. He can- alot stay at home and find pleasant occupation about the house. He has no dolls to dress, no fancy work to em- ploy himself with-, therefore he ought to have amuse- ments found for hira, for he must be amused. Amuse- ment is as necessary for the young as raindrops are to towers. Without etre the flowers grow stunted and ill- favoured. Without amusement a child will droop and become old before -its time. I see the boys of the rich playing about the streets like young scapegraces—brave, intelligent boys, who would be good and noble if they were trained, but who, getting no training, go in like the rest of the world for "a good time" only, and yet, a very little bending would make those twigs grow in perfect shape. The mother is the head gardener. She is the responsible person for the acts of her boy, as a general rule. The -first lesson to teach a boy is to make him honour himself—to steer clear of falsehood as a deadly serpent, for, after all, falsehood is the lowest attribute, and leads to all kinds of sin. It is a bad plan to doubt a boy's word; -there is something in the heart of every boy that shrinks from being doubted. Never doubt him until you think him unworthy of trust. A boy, in my opinion, should never be flogged. Punished, yes; but it ogged and lowered in his own eyes—never. If the mothers would constitute themselves the friends of their -sons they would aever regret it. A boy will do almost anything for his mother. Let her, then' keep the reins in her hands unceasingly. Train a boy to look up to himself, to 'keep aloof from vicious companions, and he will grow up almost as you wish. Let him run loose, from either carelessness or weakmindedness, and he will train himself in the way he should not go. AXERICAN Eeraemn.—Mr. Lowell, the greatest and -nest realist who evet- wrought in verse, showed us that Elizabeth was still Queen when he heard Yankee farmers talk; and without .asking that our novelists of the widely. scattered centres shall each seek to write in his local,fiialect, we are glad, as we say, of every tint any of -them gets from the parlance he hears; it is much better than the tint he will get from the parlancete reads. One need not invite slang into the company of its betters, though perhaps clang hes been dropping its s and be- cong language ever since the world began, and is cer., thinly sometimes delightful and forcible beyond the reach of the dictionary. We would not have anyone go about for new words; but if one of them came aptly not -to reject its help. For our noveEsts tortry to write Americanly, from any motive, would be a dismal error; but, being torn Americans, we would have them use -4' Americanisms" whenever these serve their turn; and /when their characters speak n-e should like to hear them speak true American, with all the varying Tennesseean, Philadelphian, Bostonian, and New York accents. If we bother ourselves to write what the critics imagine to be ." English." we shall be priggish and artificial, and still more so if we make cur Americans talk -"English." 'There is also this serious disadvantage about "English," -that if we wrote the best "English" in the world pro- bably the English themselves would not know it, or, if they did, certainly would Lot own it. It hate always been supposed by grammarians and purists that a language can be kept as they find it; but languages, while they live, are perpetually changing. God apparently meant them for the common people—whore Lincoln believed God liked because he had made so many of them—and the common people will use them freely as they use other gifts of God. On their lips our Continental English -will differ more and more from the insular English, and Tee believe that this is not deplorable Leet desirable.— W. They who forgive most shall be most forgiven. A kind word will always go further than a flat-iron. A powerful propellor on the screw-principle—Hunger. Something highly prized, yet always given away—A bride. No man can so injure us as we injure ourselves by living for ourselves. Only what we have wrought in our characters during life can we take away with us. Not .earthly suffering opens the way to heaven, but the manner in which it borne. No life can be utterly miserable that is brightened by laughter and love of one little child. The higher life begins for us when we renounce our own will to bow before a Divine law. More men are wanted everywhere with the far-reach- ing power to mind their own business. A woman has commenced to write a book, and her husband calls her Charity, because charity begins a tome. Starvation is about as good a cure for laziness as any- thing yet hit upon, and it has some sort of Scriptural sanction. We are always using the word "sympathy ;" but do we know what it means? It means "suffering with " nothing less. "Where's the bar ?" asked a dirty-looking stranger of the porter of an hotel.—" What kind of a bar?" asked the latter.—" Why, a drinking bar, of course; what else do you suppose I mean ?"—" Well," drawled the porter, "I 'didn't know but you might mean a bar of soap." Shoost !—Fair widow, examining some black dress material : "But does it fade ?" Mr. Silkenstein: " yes'm, to dell you der troot, it fades a leedle ; but it shoost goes off into a lofty violet after six monts or so— shoost lets you down mit your mourning easy and natural." The municipal authorities of a French town, having some time ago received complaints from peaceable in- habitants of the noise caused at a place of public enter- tainment by the shells supposed to be discharged into a mimic Plevna, issued the following ukase :—" For the future, Plevna must be bombarded at the point of the bayonet." There are few better evidences of mediocrity of character and incapacity for action than a readiness to consider every question from every point of view. Action demands above all things rapidity, decision. What is most wanted in the business of iife is the instinct of affairs, experience, observation, and knowledge of human character. To- morrow may never come to us; we do not live in to-morrqw—we cannot find it in any of our title-deeds. The man who owns whole squares of real estate and great ships on the sea does not own a single minute of to-morrow. To-morrow! It is a mysterious possibility not yet born; it lies under the seal of midnight, behind the veil of glittering constellations. TFfE Max WHO OVERWORSS.—Nature is as remorseless in dealing with men as with the beasts of the field. There is nothing kindly in her treatment. If any of her laws are violated the penalty falls upon the offender, often with tenfold force upon the heads of his children. The man who regards himself as a machine calculated to do a certain amount of work in the course of the year, with no more rest than is givn to a bit of mechanism, is sure to reap the fruits of his folly. It may come in great weariness of life which leads to suicide, or in an unim- paired strength, which is a bitter caricature of his for- mer feverish energy, or in the total collapse of the whole system—perhaps the most melancholy fate of all in this world. • -

Too BITTER A DOSE.—During the recent prevalence of the dengue in Dallas, a well-known Young physican was called in to see a young lady whom he had' long wor- shipped at a distance, but to whom he had never revealed his passion. Seeing that she had but a slight attack of the prevailing disease, and was in no special need ot medi- cine, he concluded to take advantage of the opportunity for making a point for himself. So he took her hand and said impressively—" Well, I should prescribe that you —that—you—get—married." "Oh, gracious !" said the alarmed and interested invalid. "I wonder who would marry me ?" "I would," snapped the doctor, with the voracity of an office-seeker. " You!" "Yes." "Well," and she sank back with an expression of disgust which none but dengue sufferers ever wore. "If that is the alternative, you can go away and let me die in peace." —Texas Tarantula,. .

CHARLES IX.—Charles was not really vile ; the tocsin of Saint Bartholomew rang hi death bell. The blood of his friends, the blood of thousands of innocents had been shed at his command. He tried to brave it out, to make a virtue of his crime. He said, "I did it ;" but no one believed him. "It was done at first without the knowledge of the king," writes Salviati in his cypher. "All that is done they impute to you alone and to Monseigneur d'Anjou," writes Du Ferrier, from Venice to Catherine. But it was Charles alone who repented. "The Queen looks twenty years younger, as if she had recovered from a dangerous illness, and issued out of a great danger," writes the envoy of Savoy. "The king is reduced to such leanness and feebleness he cannot stand, and seems but skin and bone," we read in the account of the trial of La Mole. Bad dreams disturbed by night, fear and remorse destroyed by day, the weak, unhappy lad, who, to save the mother •he feared, had shed such wealth of innocent blood. His songs, his love oflart, his passion for hunting, his placable Marie, could not console him now. In 1574 he died—a wreck in mind , and body, and the most execrated of European kings A. It is matter of re- joicing that the talk of society is not thus printed and perpetuated. Few men, if any, could pass creditably through such a severe test. It is said that Swift, at an evening party, on one occasion retired to a corner of the rOom and commenced noting down the talk of the com- pany. Being asked what he was doing, he produced the verbatim report of the conversation which had just taken place. Each speaker felt lamentably chagrined at the superficial and trifling character of his utterances. So, doubtless, would every right-minded man feel if some disciple of the phonographic school were always with us plying his pencil whenever we speak. But there is a recording angel by our side. Every word is written, though 'not by any visible agency: Our conversation exercises a power for good or evil on the mental and moral life of others, and no word as the vehicle of a thought can pause in its relative effect. —Rev. div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1886.
THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

COTTAGE GARDENING. A fine dry week has permitted all kinds of seeds to be sown in a satisfactory manner, and the slight shower or two that fell, instead of being an impediment (as is fre- quently the case while such operations are being pro- ceeded with), rendered, in many instances, valuable service, by moistening and softening the small lumps of soil that give so much trouble when seed covering has to be performed. The ground of the farm and garden never worked better than at the present time, and the labour of preparing seed beds will be far less irksome than it is in some seasons. The planting of Second Early Potatoes should be proceeded with, and speedily brought to a close. Late Potatoes are unsuitable for small gardens on account of the late period at which they are in the ground, which precludes the possibility of a second crop. A few may, however, be planted between the rows of Broccoli, and Borecole, or the Kales ; and if the rows of these are nearer than two feet, the Potatoes should be every alternate two rows, so that they may have from 2ft. 6ins. to 3ft to grow; for it must be observed that the tops of these, like all other Potatoes, extend a much greater distance in nearly all gardens than in fields, which may be attributed to richer soil, the shade from surrounding buildings, and the fruit trees. The ground between the crops named is usually very hard, and the planter must adopt a course to get in the sets quite dis- tinct from all other methods, and, after deciding the distance he is going to allow between the sets, he sh.-uld make a hole six inches deep to receive each set. After they are covered the work is completed till 'the green crops are off the ground and the Potatoes are making their appearance above the soil. Then the ground be- tween them must be well forked, and, if necessary, manure added. Those who have not got their own favourites might try Lapstone for culinary purposes; and for exhibition, International, Snowdrop, and Wood- stock—all Kidneys. The following will also prove a good selection from the host of round ones :—For culinary purposes, Fortyfold; and for exhibition, Reading Russet, Vicar of Laleham, and Bedfont Prolific. None of the above are late, and those intended for exhibition should be treated with fresh soil, such as road parings or chopped turf, round each set. Good late sorts to plant amongst Broccoli &c., will be found in Victoria, Dunbar Regent, and Reading Hero., THE FRONT GARDEN.—Annuals : Asters, Stocks, Zin- nias, Marigolds, Scabious, and a few others should have glass protection to start them, and a compost lighter and richer than the ordinary soil of the garden should be pro- vided for them. The interior of the frame should be filled so:as to bring the soil within two inches of the glass, so that the plants may not grow spindly through being so far from the glass. If the glass cover is kept close during the night and day the seed will quickly ger- minate, and when well above the soil air must be ad- mitted, and the quantity increased as the plants make progress. Before they are planted out the glass should be kept off for some days in order to inure them for colder quarters. Half-hardy and hardy Annuals may be sown out of doors where they are to flower. For a shilling many a garden may be made gay and cheerful by making a judicious selection of, these. True, many have a weedy appearance, which is aggravated by too thick sowing and not thinning sufficiently early, as well as not sowing them in the most suitable positions. All the Annuals like the full sun, but there are some that will succeed better than others when partially shaded. They are also, as a rule, more floriferous on poor soil than on rich, and as there are poor patches of soil in all mixed beds or borders, they should be marked out for gross growing Annuals. Virginian Stocks, red and white, may be sown to form a narrow band in front near the walk, or in round patches, and a little behind these Saponaria Calabrica; others must be arranged according to height. THE GREENHOUSE.—The greenhouse that is used to shelter the class of plants required for the front garden will be comnaratively empty after planting out takes Place, and the vacancy thus created may be filled by sowing the following Annuals :—Phlox Drummondi, Salpiglossis of Sorts, Prince's Feather, Silene Pendula, Saponari Calabrica, and Balsams. The latter are best sown two or three seeds in 2iin. pots, and when they are up pull out the weakest and leave one as near the centre of the pot as possible. This method of sowing does away with damaged roots when they have to be potted, but it necessitates as many pots being sown as the num- ber of plants required. The pots should be placed on a shelf as near the glass as possible as soon as the plants are above the soil.

div.head: PIT BROW WOMEN. TOWN'S MEETING AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: PIT BROW WOMEN. TOWN'S MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

An enthusiastic town's meeting to protest against the proposed abolition of female labour on pit brows was held in the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The gathering had been called by His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Mcßryde) in response to a requisition pre- sented to him, and the large assembly room was well filled by a respectable and thoroughly unanimous as - semblage. Nearly half of those present were well- I dressed women ot whom nearly 300 were employed on pit brows. The Mayor (Alderman Mcßryde) pre- sided, and was supported on the platform by the Rev Harry Mitchell, vicar of Pemberton, the Rev. Canon Carr, L.L.D., Rev. J. C. Pigott, vicar of St. Thomas's, Rev. A. A. Nunn (Parr), Rev. W. Flaherty, Rev. W. Edmondson (Church of England), Rev. W. C. Tayler (Baptist), Rev. R. J. Ward (Congregational), Rev. Father Dignam, Rev. Father Mordaunt, Councillors J. C. Gamble, J.P., A. Hanson, J. Forster, and F. J. Brown, Messrs. A. Sinclair, J.P., R. Bel- sher, W. Wogan, T. Glover (miners' agent), &O.

• The MAYOR first called upon Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk) to read a number of letters of apology. Mr. William Pilkington, J.P., wrote that he cordially sympathised with pit brow women, and thought it very unfair to try and in- ' terfere with their right to labour if they wished to do SO. Colonel Gamble, J.P., who signed the requisition calling the meeting and sympathised with its objects, expressed his regret that his absence in the south of England preven- ted his taking part in the meeting. Dr. McNicoll wrote regretting that he was not able to be present. He regarded the present employment of women at the pit bank as a fit and proper occupation for them, and the objection raised was purely of a sentimental character. It was well to have Acts of Parliament to protect small birds from cruel hands and to suppress cruelty to children—that was humane in the highest degree, but there was no need to deprive the pit women of their honest labours as they were well able to protect themselves. The exposure necessary to outdoor work had doubtless some risks, but taken as a whole the advantages greatly predominated. To deprive that class of bard working and honest women of their daily bread was a very serious matter and amounted in his opinion to an act of cruelty. Dr. Garton was very sorry he could not attend the meeting, but his sympathies were entirely with the movement. Dr. Jamison wrote sympathising with the object of the meeting, remarking that there was nothing in work on the pit brow worse for women than in many other occu- pations, and fie was quite sure from a lengthened observa- tion that pit brow workers enjoyed better health than almost any class of female workers in St. Helens. The Rev. H. S. Bolton, vicar of Ravenhead, also regretted his inability Ito attend.

I The MAYOR said he had convened the meeting in pursu- ance of a very numerously signed requisition for the pur- pose of considering the threatened interference by Act of Parliament with the employment of women on pit brows. The subject was one which had engaged the at- tention of people residing in the mining districts in which for a very long time past women have found employment on pit banks, and from what he could gather the unanimous Opinion seemed to be that the proposed prohibition would be unwarranted, and an unnecessary interference with women's right of earning a honest and honourable living. (Applause.) The Rev. H. MITCHELL, vicar of Pemberton, then ad- dressed the meeting at considerable length. He said it was a very wide question of the rights of women which had been raised over that pit brow controversy, which was only the first instalment of an attack upon all outdoor female labour. If Parliament ever passed a bill which would limit or destroy the right of women to that kind of work it would have passed a bill which would disgrace the nation. (Ap- plause.) He declared that 99 out of every 100 persons in Lancashire would find it difficult to believe that any sane man could ever propose such a bill. Outside the district in which pit brow girls worked they were an unknown class. The cry against them at present lived on ignorance, and they wanted to dispel that ignorance. (Applause.) He referred at some length to the action of the Miners' Union in reference to the question, and asked if men had any more right to interfere with the honest and respectable labour of women than women, on their part, had to interfere with similar labour on the part of the men? (Applause.) ' Councillor Join; FORSTER thought it would be an injus- tice to prevent women working on the it brows. He pro- posed "That the Mayor be requested to prepared and sign on behalf of this meeting a petition to Parliament against the passing of any measure for the prohibition of the em- ployment of women on coal pit brows, and to forward such petition to the member for this borough for presentation." (Applause.) He remarked they had it on the authority of doctors and some of the best citizens in St. Helens that the work was healthy, that the people who followed it and the women who worked on coal pit brows were as honest and respectable citizens as other people were. (Applause.) He objected to any measure of that description, because it was impossible to draw the line at pit brow girls, and if the present proposal was passed they would soon have another to put down female labour in glass works, and they then would have 500 women in St. Helens thrown on the streets to get their living as best they could. (Applause.) The Rev. A A. NuNte, in seconding the resolution, ex- pressed his cordial sympathy with pit brow girls, and said if working on pit brows was not fit for females it could with , very much more truth be said that working at the large I plates of glass in the glass works was not fit for females. Though the pit brow girls might have black faces and hands, he believed they had as clean and pure hearts as any women in the community. He trusted no British statesman or British legislature would ever interfere with the honest work of women on coal pit brows. (Applause.) Mr. Wm. Battershy, Mr. W. Wogan, and Mr. Thos. Glover supported the resolution, which was carried unanimously and enthusiastically. Votes of thanks to the Rev. H. A. Mitchell and the Mayor concluded the proceedings,

div.head: CATCHING A. SNAKE AND WHAT
div.p: CATCHING A. SNAKE AND WHAT

THE ORIGIN OF THE DOMESTIC FOWL. It is evident from the tone of Darwin's works that he was well aware of the somewhat slender evidence in support of the theory that the domestic fowls are all descended from one species, for he says in his "Varia- tions of Plants and Animals under Domestication" (page 251, vol. 1.),—" We have not such good evidence with fowls as with pigeons, of all the breeds being descended from a single primitive stock. In both cases the argu- ment of fertility must go for something; in both we have the improbability of man having suceeeded in ancient times in thoroughly domesticating several sup- posed species—most of these supposed species being extremely abnormal as compared with their natural allies,—all being now either unknown or extinct, though the parent form of no other domesticated bird has been lost." The remarkable variations in many species led the great naturalist to the belief that his opinion was the true one, and that all fowls °iv° their origin to the Gallus Bankiva. It has already been mentioned that poultry breeders, as such,—that is, those who did not pretend to be natu- ralists,—have held the opinion that all our races of fowls were not due to one species, at least, not to one of the species now extant. Mr. Lewis Wright puts this opinion into form in his "Book of Poultry," published in 1872. To this we shall refer again presently. Natu- ralists, however, have until lately accepted Darwin's theory, but in the Field newspaper of Sept. 26th, 1885, there appeared a letter from the pen of Mr. W. B.:Teget- meier, F.Z.S., the eminent naturalist, who was an asso- ciate of Darwin in many of his researches, which is an important acknowledgement that the generally accepted theory may after all be wrong. In this latter Mr. Teget- meier says : " The origin of all the different varieties or breeds of the domestic fowl is usually believed to be the common wild Indian mungle cock, the Gallus Ferruginous of modern naturalists, but known also as the Bankiva fowl (G. Bankiva in the older b-oks). This bird may be readily described as closely resembling a small black- breasted red game cock, with a tail carried more hori- zontally than usual. "It may be regarded as most presumptuous in me to dare to contest the conclusions arrived at by the honoured master Darwin, with whom and for whom it was for some years my privilege to work; but a careful and ex- tended consideration of the facts has led me to a differ- ent conclusion to that arrived at by him. That the domesticated fowl in India is derived from the firs species is evident from the fact that sportsmen occasion- ally confound the wild and the tame birds. This, taken into conjunction with the fact that hybreds with the other species bred in confinement have not been remark- ably fertile, has led probably to the conclusion which has been arrived at; but this want of fertility has been , due to the unnatural conditions under which the birds have been placed. Everyone at all conversant with poultry keeping knows that eggs laid by fowls in con- fined runs are mostly sterile, and it could hardly be ex- pected that cross-breeding with distinct species would, under these conditions, conduce to greater fertility. The hybreds between the different species of Gallus are in many cases perfectly, fertile. Some years since I saw at .Clumber numerous Game Bantams roosting in the trees that had for several generations been bred from a Son- nerat cock and domestic hens. "Last season, 1884, at the Zoological Gardens, numerous half-bred birds were reared from G. Stanleyi, and in former years many were bred from a single specimen of G. Furcatus. There is no doubt that the several wild Galli will inter-breed and produce fertile offspring as readily as do the corresponding and closely allied phea- sants, in which the three species—the Chinese, the Versi- colour, and the Colchican—have become so mixed that pure birds are rarer than mongrels. I have no doubt in rev own mind that the wild Galli have intermixed in not a few instances, and perhaps through not a few cen- turips, in producing our domestic breeds. "But it is with regard to the Eastern Asiatic type of fowl (absurdly known as Cochins and Brahmas) that my doubts as to the descent from the G. Ferrugineus are strongest. We have in the Cochin a fowl so different from the ordinary domestic birds that when first intro- duced the most ridiculous legends were current respect- ing it. Putting these on one side, we have a bird with many structural peculiarities that could hardly have been induced by domestication. Thus the long axis of the occipital foramen in the Cochin is perpendicular; in our old breeds horizontal, a difference that could never have been bred for, and which it is difficult to see could be co-relative with any other change. The same may be said respecting the deep sulcus or groove up the centre of the frontal bone. The extraordinary diminution in the size of the flight feathers and that of the pectoral muscles could hardly have been the result of human .selection and careful breeding, as the value of the birds as articles of food is considerably lessened by the absence. of flesh on the breast. Nor is the extreme abundance of fluffy, soft body feathers a character likely to be desi- derated in a fowl. The vastly increased size may have been a matter of selection, although, as the inhabitants of Shanghai feed their poultry but scantily, and, accord- ing to Mr. Fortune, mainly on paddy or unhusked rice, iit s not easy to see how the size of the breed was ob- tained if, as is generally surmised, it arose from the little jungle fowl. "Taking all these facts into consideration, lam induced to believe that the birds of the Cochin type did not descend from the same Species as our game fowl. It may be asked what bird I would suggest as the origin of these Eastern Asiatic breeds. In reply I would suggest the possibility, or even probability, of their being descended from some easily captured and readily domes- ticated short-winged species that may have entirely passed into a state of domestication, as has the camel and the horse. I can see no inherent impossibility in this suggestion, nor any fatal objection to the theory I have advanced." We have, therefore, got Just thus far, namely, that there is more than a doubt in the minds of naturalists, for Mr. Tegetmeier is not alone in his opinion as to the theory advanced by Darwin. The idea is that we must go farther back to find a common progenitor, one which was the parent of all the four species of Galli that have been named. It is very interesting to note that the first advancement of this view was not from a naturalist, but a poultry breeder. In the first edition of 'Wright's Book of Poultry we find the following "There are tendencies in some of our domestic breeds which certainly are not due to the Gallus Bankiva, and which, as they are found in the Gallus Furcatus, are pro- bably the result of natural rather than artificial develop- ment, a conclusion which is strengthened by the fact that another feature of Gallus Furcatus, not usually found in the domestic breed most resembling it, still ap- pears occasionally by reversion in that same breed. Hence, we are disposed to think that the original type can only be found still further back; that it diverged into various sub-types, including the four wild breeds still known, and developed through the Gallus Bankiva, into the Games, while other breeds were reached through collateral branches, now either extinct or possibly still further modified into the present other three known races. . . . It is possible enough that some wild species or variety of greater size than any now known may have either disappeared or become degraded." To sum up, therefore, it may be taken that with the domestic fowl, as with many other things in nature, we can go so far back but no farther. But the probability is that, as in the case of dogs, all the varieties of poultry do not owe their origin to any one species, at any rate of those now extant. In all yards where there are chickens, it is important at the present time of the year that they should have special attention. They must be regularly fed, be housed in a comfortable manner, and at the same time have plenty of fresh air. The weather is gradually getting warmer, and more fresh air is needed. Too much can- not be given in fine weather, so long as the birds are not exposed to draughts, and it is as dangerous for fowls to breath the same air over again as it is for human beings. If there are trees about, and the birds prefer roosting in them to being in their own houses, they may be allowed to do so, as it will make them all the hardier and stronger. They must be fed well, but at the same time it is necessary to take care that they do not obtain too much food—a prolific cause of disease and death.

CAME OF IT. There was consternation in the little village of B—, owing to the alarming fact of a real live snake having escaped from a wild beast show which had taken up its abode there for a short time. The proprietor, who was naturally in a fine state of excitement, had sent several of his men out in search of the missing reptile, but as yet their search had proved futile. The simple rustics were in grelt terror of the wandering snake, keeping as much as possible within the precincts of their homes for fear they should un- expectedly cross its path. Now in the village resided an old married couple known respectively as Jack and Sally Brown. They had an only daughter who, having long ago given up all hope of ever brightening the home of any of the village bachelors, spent her life in looking after the wel- fare of her aged parents. On the day on which our story opens, the spinster, Mary by name (but more generally termed " Melly ''), had been out on an errand in the villag, and, as a matter of course, came home fall of the news of the missing snake. "Oh, fayther!" exclaimed she to her parent, as he sat smoking his pipe by the fireside, " han yo' yeard abeaut a snake ut's getten away fro' th' wild beeust show ut's neaw performin' on tie' green ?" "Well, aw did yer summat abeant it when aw're at owd I Jim-o'-Jack's this mornin'," rejoined Mr. Brown, as he calmly smoked his pipe. "AW dunno' think, heawever, we neect t' pat eawrsels eawt o'th' road abeawt it; it'll noan come here theau may tak thi davy on that, Mally." e Aw shouldeo' bi t' sure fayther, if I were yo', becose aw yerd Dicky Hill say he seed summat like a snake creepin' past th' field ut th' back o' eawr heawse this mornin', but didno' like t' say owt abeawt it for fear o' free- tenin' ns." " Did he try to catch it, Melly, us thaw knows on?" was the rather ironical query of the old man, his eyes resting with a twinkle upon his daughter's countenance. " That he didno', fayther !" replied Melly. "He said he met ha' tried to kill it, but he hadno' time t' bother wil just then, but ud come agen later on when th' reptile had filled his stomick wi' mate and drink, an' then it wouldno' be as savage as it wur when he seed it." ' Oh, that's it, 13 it, Mally? Dick didno' seenm t' care mich heaw folks went on in th' meeuntime," said her father, as he re-charged his pipe. "Aw conno' blame Dick for lookin' afther his own sel', fayther," rather warmly responded Melly, who, rumour whispered, had a sneaking regard for the said Dick, and would have had no objections to transfer her chaste self and belongings to his protecting arms had he so wished it; but as yet Dick's eyes were not opened to the value of the prize which had been for so long in the matrimonial market. Tea brought the above discussion to a close, and no fur- ther reference was then made as to the snake and its whereabouts. It so happened that on the night in question Mally had determined to sit up an hour or so later in order to darn some stockings. Her parents had retired to rest, and so Melly had the kitchen so herself. By degrees her mind reverted to the escape of the snake from the menagerie, and though the was not generally of a timid nature, it must be confessed that she began to wish she had put off her stocking-mending till the morrow. She woe in the act of putting the finishing touches to the stockings when she suddenly heard a crash which appeared to proceed ' from the little scullery adjoining the kitchen. Full of terror Melly threw down the stockings, and, seizing the poker, stood prepared for she knew not what. "Oh, dear! oh my !" she groaned, "surely it conno' bi that theere snake getten in th' heause ! If it has, aw'st bi etten up afore mornin', an' when mi fayther and mother come deawn guts they'll find nowt o' me but ml clogs." i Rather to Mally's astonishment, no snake appeared, and as her fright began by degrees to abate, she determined to search the kitchen and scullery to make sure there was no ' further cause for alarm. Cautiously entering the scullery, i she looked around and found that the crash she had just heard had been caused by a couple of plates having fallen from one of the shelves. " Th' snake hasno' canoed that at any rate," was her com- ment, as she proceeded to collect the broken pieces from the floor. "But, t' mak sure, aw'll look under th' drawers, an' then aw'll go ml ways t' bed." Re-entering the kitchen, she stooped down, but no sooner did she cast the light of the candle underneath the drawers than she uttered a shriek of dismay. Rushing to the foot of the stairs, she yelled : " Fayther ! fayther! ger up, ger up! th' snake's hidden under th' drawers here-0 do bi sharp afore it bites ml to th' deeath !" .1 It was the work of a few minutes for old Jack to leave his bedroom, his wife, meanwhile sitting trembling by the bed- side in an agony of fear lest her husband and daughter I should be killed by the snake. Creeping cautiously down the stairs until he reached the last but two, Jack rather timidly asked: "Many, is th' snake wheere theme seed it fost ; theere yet ?" "Aye, fayther, it is; but aw'm sure aw seed it stur just neaw !" was his terrified daughter's reply. "Well, Melly, aw cudno' kill th' varmint misel, an' so thee step up sturs t' thi mother while aw run for th' keeper o'th' wild beeust show, an' then he'll happen catch it alive!" But Melly did not dare to stir from her present position, so much afraid was she of drawing the attention of the sup- posed snake in her direction. "Oh, fayther! fayther! (Immo' leeuve us here by eaur- sels wi' th' snake," screamed his daughter, reaching over to her father, thereby causing him to lose his balance, and to come with a loud thud upon the kitchen floor. With a yell of fear Jack sprang to his feet—his daughter at the same time running shriekingupstairs to her mother— and gaining the front door in far lees time than it takes me to record the fact, poor Jack, with his night-cap (which he had forgotten to remove on leaving his bedroom) still re- posing upon his head, was soon rushing, as fast as his legs would carry him to the place where the proprietor of the the menagerie lodged. A startling knock upon the door had the effect of bringing the inmates—amongst them being the owner of the wild beast show—forth into Jack's presence. " 0 ! mestur show-keeper !" gasped Jack, "do bi sharp an' come to eaur heanse, afore that snake o' yo'rs eyts us o up!" 'ls it in your house, my man?" asked the showman, gazing with astonishment at the nondescript appearance of Jack. "Aye, it is, mestur," was the reply. • In the course of a very short time the showman and a number of his men, together with a small crowd of curious villagers—for by this time the report that the snake had fonnd a temporary resting-place in Jack Brown's house had rapidly spread about—proceeded to the latter's place of abode. Many of them had hastily provided themselves with weapons of various kinds—pokers, frying-pans, brush- stalls, guns, and swords being amongst the number. Arriving at Jack's residence, the showmen stationed his men at different points of vantage in and about the house. As a true hero should, the owner of the supposed snake led the way to the kitchen, and, having procured a candle, looked under the dresser. As for Jack, he had managed to get upon the stairs' his idea being, no doubt, to valiantly defend the lives of his wife and daughter at any cost should the snake make any attempt to go upstairs. No sooner had the showman looked beneath the dresser than with a broad grin upon his countenance he brought forth—not the lost snake, but old Jack's walking-stick! Suddenly Jack remembered having thrown it there when he had come in from a visit to one of his friends during the day, and as the top part of it was in the shape of a snake's head, Mally's imagination had jumped to the conclusion that it was the snake which the showman had up to the pre- sent net been able to find. It was some time before Mrs. Brown and her daughter could be induced to venture downstairs, but at length it was accomplished, and you may be certain that both they and Jack were subjected to remarks of a very uncomplimentary nature for the trouble and annoyance they had caused. Jack was sometime before he heard the last of the affair. If any of his cronies wished to get him in fighting posture, they hadbuytetrto gently whisper to him, "Jack, haste catcht th' snake In conclusion, I may mention that the showman had the good fortune to recover his lost treasure, it having wandered miles ef kr oem., , It of the ee showmanconfines o fwaae plantationthen kful of n e ther tits reoutskirtscovery , o ft hthe villagers village. offewthme , il e were more so, and no regret was evinced when the menagerie there m ov villagee removed to whichsome wmoreitne scongenial s"catching"potsome —J. A gentleman writing from Chicago, on the questiOn of who is the largest beef dealer in the world, says that there is a man in Chicago whose cattle business the past

year amounted to 429,483 head. These he bought, brought to Chicago, and slaughtered in his own estab- lishment. This man was a few years ago a retail butcher. lie began slaughtering in 1878. He has buyers in Kansas and other Western States.

The total number of horses in Europe is estimated at about 30,000,000. On calculating the numerical relations subsisting between the equine and the human popula- tions of the different countries of Europe we find that for every 1,000 inhabitants there are :—ln Russia, 235 horses; in Denmark, 177; in Sweden 105 in Austro- Hungrav, 99; in Norway, 85; in Engl ' and, 83; in Ger- many, 8-1; in France, 79; and in Italy, 27. HORSES ON A JOURNEY,—" It is the pace that kills." A horse may trot and canter 60 miles in one day, or more, but he cannot ?.(3 on repeatinc, the distance at those Daces day after day. On the London stones it is found that 13 miles a day for five or six days is as much as the average omnibus horse can do and keep in condi- tion. The jog trot—the huntsman's pace—about five miles an hour, is that at which a horse can do the greatest distances for the greatest number of consecu- tive days, with the least fatigue and loss of condition. The rider may be relieved by the horse occasionally walking, but not at the horse's best walking pace. STCMBLING HORSES. Improper shoeing sometimes makes horses liable to stumble. If horses be'sound and can bond their knees this is not a natural habit.. But a _ _ _ _

horse that does frequently stumble should not only have his hoofs well pared under the front part and allowed to grow freely behind, but he should have (at least till his fore feet have grown to a suitable form) his shoes made twice as thick behind as they are in front. You will readily see how such a method of shoeing would act, by the horse being less liable to strike his "toe," as the front of the foot is termed, on the surface of the road.— , V. A. L.

DEPRESSION.—The Prussian Govern- ment has just determined to institute an official inquiry into the alleged grievances of the agricultural and landed interest, in order more especially to ascertain what foundation there may be or the complaint that the land is unduly burdened with taxation. If the re- sult of the investigation should be to show that the complaints are well founded, and that the landed in- terest is really o7ertaxed, the Government will proceed to redress the grievance by reducing the burdens im- posed on land, and making up for any loss thus arising; to the revenue by levying additional duties on commo- dities. A DAIRY SCHOLARSITIP.—A sum of £2O is offered by the British Dairy Farmers' Association to provide a scholarshb to be competed for by dairy farmers or per- sons intending to start upon the business of dairy farm- ing or dairying. Candidates must be not less than 18 years of age. They will be subjected to a written and a viva voce examination in butter-making at the society's rooms, 191, Fleet-street, London, on Thursday, May 13th, and a practical examination at Mr. Tisdall's dairy, Ken- sington. The successful candidate will be required to devote at least two months to the acquisition of know- ledge of butter-making in Normandy, and to keep a journal of his experience during the whole period of his scholarship, sending a copy of it weekly to the British Dairy Farmers' Association.

div.head: FOOD FOR FATTENING.
div.p: FOOD FOR FATTENING.

Mr. Jos. Long, -writing to the Manchester Guardian. says :—" I have received a letter, signed Lancashire,' asking for particulars of the actual quantities of the best and most economical foods for cows and for fattening bullocks. The writer says he is ignorant of chemistry, and cannot take advantage of my remarks under this head, and especially those contained in this column last week, in which I stated that a cow weighing 1,000113. is believed to require 211 b. of dried food, which should con- tain 211 b. of digestible nitrogen and 1211 b. of digestible carbon. Knowing that the majority of people do not understand these terms, I took the precaution to explain that nitrogen was the constituent of food which forms the flesh or lean of the beast and the casein of milk—the casein being the substance of which cheese is composed when deprived of the fat. I also said that the carbona- ceous foods were the fats, starches, and sugars, which almost all cattle foods contain and which are respon- sible for the combustion and the provision of the fat and sugar in milk and the fat in the beast. I have frequently stated that if a person intends to feed to the best advan- tage he should thoroughly understand this point, and, doing so, he should take care to use such foods as, pro- perly mixed, would provide for the actual requirements of his beast. For example, he is told that a cow of I,ooolb. required 241 b. of dry food, containing alb. of nitrogen and 12lb. of carbon. A cow of 7501 b. would therefore require exactly three-parts of these totals. How, then, are they to be provided? A reference to a standard work upon feeding cattle will show the compo- sition of almost every known cattle food. Therefore it is within the power of the feeder to select the foods he prefers and to mix them in the proper proportions, giv- ing such a total weight as will provide the dry consti- tuents he desires. When I say dry' constituents, it should be understood that water forms a very large pro- portion of all foods. For instance, the swede turnip con- tains 891 percent., leaving 14 per cent. of dry matter or food; wheat bran contains 13 per cent. of water, the potato contains 75 per cent., maize contains 144 per cent., meadow grass something like 80 per cent., hay 16i per cent., and green clover 78 per cent. There are cer- tain foods h are called carbonaceous food, because the principal feeding constituent is carbon, the nitrogen being small in proportion. Among these are— Proportion

.. Nitrogen. of carbon. Peas Ryegrass Oat straw 1 Potatoes Turnips Wheat . Barley Oats Maize 1 Wheat bran 1 The figures quoted are not exact, as if the correct ones were given decimals would be required, which would possibly complicate matters in the present instance, as I am writing for such readers as 'Lancashire,' who evi- dently wants the case put as simply as possible. Among the nitrogenous foods may be mentioned : Nitrogen. Carbon. Peas ' 1 _ f

Cotton cake (decorticated) Linseed cake 1 Rape cake Malt dust 1 Grains 1 Bean meal 1 Almost every known cattle food contains more carbon than nitrogen, the latter being always a small ingredient. Now, in order to show how a scientific ration based upon the above suggestions is made up, I will quote one which I arranged a short time ago. It is as follows :- 561bs. of silage, at 10s. per ton, cost 281bs. of straw, at 355. per ton, cost 11b. of malt dust, at 100 s. per ton, cost id. 21bs. of cotton cake, at 140 s. per ton, cost lld. ---- 31bs. of Indian meal, at 1255. per ton, cost l4d. This ration consists of 901bs. of food, containing nearly 20 per cent. of dry matter, the cost being llid. a day. The analysis would be about as follows : _

Carbo- ' Albumin oi ds. Fat, hydrates. Silage Straw Malt dust Cotton cake Maize meal Totals -76 The malt dust acts both as a food and as a condiment, and is used accordingly. The straw is introduced in a large quantity because it is cheap and helps to reduce the cost. The same may b 3 said of the silage, and if the whole were cooked or steamed the bulk might be di- minished without suffering in loss. I do not wish to further complicate these data, but it should be under- stood that there is a large proportion of the dry consti- tuents of food which is wasted because it is not digested. Cooking enables much of this fibrous matter to be di- gested and utilised, -.nd in this way straw might be much more generally given in rations than it is. There are so few foods that contain the actual proportions of nitrogen and carbon that it is invariably necessary to mix, and this mixing necessitates a knowledge of the constituents of each food in order to prevent a loss. If it were other- wise, feeders might use two or three foods which were wholly carbonaceous or the reverse. Again, much de- pends upon the condition of the beast and the purpose to which it is put. The fattening beast requires a larger proportion of fat and of carbo-hydrates, starches, sugars, &c., and these should be increased week by week until the maximum is reached. A cow which is not giving milk, and is simply being kept in store condition, re- quires less carbon, and of course less nitrogen. On the other hand, a cow giving an abundance of milk should have an extra quantity of nitrogen given her in order to provide for the extra amount of casein which that milk requires, otherwise it must be poor. In a butter dairy an extra amount of fat should be given or the butter per- centage will fall off. In answer to a turther question, I have often spoken highly of the Danish separator, which I have frequently worked with the best possible advan- tage with a pony. A steam-engine of one-horse power is amply sufficient to work it. I speak of the small size machine skimming up to thirty gallons of milk per hour It would pay well for twelve large or fifteen ordinary cows."

DEATH OF LORD REDESDALE.—The Earl of Redesdale died on Sunday at his residence, Vernon House, Park-place, St James's-street, London. Immediately on the earl's decease a telegram communicating the sad intelligence was, despatched to her Majesty, at Windsor. Lord Redesdale, who attained his 80th year last September, had been chair- man of committees and Deputy Speaker of the House of Lords since 1851. He succeeded to the title as Baron Redesdale in 1830, and was created Earl of Redesdale in 1877. His lordship was never married, and the title be- comes extinct.

FOREIGN NEWS. THE GREEK QUESTION.—CRITICAL SITUATION. PARIS, SATURDA.T.—The following telegram from Athens of to-day's date has been received here:—" M. Delyannis Yesterday had a long interview with Count de Mouy, in Which he protested energetically against the language at- tributed to him in replying to a recent deputation of citizens, as also against the interpretation placed upon his circular to the prefects. The Greek Premier declared that 'lino case bad be mentioned any undertaking on the part of Prance towards Greece and till less any mediation of France in the Greek question. M. Delyannis described these "Ports as having been propagated by his political adver- saries or the enemies of Greece, and declared that he had ITtllaested the Greek representatives abroad to contradict them. Re confirmed the resolution already expressed by the Government to disarm very shortly, and added that as soon With° difficulties just now standing in the way were re- 'toyed he would dismiss the reservists to their homes at the rate of two classes at time, measures beina taken to %Void any disorder arising in consequence." The following thi text of the brief reply which M. Delyannis made to thO Count de Mouv on the 26th ult., and which he corn- Inunicated to the representatives of the Powers some hours be. fore the presentation of the ultimatum ::—" I hasten to Inform you that the Royal Government has decided to adhere to the counsels of the Government of the French Republic." A"ThNs, MONDAY.—Tha situation is becoming compli- cated and critical. The Government does not appear to be willing to make any further concessions, since it considers it impossible to complv with the demand of the Powers to fix a term for disarmament, such a demand constituting, irk, its opinion, an interference in the internal affairs of Greece. VIENNA, MONDAY.—According to a despatch from Canes, the French Consul at that place has given an official con- tradiction to the report that the French Government had Promised any extension of territory to Greece in the event Of disarmament. The Consul added that Count de Mouy Was making strong efforts in Athens to induce Greece to Irlake the Powers a promise of immediate disarmament. Arrtstes, TUESDA.Y.—LISt night it was pesitively asser- ted that the representatives of the Powers would embark on mud the allied fleet early this morning. The tension on all sides was great, and it was therefore with peculiar relief this morning that an authoritative announcement to the effect that the foreign Ministers were not after all to leave Athens was received. So far as can be learned definitely, the Ministers will not leave for some days to come, if at all, „freah instructions having been received from the respective r owers ordering their representatives to remain at Athens Pending the receipt of further instructions. This change, of front, it is stated, is due to a desire on the part of some of the Powers to avoid pushing matters to extremities with Greece. It is believed here now that the Powers will be content with the guarantee of France that Greece shall disarm according to the promise already made, and that the Powers will refrain from specifying any period in which it is to be completed. It is believed that ftother communications are passing be' tweet' the Powers to ensure a peaceful solution of the Greek difficulty. In the meintime the renresentatives of the Powers have been instructed to rennin at Athens, pending further collective action. The Powers are understood to be • willing to take into consideration the susceptibilities of the Oreeks, and to make allowAnc.4 for the difficult position in which the Greek Government finds itself; but no arrange- ment can be satisfactory which does not provide sufficient guarantees for speedy lisarmament earl demobilisation. VMS, WEDNESDAY.—A. Collective Note, signed by the representatives of England, Germany, Austria, a.nd Italy, drawn tip on the initiatiee of England, is to be pre. Sorted to-day or to-morrow to the Greek Government. The Note, while reco,emieiree the friendly intervention of France, requires the Greek Government to give more precise asmr- wnces in regard to disarmament. Should this not be Promptly acceded to, the sienatory Powers will withdraw - their representatives from Athens. ATHENS, TRIIRSDAT.—a ministerial journal states this Morning that so long as the pressure of the ultimatum re- Mains the Greek Government will not disband a single 301dier.

ANOTHER ULTIMATUM. ATHENS, THURSDAY EVENING.—In the Collective Note delivered to-day to the Greek GOVOTTIMent the represents- tivee of the five Powers acknowledge the receipt of M. nelyannis's reply of April fa and take note of his pacific assurances, but their instructions direct them to state that the Hellenic Government must, during the day, give more definite and clearer assurances. The answer of M. Delyan- Ills has just been delivered, and is regarded by the Legs- tione as not satisfa&ory. The foreign Ministers will conse- luently leave to-morroer morning. The troops forming the Athens garrison are being sum- teoned to their barracks, and it is rumoured they will go to the front to-morrow. Several deputies, whoeare also offizers in the army, have re,oeived orders to leave. A despatch from the General commanding the Greek army on the frontier has been published, which reports the concentration of Turkish troops. Orders have been sent to him to move up his force and likewise effect a con- centration. A Turkish despatch vessel has arrived in the Piraras. The etoitetneat then is vest.

ENGLAND AND EGYPT. CAIRO, SII/gDAY.--Nlakhtar Pasha yesterday declared that as the Turtish scheme had been rejected the British Govern- ment ought to suggest a counter propr)sal. Sir H. D. Wolff replied that the rejection was sufficient. Great satis- faction is felt everywhere at Lord Roseherv's remark that tke population of Egypt does not itant Turkish rule direct or indirect. Muktitar Pasha sends private despatches to the Porte stating that it is evident the British intend to have their own way, and that therefore further parleying is useless. ENGLAND, GERMANY, AND THE PACIFIC. BERLIN, MONDAY.—A line of demarcation defining the British and German spheres of action in the Western Pacific was agreed upon on the 6th ult. between Sir E. Malet, British Ambassador, and Count Herbert von Bismarck, Under-Secretary of State. Colonies which already possess fully established Governments with Legislatures do not come within the scope of the deciaratien. THE AUSTRALIANS AND GERMANY'S COLONISING

SCHEME. BERLIN, SUNDAY —The semi-official IVOth German Gazette to-day publishes a letter from Sydney', stating that the German squadron under Rear-Admiral Knorr, while in the waters of New South Wales, was the object of frequent marks of attention on the part of the Government and the municipal autholities. These courtesies, adds the writer, have been doubly appreciated in view of the aitation lately carried on by the leading newspapers of Queens- land against Germany's colonial aspirations in the c'outh Seas.

GERMANY AND THE VATICAN. BERLIN, SATURDAY.—The Minister of Public Worship has officially informed the President of the Lower House of the Prussian Diet that the Government in a Note to the Vati- can, dated April 23,d, expressed its willingness to proceed to a further revision of the Church Laws, and on April 25th, to its great satisfaction, it received a reply from Car- dinttl Jacobini which ran as follows:—;" In order to give the Prussian 'Government a new and special proof of his confidence and conciliatory disposition, the Holy Father has empowered the undersigned Cardinal Secretary to infotm the said Government that it is his intention that the notifi- cation of appointments to the now vacant cures shall begin from the present time, and shall take place without delay. When your Excellency makes this communication to your Government you will not fail to lay stress on its special value, particularly in relation to its establishment of final religioas peace." Cardinal Jacobini's note was addressed to Dr. von Schloezer, the Prussian Minister to the Vatican, who forwarded it to Berlin without delay. THE LABOUR QUESTION IN AMERICA. NEW YORK, SATURDAY —The working-men's movement in favour of the eight hours' working day was inaugurated to-day in various places. Some of the employers acceded to the demand and others refused, whereupon their men struck work. Tee movement is most extended at Chicago, where thousands of men, including many of the bands em- ployed in the railway freight yards, went out on strike and paraded the streets in immense numbers. One party carried a red flag. There was, however, no disturb- ance. NEW YORK, MONDAY.—Further strikes for shorter hours and batter pay have occurred at various places to-day, and at Chicago the movement bas become more extended, seven thensand sausage makers employed in the stockyards having struck. Strikes are also reported among the working-men of Boston to the number of 4,000 ; and at Pittsburgh among the stonemasons and carpenters, the number of men who have joined the movement in this case being 1,800. The railways are able to carry on only a limited traffic owing to strikes among the freight handlers; and the Wabash Company have asked for Federal protection. In some cases the strikers have tried to force the workmen to quit the lumber districts and to remain idle. One great iron factory has been Clasen in consequence of the move- ment, while in some places the employers have acceded to the demands of the men. LABOUR RIOTS.—SEVEN MEN SHOT. NEW YORK, TUKSDAY.—It is officially announced that the strike on the Missouri Pacific Railway bas ended, the Knights of Labour having yielded to the company. CHICAGO, MONDAY. The men who have struck work here for the eight-hours system became very violent to-day, and attacked the M'Cortnick Reaper Factory. The police defended the place, and in the fighting which ensued five strikers and fonr policemen were shot, two of the former fatally. One policeman was captured and beaten by the mob, and an attempt was made to hang him. The man, how- ever, was ultimately rescued. The situation is threatening. At Milwaukee the strikers have visited the workshops and forced many of the men to stop work. CHICAGO, TUESDAY.—A battalion of militia is ordered to be ready to proceed to Milwaukee. Yesterday's disorders were due mainly to foreign Socialists. MORE RIOTING.-50 PERSONS SHOT. CHICAGO, WEDNESDAY.—A desperate encounter occurred here last night between tte police and the Socialists. The latter, to the number of 15,000, were holding a meetieg, when the police appeared on the scene and ordered them to disperse. The Socialists, however, refused, and in the con- flict which ensued several dysamite bombe were thrown. ISeveral policemen were killed and many wounded. Nearly 50 rioters were shot, several fatally. The Inspector of Police says that when the principal speaker was ordered to desist he shouted "To arms," where- upon several bombs were thrown from behind the waggon on which he was standing. The losses sustained by the police from bombs and revolver fire comprise three men killed outright and 37 wounded, four mortally. Of the Socialists one was killed and one is in a dying state; 25 others are also known to have been wounded, besides those who were taken away. CONCENTRATION OF ARABS AT DONGOLA. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—The Khedive ha ta received a tele- gram from Korosko stating that the Mandi's lieutenant at Berber is ordering all men arriving from Khartoum to march as rapidly as possible to Dongola. He himself will start for the latter place with the last batch. It is believed that a large rebel force is assembling at Don- gels.

div.head: SERIOUS PRISON REVOLT.
div.p: SERIOUS PRISON REVOLT.

PARIS, THURSDAY. A mutiny broke out yesterday in the prison of Grand Royalette. The gaolers were attacked and three of them injured. The governor also was woun- ded. Troops were sent for, and on their arrival quelled the mutiny and placed the ringleaders in solitary confine• merit.

VESTRY MD,TING AT LATCHFORD. A POLITICAL BELL-RINGER. The annual vestry meeting of Christ Church, i Latchford, was held n the schoolroom, on Monday evening. The vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott. presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. M. Prescott, Captain Reynolds. and Messrs. J. White, H. Woods, J. Lee, W. Pierpoiut, R. Gorton. W. Wallace, J. Lowe, T. Lloyd, and T. Norman. Mr. Gorton, one of the retiring wardens, read the churchwardens' statement of accounts, which showed that the total receipts amounted to £l9O 75 31-1, and that after meeting the expenditure there was a balance due to the wardens of £l6 13s S. The balance due to the wardens the previous year was £2l 6s Gd, so that it had. been slightly reduced.—Mr. W. Pierpoint, referring to an item in the accounts for bell-ringing, said his main purpose for coming there that night was to men- tion the fact .that when his party were beaten at last general election one of the sounds that saluted his ears after the declaration of the poll was the ringing of the church bell. He did not know that it mattered very much, but lie must say that it came in very bad taste. He was a Liberal member of the congregation ; he held land in the parish, and he paid tithes to the rector of Grappenhall, and he did hope that the bell was not rung with the cog- nisance of the vicar and churchwardens, or any of the offi- cials of the church. He did not think he was an enemy of the Church of England in any respect, and he did not want the Church of England to treat him as an alien. He felt sorry that the bell was rung, because there were other Liberals who lived in Latchford, although they happened not to oe in a inajority as their friend Captain Reynolds knew, hut who would be as much hurt as be was by hearing the bell.—The Chairman, in reply to Mr. Pierpoint, said that the churchwardens had no power over the hell, there- fore it was not rung by their orders. He might also say that the bell was not rang with his wish or his consent. When the sounds of the bell first greeted his ear, he hap- pened to be in the vicarage engaged in family prayer, and as soon as the prayers were over he:rushed out to the belfry and found that it was the bellringer who was ringing the bell. He told him to stop at once and that it was very much against his (the chairman's) wish that he had gone up into the belfry to ring. If Mr. Pierpoint had kindly in- quired of him why the bell was rung, he (the chairman) would have been much better pleased • than by having it , brought forward at a vestry meeting although, no doubt, that Wa9 the opportußitv. If that had been done he would no doubt have been able to smooth all difficulties by explain- ing the matter satisfactorily as be had done to one gentle- man of the parish who, with Mr. Pierpoint, wee very mucn annoyed when he heard the bell ringing on the night in question.—Mr. Pierpoint said he was much obliged to the chairman for his explanation, which was entirely satisfac- tory to him,—Captein Reynolds said he felt glad the chair- man had speken as he had done. He (Captain Reynolds) did not know the bell had been run, but be hoped the same spirit that Mr. Pierpoint spoke for that night would be mani- fested by his party in the feture; certainly it had not been in times past. —The matter then dropped, and the accounts were pieeed.—The Chairman then stated that he had not been able to prevail on Mr. John White to allow himself to be nominated vicar's warden again, and therefore he would nominate Mr. Herbert Wood. The Chairman also spoke in high terms of Mr. White's services to the church.—Mr. Gorton also expressed his intention of withdrewing from the office of churchwarden, and on the ruotion of Mr. W. Pier- point, seconded by Captain Reynolds, Mr. Lee was elected ' to the office.—Captain Reynolds then moved a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Gorton for his services as churchwarden during the seven years he had held the office, and this pro- posal was seconded by Mr. Lee, and carried unanimous.On the motion of Mr. H. Wood, seconded by Mr. Gorton, a similar compliment was paid to Mr. White, who, in reply- ing, referred to the improvements that had been made in con- nection with the church, and to the increase in the number of the coneregation.—Mr. John White and Mr. Lowe were next appointed lay delfe.,ates ; the organist's salary wtl9 fiz,.cle.at 00, with a gratuity of £10: and a vote of thanks was passed to the choir for their services. Votes of thanks were also passed to the Rev. J. M. Prescott and the chair- man.—This VMS all the business.
