div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 8, 1886.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT-

short time, and should the answer of the Greek Govern- ment not be sufficient, steps would at once be taken of a nature which would, in the judgmeut of the Powers, tend to secure the great object which they all had in view. . THE EGYPTIAN ARMY..ReplYing to a qtiesiion as to the mission of Muklitar Pasha and Sir H. Wolff, the PRIME MINISTER stated that after a very careful examination of the plans of Mukhtar Pasha for the reorganisation of the Egyptian army the Government had come to the conclusion , that they could not prop, rly agree with them, and in con- sequence Sir H. Wolff had beeie asked to inquire of Mukhtar Pasha whether he could so modify them as to meet the ob- jections which the Government had taken.—Mr. H. GLAD- STONE informed Mr. Labouchere that there were at present 14,000 British troops in Egypt. and that orders bad been issued to reduce the nueiber to 9,000. RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC.-011 the motion for the second readiug of the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill, Mr. J. C. BOLTON moved as an amendment—" That while this House desires legislation with the object of securing uni- formity of classification for merchandise conveyed by rail- way, the consolidation of the toil powers of railway com- panies, and such other modifications of the existing law as experience has shown to be useful and necessary, including the establishment of a strong and per- manent court with special powers over railways and canals, it is not prepared to sanction any compulsory interference with or diminution of those powers of earning revenues granted by Parliament to railway companies. upon the faith of which eight hundred millions of capital have been expended, and upon which the security of that capital depends."—Mr. E. STANHOPE suggested that it would be wise not to take a divieion on the amendment, as by doing so the object of the railway companies would probably be defeated. Speakirg as a railway share- holder, he thought shareholders and traders alike had reason to complain of the present rate of things.— Sir Iticitann CROSS believed that in this matter the interests of the railway companies and of the traders ought to be identical, and he was desirous to see their differences settled. So strongly did he object to the clause in the bill empowering the Beard of Trade to revise the maximum rates that he would rather lose the bill than have it with that clause.—Mr. J. E. FER- GUSON called attention to the difficulty of obtaining through rates from the railway companies, and made other criticisms on the bill.—Mr. I). Plunkett having spoken in favour of the amendment, the ATTorterE,at GENERAL answered the ob- jections urged against the bill, and defended the action of Mr. Mundella in regard to the memoranda left by Mr. Stanhope at the Board of Trade, contending that Mr. Stan- ' hope hod himself destroyed the private character of the document.—Sir It. WEBSTER expressed a general approval of the bill.—Sir J. Pease, Sir B. Samuelson, Mr. Forwood, Professor Rogers, Mr. Lionel Cohen, and Mr. Mundella con- tinued the debate.—The amendment was withdrawn, and the bill was read a second time.—The Crofters Bill passed through Committee, and was ordered to be read a third time on Monday.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moernev. The House of Commons reassembled at 4-0, after the Easter recess. The attendance was small. Mr. Palgrave occupied the place of Sir Thomas Erskine May as Clerk to the House. NEW MEMBERS —Mr. Shaw Lefevre took the oath and his seat for Central Bradford. The right hon. gentleman was received with Ministerial cheers. bir U. eiay-Shuttie- worth, who was introduced by Mr. A. Morley and Mr. C. Flower, took the oath and his seat for the Cutheree Divh of Lancashire on his re-election after appointment as Chan- cellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. Lord Eleho, who was introduced by Mr. S. Herbert and Mr. R. Yorke, took the oath and his scat for Ipswich amid Opposition cLeers. Stwele—Clvte SERVICE ESTIMATES.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the remaining votes in classes 1 and 3 of the Civil Service Estimates.--On the vote of £BOO for Dover Harbour, Mr. RYLA.NDS protattA against this vote, which in principal involved an enormous sum of money, being brought forward now unexpectedly in a thin House.—Sir R. PEEL referred to the fact that when in March this vote was postponed, the Chancellor of the Exchequer promised a full explanation should he given of the pl in.—The CHANCELLOR Of the EXCHEQUER stated that the present vote was solely for the preliminary experiments and examinations.— Mr. BRADLAUGIS suggested that the description of the vote should he amended so as to read "expenses of the preliminary survey for the site of a pro- jected harbour."—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER agreed to withdraw the vote, and bring it forwaid in an amended form.--The followidg votes were agreed ti : £25,120 for a new harbour of refuge at Peterhead; £141,435 contribution in lieu of rates on Government buildings ; f £7,500 in aid of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade; £232,000 in aid of disturnpiked roads in England and Wales, and £30,000 in aid of disturnpilied roads in Scotland; £182,355 for pub- lic buildings in Ireland; £12.203 for the maintenance of lighthouses abroad ; £35,677 for diplomatic and consular buildings; £70,974 for law charges, and £179,200 for criminal prosecutions.--On the vote of £352210 for the expenses of the Supreme Court of Judicature, Mr. RYLA.NDS called attention to the large expenditure incurred in the central office owing to the redundancy of officials.—Mr. Foween said that the number of redundant cleiles was being reduced as the vac incies occurred--Several other votes were agreed to, and progress was reported. THE INCOME TAX.—On the motion for the second read- ing of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, Mr. BARTLEY complained that the income tax was in nianv cases levied I upon amounts in excess oC income.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER agreed that the burden of the income tax was heavily felt, but the tax was now permanent, and the only thing the Government could do was to take care that the tax sheuld not be levied in such a manner as to leave those who paid it under a sense of injustice.—The bill Was ! read a second time. The National Debt Bill was read a second time. THE MEDICAL PROFESSION.—Sir L. PLAYFAIR moved the second reading of the Medical Acts Amendment Bill. The bill provided that the Universities might continue to give the qualifications they now give, but that the corpora- tions must combine, so that the College of Surgeons should unite with the College of Physicians, or with some other body. The second part of the bill provided also for the registration of qualified colonial medical men practising in this country.—Sir H. HOLLAND, whilst supporting the bill, i regretted that it had not been made a consolidation bill.— ' Dr. FOSTER, on behalf of twelve thousand medical men, supported the second reading.—Dr. FARQUHARSON hoped I the bill would become law during the present session. I After some discussion the bill was then read a second time, ' the Committee being fixed for next Monday week. The Ulster Canal and Tyrone Navigation Bill was read a second time. THE BURIALS BILL.—Mr. 0. MORGAN moved the second reading of the Burial Grounds Bill, which proposed to abolish in cemeteries the present distinction between con- secrated and unconsecrated ground. It would permit the Iconsecration of any portion of a cemetery as a religious rite provided that the ceremony involved no disability.— Sir R. CROSS thought the provisions of the bill were incon- sistent, and some of them were unnecessary.—The second reading was agreed to. The Returning Officere Charges (Scotland) Bill was read a sec6nd time. The House adjourned at 12-45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TrEsnet. The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. THE IRISH LAND PURCHASE ACT.—In answer to Sir G. j Campbell, Mr. J. MORLEY said the total rental, the purchase of which has been sanctioned under the Land Putchase (Ireland) Act of 1885, is £25,714 14s 9,1 a year, and the amount sanctioned for the purchase is £617,833. To ANTI-VACCINATORS.—In reply to Mr. Robinson, Mr. , CHILDERS said as to remitting the penalties inflicted in cases I of non-vaccination he saw no reason for advising the indul- gence of the Crown towards persons who persisted in refus- ing to comply with the law. THE PEACE PRESERVATI*N (IRELAND) ACT.—In answer , to Mr. C. E. Lewis, Mr. MORLEY said he had on the paper for that night a notice of motion to introduce a bill to renew the Peace Preservation (Ireland) Act of 1881 for a , limited period should leave be given. He proposed to put down the second reading for Thursday, and as the hill con- sisted of two clauses only, he saw no reason why it should not become law before June Ist. Further particulars ho would state on introducing the bill. THE GREEK QUESTION.—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH: I gave notice yesterday that I would ask to-day whether the Go- vernment could make any statement to the House as to the relations existing between the Great Powers and Greece, and also when pipers were likely to be presented. I beg now to ask this question.—Mr; GLADSTONE: In answer to the question of the right hon. baronet I have to say, as the right hon. gentleman and the House is well aware, a Col- lective Note on the part of the Powers was addressed to Greece, and a time was fixed within which an answer would be received or other consequences would follow. That time expired at five o'clock yesterday afternoon, and since then we had received no definite news whatever. Under the cir- cumstances the House will see that it is obvious the time has not arrived for me to make any further reply, though probably I may be able to do so before Any length of time , has elapsed. THE ADULTERATION OF TOBACCO.— Mr. MACFARLANE drew attention to the adulteration of tobacco, and moved for , the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire into the effect and working of the present system of levying duty upon tobacco. From an analysis he had had made of various specimens of tobacco, it appeared that the proportion of water varied from 14 to 53 per cent. The ordinary tobacco consumed by the working classes was sold across the coun- ter at 3d an ounce, but the workingman got only 50 per cent of tobacco in his purchase, and therefore paid at the rate of Sc a pound, while the richer classes (who paid Sc a pound) got 92 per cent of pure tobacco.—Mr. RYLANDS seconned the motion, on the ground that the hon. member for Argyllshire had made out a very good case for inquiry.— Mr. H. FOWLER thought it very undesirable to disturb, even by inquiry, fiscal arrangements which were working without friction, were producing no revenue, and were inflicting in- jury upon DO class of the community. He was informed that there was no article of consumption in the country at the present time more free from adulteration than tobacco. —The motion was negatived without a division. INDIA'S OPIUM TRADE.—Sir Jos. PEASE called attention to the cultivation of the poppy in India and the manufac- ture and trade in opium by the Government of India and moved that in the opinion of the House, it was expedient that the Indian Government should take measures to ter- minate gradually its direct connection with the cultivatioa of the poppy and the manufacture of and trade in opium, and that it should use the powers that it possessed to pro- hibit in British India the cultivation of the poppy except to supply the legitimate demand of opium for. medical pnr- poses.--Sir J. SWINDURNE seconded the resolution, observing that the only parallel to the opium traffic wee the Slave trade in the West Indies.—Sir R. TEMPLE said it was a gratuitous assumption to say that the people of China were poisoned by opium. He advocated the retention of the tax on moral grounds.—Mr. MACITER, having resided for some years in Burmab, spoke of the terr ble effect of the con- sumption of opium upon the Burmese. He was, however, unable to support the resolution as India was not in a posi- tion to sacrifice seven millions of revenue.—Sir R FoWLER supported the resolution.—Mr. H. S. HOWARD said the pro- hibition of the cultivation of the poppy would be impossible, or worse than useless, for if it were stopped in one place it would be carried on in another.—Sir G. Ceettmeet was speaking in opposition to the resolution when attention was called to the fact that there were not 40 members present, and the House was counted out at 8-0. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 25 minutes to 1 O'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Irish Municipal Franchise Rill was read a second time, with the approval of Mr. J. Morley on the part of the Government.—Mr. Howard Vincent moved the second reading of the bill, the object or which is to give power to the criminal courts to place offenders for the first time under police surveillance, with the liabil- ity to be called up for sentence if it should be found neces- sary to do so.—Mr. CHILDERS pointed out that the pro- posal would involve a serious change in the criminal ad- ministration, and he asked for time to cousult the judicial and police authorities. After considerable discussion the debate was adjourned.—Sir R. N. Fowler moved the second reading of the Representation of the People Act (184 Extension Bill. Mr. Childers remarked that the nutter was one which the Government proposed to deal with, and the debate was adjourned to July.—The Sale of Intoxicat- ing Liquors on Sunday Bill, brought in bv Sir J. Pease, was advanced to the Committee stage.—Progress was made with several other measures, and the House adjourned shortly before four o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The House of Lords sat to-day for the first time since the Easter recess, the Lord Chancellor taking his seat on the woolsack at a quarter after four o'clock.—Earl Granville paid a tribute to the worth of the late chairman of Commit- tees, and the Marquis of Salisbury and the Earl of Cork also bore testimony to the high qualities that distinguished Lord Redesdale.—On the motion of Earl STANHOPE, the Drowned Persons (Discovery and Interment) Bill was read a Sfeen,l time.—Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter to five o'clock. NEW BOOKS. "CasselrB Concise Cyclopatdia " is a new work by I Messrs. Cassell and Company which is likely to have a !large sale. It is in one volutne, and therefore less costly than the run of cyclopedias, and handier for reference, especially for the general reader or the busy professional man. It is a large volume, of course, ex- tending to as many as 1340 deuble-column pages. It is not pretended that it contains as much matter as the more expensive works of this class ; but it will vie with most in the number of articles upon which it treats. When we say that there are nearly twelve thousand subjects separately dealt with, we shall have suggested to the reader that the art of compression must have been carried to a high pitch. The articles embrace almost everything of interest to humanity; but to be more particular, it may be stated that the subjects covered are " mythological, historical, biographical geographical, topographical, scientific, and technical." We have taken the trouble to test articles under each of these heads, and it is satisfactory to find that in each case they have been carefully prepared and brought down to the latest date. It is especially an- noying when some question is raised, say of the popu- lation of a large town, to find the book of reference is at least one census behind. But this is not the ease with the " Concise Cyclopedia ;" the population of parliamentary towns is given on the basis of the last census. Opening at random at the letter "M," we get in succession articles on Mezzotint° engraving, Mica Schist, a metamorphic rock, Michaelmas Day, Michaelmas Daisy, Michael Angelo, Michelet (Jules), Michigan, one of the United States of America, Micro- meter, a measure for small distances. Microphone, and Microscope. The last two articles are illustrated, and this, it may be added, is a most important feature of the work, for it need scarcely be said that an illustra- tion will often, at a glance, convey more to the reader than a dozen pages of print. Every one has heard a good deal of myrrh who is familiar with the bible ; but it needs such a picture as is here given of the tree from which it is obtained to convey a satisfactory idea to the mind. There is an illustration of the Mosquito, too, as to which it. need hardly be said that the repre- sentation is much to be preferred to the reality. The I editor of the work, Mr. William Heaton has of course drawn from all available sources of information in order to ensure accuracy; and acknowledges his special indebtedness to Mr. O. H. Botharnley, assistant lecturer in chemistry, Mr. W. E. Clarke, F.L.S., joint author of the handbook of the Vertebrate Fauna of Yorkshire, Mr. A. Denny, assistant lecturer on biology, and Mr. A. J. Read, 8.A., science teacher at the Leeds Mechanics' lustitution. The newspaper ' reader and the student will find the volume exactly what he wants—a book that will answer his questions at any time upon almost every subject. Even classical and foreign phrases are given and explained when they are of a kind that are frequently used. The book is handsomely bound in scarlet and gold; but, in addition to this form of issue, it is now being pub- lished in monthly parts at 6d. each, and will be com- pleted in 28 parts. As a specimen of the way in which even minor matters are dealt with we give the article on Easter as follows : _

Easter, the annual festival observed throughout Christen- dom in celebration of the resurrection of Christ. Easter Day, or Easter Sunday, is the firs bunday after the four- teenth day of the " calenAar moon" wh ch happens on or after March 21st. The "calendar moon" is not, however, the actual moon, nor even the mean moon of astronomers; it is an altogether imaginary moon, created for ecclesiastical convenience in advance of the real moon; and the four- teenth day of the "calendar moon "falls generally on the fifteenth or sixteenth of the real moon, and thus after the real full moon. The earliest possible day for Easter Day is March 22nd; the latest is April 25th, on which day it falls in 1889, but not again till 1943. The word Easter is sup- posed to be derived from Eostre, the Anglo-Saxon goddess of spring, to whom the month now called April (Eo4re. eionath) was deciicited, Eostre is believed by Bede and otilcts V; be the same as the Sidenian Astarte, the Hebrew Ashtoreth, the Greek Aphrodite, and the Latin Venus. The festival of Easter has been celebrated in the Christian Church from a very early period, probably from the early part of the second century.—The Easter Sitting of the Law Courts (formerly called Easter Term) begins about the middle of April, and terminates about the end of Mar. "Building Societies Acts," by E. A. Wurtsburg. Messrs. Stevens and Sons, Chancery Lane, London. The writer of this work has by its publication sup- plied a want which must of late years have been much felt by that portion of the British public which is connected with or interested in building societies. The author informs U 8 that these societies are, in the Building Societies Act of 1836, stated to have been established in different parts of the United Kingdom, principally amongst the industrious classes for the purpose of raising by small periodical subscriptions a fund to assist the members thereof in obtaining a small freehold or leasehold property. Although there can be but little doubt that this was the design in their in- ception, and that mach good was done through their instrumentality in promoting habits of thrift among the working classes, yet it is to be lamented that the original idea has in these later days been in a great measure so far abandoned as to make some of these societies into huge money borrowing and lending concerns. Probably the necessity for writing such a treatise as this would never have arisen had the original design of building societies, as set forth in the Act of 1836, been faithfully carried out. Whilst the operations of a society were confined to advancing to its members small sums of money on security of small properties (in many cases the houses in which the borrowing members resided), little danger of the societies becoming involved was to be apprehended; but as the societies prospered, and money flowed into the coffers, the directors and committees (who were in many cases inexperienced men) placed money upon property when at its most inflated price, which they were destined ,never to realise. By this action, and others of similar nature, the managers of societies involved not only themselves but many others in utter ruin. At a time when building societies are not con- sidered quite as safe as the Bank of England (as they once were), and when it behoves every man to look before he leaps into these societies, this new work comes most opportunely. Its general scheme is clear and intelligible to the ordinary reader, and the man who permits himself to be guided by it cannot get very far wrong in building society matters. It would be well if every officer of every building society in the Kingdom would not only make himself master of its contents, but what is more important, still endea- vour to conduct his society in strict accordance with the principles there enunciated. Shareholders, too, would not be doing anything unwise in making them- selves masters of the contents of the book, as by so doing they would obtain some idea of the nature and extent of the liabilities which they incur as members of a building society. It is a notorious fact that many large societies are conducted on the loosest principles. Men with little or no ability, and no aptitude for business of any kind, have a chief share in their management, and such men are only too anxi us to persuade themselves and others that they know as much, if not more, law than any lawyer Possibly can. They are the penny wise and pound foolish sort. They proceed by " rule of thumb" and rather than admit their ignorance by calling in the advice of a solicitor land themselves and their society in a delightful bungle which becomes in the end a thousand times more profitable to the man of law than a little advice in the beginning would have been. To such men this volume commends itself more than to others. Its price is 7s. 6d. (10d. more than the regulation fee of Gs. 81), but the advantage is that it may be visited again and again, and, what is more, with profit each time. Another valuable work published by Messrs. Stevens and Sons is entitled "A truide to the Income Tax Acts, for the use of the English Income Tax Paver." It is from the nen of Mr. Arthur M. Ellis, L.L.B , author of "A guide to the House Tax Acts." That it has met a want in this country is shovsu by its reaching a second edition. Sydney Smith said there was nothing certain but death and taxes; and this being so, distasteful as taxes are, it is as well that we should know something about them. Hence the "guide" before us. The book is divided into four chapters. "The first "—to quote the introduc- tion—" describes the officials concerned in assessing, charging, and collecting the tax; the second deals with the properties and profits which are subjects of the tax ; the third describes the methods of assess- ment and collection- and the fourth treats of the allowances, abatements, and relia which the in- come tax payer may claim on one ground or another, and of the modes in which assessments erroneously made are corrected." It will be gathered from this that the work is one which is likely to be of great use to those who pay income tax, and that it may be the means of "paying for itself" many times over. Some idea may be gained of the labour of the writer when it is stated that income tax enactments run through no less than twenty-four Acts of Parliament, a list of which is given in the interests of the reader who hungers for more. There is a full table of cases; and, as every page is indexed, it will be seen that 'SIr Ellis has not spared himself in making his guide alike valuable' to the legal and non-legal mind. The book, whicii is suitably bound, is published at 6s.

THE IRISH QUESTION. • The "Freeman's Journal" says :—The manifesto is statesmanlike in spirit and noble and brave in tone. Mr. Gladstone has raised the great question. far beyond the region of party recrimination to It position.where it can be discussed on its meritg. The annual session of the General Synod of the Church-of Ireland was opened in Dublin on Tues- day. Lord Plunket, Archbishop •of ,Dublin, presi- ded, and in his opening address expressed his approval of the course adopted. by the Synod in passing, at a special meeting, resolutions on the present crisis condemnatory of Home Rule. The Press Association has reason to helieve that Mr. Chamberlain and those who think with him on the Irish question will after all find themselves able to vote for the second reading of the home Rule Bill. Negotiations are in progress with respect to the modifications insisted on as a condition to giv- ing their support, and there is every prospect of an arrangement being effected. It is expected that the Land Purchase Bill will be dropped.

Sir 11. James, in a letter to Welsh correspond- ent, says he cannot define preciSely the eitent to which he agrees with Mr. Chamberlain's views on the Irish policy of the Government, but they are agreed that the bill as proposed by the Government cannot receive their support. Speaking in Dublin, on Tuesday, at a meeting of the National League, Mr. Healy, M.P., referring to Mr. Gladstone's manifesto, said that such docui ments did more to promote 'good feeling between the peoples of Ireland and England than all the so- called remediallepislation of the past century. The lion. E. B. Portman, M.P., addressing the North Dorset Liberal Association, on Tuesday night, said he would vote for the second reading of the Home Rule Bill, reserving the right to differ on details.

Mr. Pugh, addressing the East Carmarthenshire Liberal Association, on Tuesday night, declared his adhesion to the Premier's proposals, and the meeting passed a resolution unanimously approving of the principle of the Home Rule Bill. A meeting of the General Committee-of the Lon- don and Counties Liberal Union was held at the City Liberal Club, on Tuesday afternoon, at which the Irish schemes were discussed. A resolution was proposed by Mr. Charming, M.P., approving the principle of the Home Rule Bill, but with the reservation that the Imperial Parliament should have supreme control over all matters of Imperiar concern. A discussion ensued, in which much diversity of opinion was shown. Mr. Caine, M.P., moved is an amendment a rider to the original resolution, to the effect that Ireland should con- tinue to have representatives in the Imperial Par- liament. This, on a division, was lost by 25 votes to 10, and the original resolution was then carried. It was afterwards resolved to hold a meeting of the Council of the Union on the, 12th instant, for the further discussion of Abe bills, and it is ex- pected that Mr. John Morley will then deliver an address. , Mr. Goschen, speaking at a Loyal and Patriotic Ynion meeting at Leeds on Tuesday night, declared that Mr. Gladstone by his manifesto had practic- ally withdrawn his bills, and left the matter in the form of an abstract resolution, which it was not practical to give effect to. Lord Punraven 05.% spoke against the bill. A special Meeting of the Council of the National Liberal Federation was held-in London on Wednet- day afternoon; Mr. James Ki'son, of Leeds. pre- siding. Delegates attended from all parts of the kingdom.. The Chairman explained that he could not adopt the resolution proposed by the officers'of the Federation, nor could he follow Mr. Chamber- lain's lead. He believed Mr. Gladstone would c arty his Irish policy to a successful issue, and that -the safeguards proposed would be ample. Mr. William Harris, chairman of the Committee, moved the resolution of the Council in an amended form, amid considerable 'interruption. It expressed a desire for the permanent settlement of the Irish question, but urged Mr. Gladstone to accept the ainendinent retaining the Irish representatives at Westminster. Mr. P. Stanhope seconded the resolution. Mr. Ellis, M.P., moved an amendment thanking Mr. Gladstone for the scheme as tibasis of settlement, and expres- sing unabated confidence in the Government. Mr. Matthews, Leeds, seconded this, and a warm discus- sion ensued. The original resolution was then ' negatived by an overwhelming majority, and. the amendment was carried amid some confusion. •

Mr. Trovelvan, addressing his constituents at Hawick, on Wednesday night, said the simple and practical alternative was to keep in the hands of the central Imperial Government the maintenance of law and order, and so avoid the necessity of buying the land. As a Radical and economist he opposed both bills.

Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledging receipt of an ad- dress from Archbishop Croke and the Roman Catholic clergy of Cashel, says he is confident that those who signed the address "agree with the .body of their Bishops in the belief they have ex- pressed that the policy now proposed to Parlia- ment will, if happily accepted, conduce alike te the happiness of Ireland and to the unity of the Empire." A largely attended conference of - representatives from the leading Liberal Associations of •Scotland was held on Wednesday in Edinburgh. After con- siderable discussion resolutions affirming that the demand of the Irish'people for Home Rule was just and reasonable, and also that the Government bills, as containing the basis of a settlement calculated to restore order and prosperity to Ireland and strengthen the Union, deserved the support of all Liberals, were adopted—the first unanimously and the , second by an overwhelming majority. Two largely attended meetings were held in the evening. MR. GLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.

Mr. Gladstone on Mon'day issued an important , address to his constieuents with reference to his Irish measures. The right lion. gentleman says some differences of opinion prevail amongst friends of the Irisi. Government Bill, as was to be expected, but he looks upon the wide and warm approval given •to the measure in the eountry, as showing that the principle of Home Mule for Ireland is re- garded as reas3sablei and that the demands of Im- perial unity have at least been carefully studied.. Mr. Gladstone is not disposed to ,under-estimate the grave importance of the differences Of opinion exhibited within the Liberal party, but he Ands in histcrical parallels .Viat as a rule the body of the party have been right and the seeesgidn 'Wrong, even where, as is .not the case at present, the seceders were agreed upon an active and sullStan- live policy. The secession now, however respectable and estimable in other ways, is as to positive policy for Ireland a perfect Babel. It offers either a hun- dred conflicting remedies for reitiiiiiig-secial order or no remedy at all. ..'Nhe real question before the Country is not the triumph( elriSh autonomy, but the • length and character • of the struggle by which it is to be preceded. A new terror is brought uptui the stage in the shape of Honig Rule for Scotland, and, some_add,:. forNales, but this suggestion brings no alarm to Mr. Glad- stone, who asks fortinie to look at each question in its order and on its merits. In the 'present conflict he finds with 'sbirovr that title,'wealtli,sOcial influ- ence—in a word, the spirit and power of class—are adverse to the Government. But clam has. before now been opposed to and been beaten gy the upright sense of the nation, and he agrees with Lord Har- tington that-this Irish question can .nnly beAgtled and set at restby the nation. 4 Tliti establishment ifl Dublin of a legislative body empowered to-niake laws for Irish as contra-distinguished from Imperial affairs is the issue now before the country, and not the details and particulars of the scheme. Those details 'are being artfully einproye4 to bewilder un- wary souls, but What the Itottse of Commons has to decide is whether we should or should not have re- gard to the prayer of Ireland for the manageinent by herself of affairs specifically and exclusively her own, and with the mass of English and Scotch people rests the answer. Mr. Gladstone's sole refer- ence to the Land.- P.'urchas,e. Bill is that he "leaves the bill to stand en the deelarations 'already made,* with an expression of regret that the Irish land- lords have as yet given no indication of -a desire to accept a proposal framed in a spirit of the ut- most allowable regard to their apprehension i and. their interests.

div.p: THE PAID ON THIEVES AT
WARRINGTON. A YOUTHFUL TRIO.

On Monday, at the Warrington Borough Court, three boys named Patrick Fallon" Thomas Edward Duffield, and Thomas Fairhurst were charged with stealing a knee rug, value 15s, the property of James Kenworthy, timber merchant, Brown-street, off Bewsey-street. Police-constable Bickley was on Sunday night near the railway bridge in Bewsey- street, when his attention was attracted by a noise in the adjoining timber yard of Mr. Kenworthy. The prisoners were on the premises, and the rug in ques- tion and a bunch of keys had been dropped. Another bunch was found on another of the prisoners. The boys, who now said they went on the premises to sleep, received a very bad character. Fairhurst was sent to prison for a month, to be followed by five years' detention in a reformatory, and Fallon and Duffield were each sent to prison for a month. THE SUPPOSED THEFT OF A WATCH AND CIIAIN. At the same court, a man named Martin Smith, for- merly a soldier inthe Grenadier Guards, was charged on remand with being found in possession of a gold ! watch and gold albert cu sin, supposed to have been stolen from some person unknown. Inspector James , said that information had been received from Lon- don that the watch had been stolen, and Chief Con- stable Hunt asked for a further remand until Friday, which was granted. THE SHOPBREAKING AT MR. MORTON'S.

Another case of robbery was also heard on Mon- day afternoon. Three youths named John Wilson (18), labourer, of no fixed abode, William Hickman (20), labourer, lbydock-street, and William Ellis forge-hand, Turner-street, were brought up on re- mand charged with breaking into the shop of Mr. Edgar Valentine Morton, Winwick-street, and steal- ing a half sovereign, 18s in silver and copper, four gold rings, a pair of trousers, a hair watch-guard, and a lady's silver geneva watch, the whole of the , value of .-05 is 3d.-- Mr. Lyon Whittle (deputy town clerk) prosecuted on behalf of the police.—Frederick Tyrer, assistant to Mr. Morton, said that on Tues- day the 20th April he locked up the shop at ten minutes to seven in the evening, and saw that every , thing was safe. He returned at 11-50 the same ;night and found the back door open, and that a small window had been taken out bodily. He missed 28s 6d from the money drawer. He identi- fied the four rings and the silver Geneva watch pro- duced as his master's property. They were also safe ,in the shop on the Tuesday night in question.— William Briggs, pawnbroker, Powys-street, said that on Monday the 26th April a lad named Troy came to his shop with one of the gold rings produced and asked 7s on it. He said it belonged to a man out- side. Witness had received notice from the police of certain things having been stolen. He went away and returned accompanied by P.C. Monoghan. Hickman and Ellis were standing near the shop, and Monoghan detained them. He found two rings in the street. All the rings. were handed to the constable.—Thomas Troy, who had been pre- viously charged with having been concerned in the robbery, was now called as a witness, the charge against him having been withdrawn, lie stated that on Monday the 26th April, Hickman told him he had four rings, and asked him to pawn them. —A clogger from Salford gave evidence to the effect that several days ago Wilson came to his shop and exchanged the pair of boots now produced for a pair of clogs.—P.C. Monoghan olive evidence with reference to the apprehension of the prisoners, who, when charged with the robbery, admitted they were guilty.--Prisoners were committed for trial to the Assizes.

ROBBERY OF BOOTS. The prisoners John Wilson and William Hickman were then charged with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of Messrs. Freeman, Hardy, and Willis, boot and shoe dealers, Bridge-street, between 4-15 p.m. and 8 -55 p.m., on Sunday, the 18th April, and stealing about 21 pairs of men's and girls'boots, of the value of £3 8s Bd. Mr. Whittle prosecuted. The manager for Messrs. Freeman, Hardy, and Willis now stated that although a large number of boots had been stolen, he could only swear to one pair (now produced) as belonging to the firm. Evidence was given to show that Troy attempted to pawn a pair of boots at the shop of Mr. Morton. They were handed to the police. Troy said on the 20th April he met the pri- soner Wilson, who asked him to pawn a pair of boots for him. The boots produced were the same he pawned at Mr. Morton's shop. P.C. Monaghan said that on Sunday night, the 18th April last, he was on duty in Bridge-street when his attention was called to the shop of the prosecutor. A light was burning in the back shop: lie examined the back premises and found• a step-ladder reared 1113 and leading on to the roof. He went on the roof and noticed that one side of the window had been , taken out, lie got through, went downstairs, and found that a square of glass had been taken out of the window between the back and front shop 3. A person could reach boots by putting his hand through the broken square of glass. P.C. Neill said he charged the prisoners with the offence. They were in custody on another charge. Wilson said, "It is false; I wasn't in it." Hickman Pulled round and said, "You were in it; I can prove it." Wilson then said, "We only took one pair." Hick- man then replied, "I was there, and so was Wilson. We only took one pair. Wilson wore them two days, and Troy pledged them."—The prisoners Were committed to the Assizes. THEFT OF A. PAIR OF BOOTS.

At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, a youth named James Towey (21), forge labourer, was, charged with being found on the premises of Fred- ' erick Jones, 5, Froghall-lane, for an unlawful pur- pose on the morning previous, and, further, with stealing a pair of boots, value 4s, from the same premises, on the 9th April.—Chief Constable Hunt, who described the prisoner as one of an Organised gang, said that on the previous morning a daughttr of Mr. Jones, who was in the parlour; heard a noise in the kitchen. On going there she saw defendant coming from underneath the table. She said "What do you want there ?" and he replied "I have only just come for a drink of water," and made his way out of the house. Information was given to P.C. Monoghom, who afterwards apprehended prisoner. At the Police Station prisoner admitted that the boots he was then wearing he had stolen from the same house in the month of April.—lie pleaded guilty. For the first offence the magistrates sent him to prison for fourteen-days, and for the second he was committed to gaol for three months. It was mentioned that he' had several times been con- victed. •

This committee recommended that the following plans Pe approved :—Alterations and extension to soap works at Bank Quay for Messrs. Lever Brothers; ten houses in Latchford-road for Mrs. C. Stirrup; addition to 26, Rolles• ton-street, for Mr. Francis Jolley; scullery to house and shop in Chorley-street for Mr. J. Nevins; iron stable off Church-street for Mr. Bowers ; house in Grappenhall-road for Mrs. Grounds; new shop in Horsemarket-street for Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton; a brick shed in yard off Knight-street for Mr. W. Lythgoe. Recommendation, that the plan of a "give and talc's line" for the improvement of St. Mary's-street, Latchford, be approved, tbe Corporation to rebuild the boundary wall at an estimated cost of £2o. The following report of tbe Lighting Sub-Committee was approved and adopted: The Sub-Committee met on March 25th. Present, Councillors Greening and Wright. After visiting, they recommend that the following lamps be fixed :—Bracket lamp in side street, near Mr. Greaves' prem- ises, corner of passage leading to back of new property, Bridge-street ; two new special pillar lamps. with 30-candle Bray's burners—one opposite Mr. Greaves' shop, and one GO yards to the north, both on the west side ef Bridge- street-4mile GREENING, JOHN ED. WRIGHT. Councillor GREENING moved, and Councillor Witte= seconded the adoption of these minutes. Alderman BURGESS asked if it was the intention of the Street Improvement Committee to take measures for the removal of different kinds 'of obstructions which had been erected behind cottage houses in Warrington. The com- mittee required tke owner, or the parson who built the pro- perty, to set apart a given space of land behind each dwell- ing for breathing or air space, but the tenants were being allowed to fill in these spaces to a very large extent, and Indeed' he might say with perfect safety there were hun- dreds of backyards filled in with such things as pigeon, rab- bit, and fowl cotes, and perhaps even a stable for a donkey. He (Alderman Burgess) thought the time was come woen the committee would have to take energetic steps for the remeval of these erections, which were calculated to very prejudicially affect the health of the people who inhabited the property, and of those who lived in the surrounding houses.

Alderman limits also suggested that the committee should make an inspection of the various property in a ruinous condition in the town, some of which was so ruin- ous that he was almost afraid some accident would be happening. Cooncillor JOLLEY thought there was a good deal in what Alderman Burgess said, but be hoped the committee would not deal severely with those who had erected glass frames for the purpose of cultivating a few flowers in their back yards. Alderman Horatio thought it would be too bad if a man could not keep a few rabbits or pigeons outside his bease without the Corporation coming down upon him. CouncWor GatimetNo said that the subject brought for- ward by Alderman Bargesi had been before the committee en •various occasions. After a conversation he had with Alderman Burgess, at the Sanitary Committee, some few weeks ago, where this matter was discussed, be brought it specially before the Street Improvement Committee, and Mr. Longdin received instructions from the com- mittee to get out a report .of all the places in the town at which the bye-laws were infringed to the manner described. There were no doubt a great many of such cases, and some of them would be difficult to deal with. But there was no doubt that a great proportion of them would have to be put down. Mr. Loagdin had instructions to keep the matter in hand, and to report to each meeting of the committee how things were going on. With reference to Alderman Davies' remarks, he probably referred to property in the Bewsey district. (Alderman Davies: Various parts of the town.) That had had the at- tention of the committee, and orders had been given to prevent anything of a dangerous character happening. Mr. Jolley referred to the back yards' tiovered with glass; but they could not have breathing space through glass any more than through slates, and he thought that if they took any steps at all they would have to take steps to serve one like anothet. (Hear, bear.) Alderman &mons said the answer of Councillor Green- ing was perfectly satisfactory. - The MAYOR referred to some cottage property he had in interest ha in Lythgoes-lane which he load seen the other day, and was surprised to find the houses were almost built up with wooden structures—pigeon and rabbit cotes, and. in one case positively a little donkey stable—(laughter)—and several other structures of a most mysterious character. He did not like to take action in the matter, but still it was one that would have to be dealt with. Wi,h regard to the cultivation of flowws, he was sure the committee would not interfere unduly with that if it could be allowed with- out sacrificing the public health. The minutes 'were then confirmed.
SANITARY COMMITTEE. The order for plyment recommended by the Sanitary Com- mittee included .£2BO for intercepting depot and £250 for ejectors. _ _
• On the motion of Alderman BURGESS, seconded by Councillor SUTTON, the minutes were adopted.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes contained as follows : Minute, that the Borough Surveyor submitted plan, speci- fication, and estimate for the forming and paving of Glazdbrook-street, part of Paul-str,et, and part of Eustace- street.—Resolution, that the Town Clerk serve ale necessary notices for the forming and paying of the said streets, and take all necessary proceedings under section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1875.—Resolution, that the macadam portion of the carriageway oc. Froghall Lane be replaced with granite sets.—Resolation, that the portion of Queen- street from Brown-street to Golborne-street, and from corner of Cheshyres-lane to the Fair Ground, be paved with sets. ()n the motion of Alderman DAVIES, seconded by Coun- cillor TAYLOR, the minutes were passed.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the School Attendance Committee stated that the report of the inspector showed that 9a cases bad been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 91 cases for 183 children; that 20 cases bad been. taken before the magistrat!s, when fines were inflicted in 19 cases and one ordered to the industrial school. [Note.-38 cases were brought before the com- mittee and dealt with.] Confirmed on the motion of Councillor Bizows, seconded by Councillor FLighlING.

div.head: CEMETEaY COMMITZEE.
div.p: CEMETEaY COMMITZEE.

Ths Registrar repurted to the Committee that the inter- ments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 38; minors, 36 ; stillborn and premature, 17;' and for the cprrespond- ing period last year: Adults, 43; minors, 31; stillborn and premature, 3. Note.—The receipts for the past four we ,ks were £6l 12s. 103., and for the corresponding period lest year £57 3s. 61. Confirmed on motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Coun- cillor BROWN.

div.head: MUSEUM AND LIBRARY.
div.p: MUSEUM AND LIBRARY.

The minutes of the Museum, Library and Arts Committee contained the following report of the curator for the month of March :—Visitore to the museum, compared with March, 1885,4,222; increase, 63 per cent; books issued in reading room, 2,143: increase. 59 per cent; books issued to sub- scribers, 1,802 ; increase, 8 per cent. Minutes adopted on the motion of Councillor W. PIERPOINT seconded by Councillor SurroN.

THB BATHS AND PARK. The Bathkeeper reported to the Town Ball, Park, and Baths Committee that the income from the baths for the past montb was £l2 lie 6d. Councillor Flitslicolus called attention to the bad condi- tion of the footpath through the park; from Sankey-Street to Kendrick-street, but the MAYOEI replied that the im- provement of the path was in progress.—Minutes con- firmed.
THE MARKETS. The Markets Committee reported that the total income for the pet month from all sources was £2ll 63 4d. TILE GAS. •

Alderman HOLMES moved and C,ouncillor GREENING aeconded the confirmation of the Gas Committee's minutes, which contained nothing of moment. Councillor FLzmiNG said that in the absence of Councillor Dixon—(laughter)—he should like to baye a word to say on the gas. Last March his gas bill was LS 193 11cl, but this March it was £lO 15s 3d, and he sheald like to ask the chairman of the committee how that was, because they had just used the regular number of burners and observed the same regular habits. (Hear, bear.) Alderman DAVIES said the best thing to do was to refer Councillor Fleming to Mr. l trson, who would give him the utmost satisfaction. (Laughter.) He had experienced it himself. (Laughter.) Alderman BoraEs thought the answer of Alderman Davies the best answer.that could be given. But speakinn.: seriously be supposed Councillor Fleming had used the gas, and consequently it had been charged for. Alderman DAVIES : I an only surprised he is not charged i more. (Laughter.) The minutes were then confirmed. A SUGGESTION. Alderman BURGESS said he should just like to say a few words with reference to that Corporation having an oppor- tunity to wait upon Her Majesty in Liverpool next week. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He wishedto know for the bene- fit of that Corporation if measures were being taken to bring about that desirable condition of things, and whether they might expect to appear as the mayor's guests—(laugh- ter)—on the occasion, to be taken at the mayor's Cot, or at the public cost, or at any other cost than their own. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He thought it was an aamir- able opportunity for the mayor to distinguish himself and have an opportunity of showing to her Majesty the most I admirable corporation she has within her kingdom, (Hear, hear, and laughter.)

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, MAY 8,. 1886.

MR. GLADSTONE'S Manifesto is a master- Piece, both as to rhetoric and as to reason- ing. It is as clear and luminous as it is 4rni and convincinsr. The PRIME MINISTER deals with objections with the confidence and freedom of one who is familiar with every detail, and is sure of his case. He travelled some time ago the weary road on which ,his critics now inquire their way at every mile; and looking serenely from the heights beyond, he feels that he has some title to tell others Where they stand, and whether they are on safe ground. We may now see, after all that has been said during the past few weeks, Why, when he introduced the Home Rule Bill, he courted the fullest and freest discus- sion of its provisions? He knew that reason and time were on his side—that the people might for a while be staggered with the vast- ness of his plan—but that, when they came to realise its proportions and its objects, they Would perceive that it was well conceived, carefully drawn, and likely to be adequate to the achievement of the end in view. The scheme has been subjected to ruthless criti- cism ; but it has not lost ground by being' criticised. On the contrary, there is day by day accumulating evidence from all parts of the" United Kingdom that, whatever the upper Class may say, the people as a whole are favourable to the principle of Home Rule for Ireland. Mr. GOSCHEN made himself rather ridiculous at Leeds, on Tuesday, by saying that Mr. GLADSTONE'S scheme, instead of holding the field was "hopelessly gone." tie was instantly answered at the meeting °Y cries of " No " ; but a better answer was furnished by a large and enthusiastic overflow Meeting, held out of doors, which passed a resolution almost unanimously in favour of the Irish Bills of the Government. Mr. GOSCHEN'S remedy is "firmness"—in other Words coercion, and "the suppression of the trafficking with the Irish vote." Coercion is a brutal weapon which has within the past twelve months been thrown down by both Political parties; it has been made use of fifty times in fifty years with a failure which is as distressing as it is notorious. As to "suppression of the trafficking with the Irish vote "—well, let Mr. GOSCHEN bring in a bill with that subject, and, if it is not in- stantly laughed out of existence, we shall be able to say how much of a corner of the field it is likely to occupy. Mr. GLADSTONE May well say, in view of such proposals as those of the Whig member for Edinburgh, that, except his own plan, "there is nothing in the political arena that is determined °r intelligible." The proposals of his oppo- nents "vary with every speech they make— a proof, not of the weakness of the men, but of the hopelessness of their cause." The PRIME MINISTER is not at all alarmed by the suggestion that we may hear next of Rome Rule for Scotland and Wales; for he " can draw no vital distinction of right between the case of Ireland and other cases." And why should he? If three- fourths of the people of Scotland were unanimous in demanding, through their representatives, that Scotch affairs should be dealt with bv a separate Parliament, who would venture to say that the matter was outside the domain of practical politics? And so With regard to England and Wales. It may be—and we do not think it at all unlikely— that when Irishmen have got fairly to work in a Parliament of their own, the principle of local self-government—from the application Of which we are all expecting so much—will develop in the direction of three additional Rome Rule Parliaments. It is a question, in the first instance, of what the people want, and of powers, and of a.name. Town Coun- cils have legislative powers, within the area of the general law, and they would still be What they are if they were called Town Par- liaments. If the nation, in its wisdom or un- Wisdom, should think fit to give larger powers to bodies to be called Provincial or National Parliaments, instead of National Councils, that is a matter, surely,which is perfectly le2i- titnate and perfectly constitutional. It is not, at any rate, "a new terror," except to those Who are afraid of their own shadows. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN talks of federation; but true federation is impossible except with bodies federating upon a common basis. Let him help Mr. GLADSTONE to solve the Irish prob- lem by establishing Home Rule for Ireland; and then, if it should end in our having Rome Rule for England, for Scotland, and for Wales, we may have a federation upon a sound footing which will properly constitute an Imperial Parliament—just as Congress is the outcome of the federation of the United
j

States: It may be said, and indeed it is being said, that Wales and Scotland are content as they are. Well, "If it be so, so be it ;" but it is as well to observe that we have not yet settled the bases of local self-government for these countries; and it may be found, when we come to deal with the question, that noth- ing will be satisfactory which stops short of Home Rule. Be that, however, as it may, since what is one man's meat is sometimes another man's poison, we are bound to deal with the Irish case on its merits; and if Ilishmen agree, as they seem to agree, in demanding Home Rule, we say, with Mr. GLADSTONE, by all means let them have Home Rule.

A Town's Meeting was held at St. Helens on Tuesday evening, and a strong protest ; was made against the Parliamentary proposal to prohibit the employment of women on the pit brows of collieries. There is an impres- sion abroad that the miners who advocate this prohibition are less anxious to protect women than they are to forward their own interests. It is suggested that if they can get rid of female competition in their par- ticular market, the price paid for male labour. will have a tendency to increase. This is undoubtedly true; but, standing alone, it is not an argument to which Parliament ought for a moment to listen. It is Protection in its worst form; it is a return to monoply of the most repulsive kind. The miners do not, of course, take their stand upon this ground; they R.now better. They urge that the work of pit brow girls, followed as it is out of doors, and in unseemly attire, is coarse and degrading; and that the Legislature having in the interests of the sex prohibited female labour in the pit itself, should go a step fur- ther, and put an end ,to it on the pit bank. But the cases are not analogous; it was shown before Parliament interfered with the employment of women in mines that the peculiar conditions under which both sexes were brought together, below ground, were essentially subversive of morality. This was the strong point of the prohibitionists, and it enabled them to carry the day. There is no such complaint now; the pit brow girls work together, and in the open air; and it is affirmed by those who know them best that , they are as honest, as respectable, and as moral as other sections of the community. The occupation would not be to the taste of LADY VERE DE VERB; but ovlinary mortals cannot "pick and choose." We have all a good deal to do in the way of work which we do not like; and females, who have a very narrow field of employment, are too often driven to occupations which are dis- tasteful to them. But it is just because their choice is narrowed down that we should en- deavour in the main to enlarge rather than restrict it. The miners must make out a better case than they have yet presented, or Parliament, as the meeting on Tuesday even- ing concluded, will not be justified in inter- fering with female labour on the pit banks.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

- _ From a letter in another column, it will be seen that local Tories have been vilifying Mr. Mandella, M.P. The particular piece of base coin is "nailed down ;" but, no matter— they have other counterfeits to put in circu- lation.

The Queen has of late years been too little seen of her people. A display of loyalty— such as that which took place in London last Tuesday, and will be repeated in Liverpool next Tuesday and Wednesday—is alike good for Soveteign and subject.

The Council of the London Chamber of Commerce offer a prize of Lso for the best essay on Imperial Federation. Here is a "rare opportunity" for our local essayists. Alderman Davies and Mr. J. L. Tunstall are the local secretaries.

Tne Anarchists who go "on strike "and endeavour, as they have done in Chicago, to enforee their arguments with dynamite, can- not complain if they are answered with lead. Creatures who act with the ferocity of tigers must expect to be shot down like tigers. -- Liberal organisations, great and small, are all but unanimously declaring in favour of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule scheme as a basis of settlement of the Irish question. The resolution of the Warrington Liberal Association, on Wednesday evening, was car- ried with one dissentient only.

-- " Mr, Gladstone' s umbrella" proves, after all, to be by far the biggest and the best. it covers by long odds the greatest number; and there are some indications that it may soon cover Mr. Chamberlain. All he wants is a structural alteration, which it may be possible to make. To drop the metaphor, Mr. Chamberlain will be satisfied if the principle is conceded of Ireland being directly represented at Westminster. It is gratifying to learn that Mr. Gladstone has forwarded a cheque for Lso towards the election expenses of Mr. Joseph Leicester, M.P. for West Ham. This handsome con- tribution will be especially welcome to Mr. Leicester, who as a genuine working-man is not over-blest with this world's goods. War- rington Liberals will not be the less proud of their townsman now that the Prime Minister gives substantial proof of his regard for him. Mr. Peter Rylands has not ceased to be a Radical, as some would suggest. Last evening, hr the 'House of Commons, he gave notice that on that day four weeks he should move a motion declaring that the right of sitting in the House of Lords possessed by certain Bishops of the Church of England is con- trary to public policy, injurious to religious interests, and ought to be abolished. ••••••••••••• Tipplers get at times in queer straits. A labourer at St. Helens tried the other day to get into an office with a view to " sleep- ing it off." The door being locked, he pro- ceeded to enter by the chimney, but "Stuck fast," and was imprisoned for two hours. In fact, before the man could be released, the chimney had to be, in part, taken down. He was glad to be rescued; and yet, 'tis said, he "looked black."

-- The Rev. B. B. Prescott does not appear to have approved of the action of Mr. W. Pierpoint in calling attention to the fact of the church bell at Latchford having been rung to celebrate the victory of the Conserv- atives at the General Election. But why not? It has been the means of making it known to the parishioners that the Vicar went to the bell-ringer and had the ringing stopped. The ringing was public enough, and Mr. Pierpoint has rendered a public service in asking for a public explanation,
- Sir Charles Dilke seems, the other night, to have strongly impressed his audience with a belief in his innocence, Pity he didn't

thus speak out in the witness box. He is either a much-abused man, or, as Carlyle de- scribed- the Turk, unspeakable." He is pay- ing a terrible penalty for the mistake he made in nc,t insisting upon denying, on oath, the charge made against him; but he is seeking now to repair the error. If he should estab- lish his innocence, he may count on a great revulsion of feeling in his iavour.

The Liberal electors of the Newton Divi- sion demonstratcd, at the presentation to Colonel AlcCorqundale on Thursday evening, that they have more than an admiration—that they have an affection for him. Such men as he, as Mr. William Crosfield appropriately ob- served, do indeed brighten and enrich the public life of the country. A resolution was unanimously passed expressing confidence in the Government. The demonstration would be " simply perfect" if it should result in Colonel McCorquodale concluding', with the electors, that he " must stand again."

The congregation at 4 Helens Parish Church are not satisfied With the singing. Canon Carr admits that it might be better ; but howling precedes singing. The worthy canon says "They had a voluntary choir when he first came to the old church, and their music was like a Dutch concert." To know what a Dutch concert is like, another reverend gentleman—the Rev. Dr. Brewer— says you must imagine "a party of Dutch- men in sundry stages of intoxication, some singing, others quarrelling, speechyfing, wrangling, and so on." Now, the choir at St. Helens Parish Church have got beyond that ; give them time—they are progressing.

WIDNES BREAD DEALERS IN TRODBLE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday Francis Cooke, provision dealer, Alforde-street, was convicted on the evidence of P.C. Chambers of selling biead withowt weighing it. A 41b. loaf, Cur which the officer pat,: 412-d, was 4-1- ounces short. A line of 103 and costs, 123, was unposed. A sitnihr penalty was inflicted upon Win. Rodgkinson, provi:ion da let, Albert- road, for a like offence. P.C. Chambers paid 311 Cur a 41b. loaf that was four ounces snort. WrntsEs :_:ClIOOL BOARD AT Won.—At the instance of the School Board, Mr. G. U. Danby, cletk, sir mooned the following persons for neglecting to sena their children regularly to school : E Mulvey (two cases), Christopher Buc'xnan, John, Fennev, Walter Burchell, Frank Garlsutt, James Cummins (two cases). Michael Murphy. John Murphy (two cases) James Malian (two cases), Charles McKenna (two cases), James McCann (two cases), William Fallon (two cases), and Peter Connor. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each case. THEvr OF A WATCH.—At Widnes I'olice Court on Mon- day, three boys named Roberts, Pace, and Smith, were charged with stealing a silver lever watch, value 40s, the property of Thomas Roberts. from the schooner Chester, lying in West Bank Dock. Tne watch was safe in the cabin on Friday night, but had disappeared next morning. On Saturday, P.C. Davies apprehended the prisoner Smith in the act of pledging the watch at a ptwnshop in Ann. street West. He said Roberts gave it to him. In the even- ing Roberts and Pace were apprehended, and the former confessed he was the culprit, but added that Paco was with him. Pace was ordered to pay 303; or go to gaol for 14 days; and the other boys were sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod. ALLEGED NEGLECT OF FAMILY.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions on Monday, .18,rnes Tudor, of Weston, was charged under a warrant with neglecting to maintain his wife and
'amity, whereby they had become chargeable to the corn- __ .
mon fund of the Runcorn Union.—Mr. T. Houghton, who appeared for the Guardians said tho woman had gone to the workhouse through some disagreement. He did not
;hink the man had refused to maintain his family ; and he

was willing to come to some arrangement. He was in the employ of Mr. Kirkhana,•chemical contractor, and he might be working in Runcarn to-day and in the sou. 11 of England to-morrow. At the time in question the defendant was working in Dublin. He had to leave suddenly, and he sent his wife money to enable her to return. When she arrived, instead of going to the house of the defendant's mother, where the defendant lived, she went to the workhouse. The defendant was quite willing to pay the amount due with casts.—The defendant said from the way his wife had been going on, drinking and running him into debt, it was im- possible for a working-man to support her.—The Bench allowed the defendant to come to a settlement with Mr. Houghton. WOUNDED WITH A TUMBLER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Bridget Mullen, a young married woman, living in Grove-streen, was charged on remand with unla Nfullv wounding Ellen McCal)e, wife of Hugh Mc- Cabe, of Warrington-road. The evidence for the prosecution was that between ten and eleven o'clock on Saturday night, the 25th April, McCabe heard music and dancing in the prisoner's house, and went in. After being there a quarter of an bow, a woman named Mrs Connor said "What is that Manchester street-walker doing here? " Mrs McCabe said she would make her prove her words. Whereupon Mrs Connor and Mrs Mullen struck her. She declared her in- tention of summoning them and left. Meeting P.C. Bruce she returned with him, and the door was no sooner opened than the prisoner sent a tumbler at her face, inflicting several wounds, which Dr. MacLennan attended to and de- posed were not dangerous.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the prisoner. contended that Mrs McCabe was the aggressor, characterised the case as a paltry one and asked to have it dealt with as a common assault.—The Bench committed the prisoner to the assizes for trial, but admitted her to bail.

CADISHEAD POOR'S LAND.—The Guardians re- cently made their annual inspection of the poor's lots. Among those present were Messrs. J. C. Mather, J. Pearson, Adam Stott, and W. Stott, and the war- dens J. Thompson and John Taylor, Wooldin The usual business took place of drawing the year's rent and re-letting the lots for the ensuing year. The authorities afterwards had dinner at the Coach and Horses Inn, Cadishead. Tam HAYDOCK PIT BROW WOMEN.—A fortnight ago a meeting was reported of the Haydock pit brow women at which a petition against the pro- posal to abolish female labour on pit brows was directed to be sent to the Home Secretary. This was done, and the following acknowledgment has been received :--" Whitehall, London.—Sir, I am directed by the Secretary of State to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 14th inst. forwarding a copy of the resolution p,ssed at a meeting of pit brow women on the 13th April on the subject of the proposal to abolish female labour at the pit brow.— I am, sir, your obedient servant, Godfrey Lushing- ton. R. AL Prescot, Esq., Lyme House, Haydock."

MILLING AND PARTNERS, LIMITED.—Mr. John Milling, trading as John Milling and Partners, of Leeds, warehousemen, general drapers, and house furnishers, has, like many other well-known firms, converted his business into a limited company. The business is well and favourably known in the North of England, and has been successfully carried on for many years past by the founder. It is unique of its kind, there being no other general drapery estab- lishment in the town at all approaching i it in mag- nitude or having so wide a connection n the sur- rounding districts. The company have secured the services of Mr. Milling and Mr. Colquhoun as direc- tors, and no fees will be taken until the share- holders have received a dividend of at least 15 per cent. in each year. This company affords to those who desire a good investment a prospect of a hand- some dividends without serious risks. WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.—On Thurs- day, at Warrington County Court, Joseph Heywood, wheelwright, Preston Brook, appeared before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes,for his public examination in bankruptcy. Mr. Worsley, deputy official receiver, put a number of questions to the bankrupt as to his affiairs, and the answers he had given to questions that had been put by the Official Receiver. Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of a creditor, put one or two ques- tions. The examination, which lasted over an hour, was adjourned.--Arthur Edwin Hawkins, clothier and tailor, Bridge-street, Runcorn, was also ex- amined. He said that he commenced business in 1884, with a capital of £6OO. He had done his best to struggle on with the business. He attributed his failure to difference in valuation, fixtures, and good will £2OO, discount on bills £25, and interest paid £4O. The takings had not been what he had antici- pated. He had paid too much for the business, and had bought his experience dearly. The examination was adjourned.—The examination of Edward Pen- nington, wheelwright, Preston Brook, was closed. SLANDERING Mn. MUNDELLA.—A story has been circulated in a local journal that Mr. .Mundella, whilst preaching Free Trade, was interested in a continental factory which sent hosiery to this cotin- try. This having been made use of by Tory work- men engaged in the wire trade, with the addition that the President of the Board of Trade had exer- cised his influence in causing a Government order ' for wire rope to be sent to Germany, a Liberal working-man wrote to Mr. Mundella, on the sub- ject, and has received the following reply :
Bcard of Trade, Whitehall Gardens, BM., May 5, 1886.
My Dear Eir,—These statements to which you refer are of the usual Tory character, and are utterly untrue, so far as I am concerned. .

The Board of Trade has nothing whatever to do with any contracts for the public service. It is not even consu:ted upon them, and has no cognisance of them in any respect. Personally I have nothing to do with business, and have had nothing to do with my former manufacturing business for the last fourteen years.
Faithfully yours,

A. J. DITTNDELLI.: AFFILIATION CASE.-At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday Isabella Ann Woods sum- moned Charles Smith Bennie to show cause why he should not contribute to the support of her illegiti- mate child, of which she alleged he was the father. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and stated that she was formerly a domestic servant in the employ of Mr. Thompson, surveyor to the Warrington Highway Board, and the defendant, Mr. Charles Smith Bennie, was Mr. Thompson's stepson. He had evidence to prove the paternity of the child, but did not propose to go into details.—The complainant stated that she now lived at Sandy-lane, Orford, was 18 years of age, and was single. She was formerly in the service of Mr. Thompson, with whom defendant resided. De- fendant had paid ..C1 after the birth of the child and .E 5 before. He had formerly made her an offer of marriage.—Mr. Browne said that defendant had written to Mrs. Woods, complainant's mother, say- ing that he would do all that he possibly could, and that the child should never want. His proposal was to pay .Cl 3 annually, at 12 instalments, to be remitted on the first day of each month ; what little he had already done he would leave out alto- gether. Defendant, in the letter, added that it was entirely against his principles to make reparation in that way, but lie did think it was for the best.— In answer to the magistrates' clerk, it was .stated that the defendant was deputy surveyor to the highway Board and also surveyor to theGolborn.e Local Board.—The mother of the complainant said that defendant had to her admitted the paternity of the child, and said that he would marry com- plainant and take a house in Warrington.—,The Bench made an order for defendant to pay as a week.
