ITHE CHESHIRE TRAGEDY.—After an inquiry ex- tending over some hours at Broxton, on Wednesday, the Cheshire justices committed Mary Chesworth to take her trial for the wilful murder of her child at Hampton Heath. The prisoner, in reply, said that she did not murder the child. She was starving at , the tim6, and being weak and faint, fell into the pond as she was passing, and had a very narrow ' escape of her own life. GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday after- noon, in the Schoolroom, Great Sankey. There were present Messrs. lierfoot (in the chair), Cook, and Ridgway; S. Sutton (clerk), and Nodal (architect). —The Clerk reported that there was a balance of £954 in the hands of the treasurer, including the ' amount outstanding upon the loan for school build- ing. A precept for the sum of £lOO upon the overseers of Great Sankey was allowed and signed. The tender of Mr. Ramsbottom, builder of the schools, amounting to £57 10s, for brick and stone ; work in connection with the erection of boundary walls, with wrought-iron railings, &c.,was accepted, as was also that of Mr. James Bridge, of Warring- ton, amounting to £l•2, for ironwork. The architect stated that he considered the whole of the interiori work would be completed and the workmen away by the end of next week, and the children would be ' able to occupy the premises the following week. 1

• said until there was an understanding be should refuse to sign any cheques except they were merely for wages. He thought the Board should pass a resolution making it equally binding upon each member of the Board.—lbe Cnairman said he thought they had sufficient honour amongst them to sign without passing a resolution.—Mr. Shaw suggested that the chairman and two members of the Finance Committee, who were well acquainted with all the money affairs of the Board,should sign the cheaues.--Mr.Prit- chard asked why there was this reluctance to sign cheques. —The Chairman replied that be had no doubt it was due to the fact that one or two members, in fact three or four, had been surcharged, and were acquainted with the difficulty there was of getting out of it. The Local Government Board did not hesitate to say persons would be brought before the magistrates. He thought Mr. Shaw's idea a good one.—Mr. Shaw: The Chairman was surcharged, ouly he got someone to pay it. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said he was surcharged, but unfortunately he did not get anyone to pay it. He had to pay it himself.—Mr. Imisou said be had that morning refused to sign some cheques, because he thought the chairman of the Finance Committee and the chairman of the committee to which the account had refer- ence should sign the cheques.—Mr. Dobson said he was the oldest elected member of the Board, and he had never before heard a discussion regarding the signing of cheques. He thought every member of the Board ought to take his share of the responsibility of signing cheques.—Mr. Grice believed there were some members who bad neveroigned a cheque.—The Chairman remarked that after that difscussion the members would be prepared to do their duty.

div.head: OUTRAGEOUS STABBING CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: OUTRAGEOUS STABBING CASE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday morning, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and T. Sutton Timmis, a young man named Alfred Jackson, labourer, of 64, Beaumont-street, Was charged with having stabbed Samuel Woodyer, labourer, 47, Beaumont-street, on Saturday night —Samuel Woodyer said that on Saturday night, about half-past ten, he was standing at the door of hi) house talking to his wife and another woman, when he saw the prisoner coming across the street. He was saying, "Pil rip his liver out." He did not know the prisoner, and did not think that he was referring to him. He came up to him and said, " Now, Davy," to which wit- ness replied. "Go home, man, there's no one here that wants you." Prisoner then rushed at him, and stabbed him on the left arm. He pushed him away, but he again rushed at him,and struck him on the left shoulder, main which he (witness) exclaimed, "I am stabbed." He fell, but got up, again. The prisoner ran away to his own house. He felt ' a pain in his shoulder, and had lost a large quantity of blood. He afterwards found that he had been :tabbed on the arm and the shoulder. He went to Dr. McDonnell's surgery and had his wounds dressed. He could not explain why the prisoner attacked him.—Margaret Mullineux, a married woman, living at 16, Beaumont-street, gave evi- dence in corroboration of the above statement. She added that prisoner had been fighting with another man named Davy, on Saturday afternoon, and that Woodyer lived with Davy.—Dr. McDonnell said about a quarter to eleven on Saturday night the man Woodyer came to his surgery and complained of having been stabbed. On examination he found that he was suffering from two wounds. One was a large incised wound, about three inches long and three inches deep. on the back part on the left arm, which was bleeding freely. The other was in the anterior part of the rigbt arm, about the middle of it. This was also an incised wound, but superficial. It was bleeding. The large wound be stitched up. He was in a very weak condition, and had evidently lost a considerable quantity of blood. The large wound was in a dangerous position, but the smaller one was not so dangerous. He had examined the shirt produed, and found a hole in it corresponding to the wound in the shoulder. A knife like the one produced would be able to inflict such injuries. They were undoubtedly stabs. He was of opinion that great force must have been used, and it would be some time before the man would be able t resume work. Even if the wounds took a favourable turn it would be ten days or a fortnight.—P.C. Cummins deposed to ap- prehending the prisoner on Saturday evening, in his lodg-4 ings, at 64, Beaumont-street, where he searched him, and found the pen-knife produced in his right-hand trousers pocket.—ln reply to the charge, prisoner said, "I was drunk at the time; I did not intend to stab anyone."—Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the assizes.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. P. Speakman, chairman, presided, and there were present— Messrs. R. Shaw, Dobson, Grice, Pritchard, Pnison, Taylor, Farrell, White, Lake, Dr. McDougall (medical officer), W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marsjlall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: 'MEDIC tL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: 'MEDIC tL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths registered during the last month amounted to twenty-five. One was an inquest case, and of the remaining twenty-four three were due to consumption, three to convulsions, two to croup, two to senile decay, two to inflammation of the lin- ing membrane of the brain, two to bronchitis, two to measles, two dropsy, and one each to paralysis, rheumatic fever, congestion of the lungs, premature birth, disease of blood, and one of uncertain origin. The above twenty-five deaths showed an average death-rate for the twelve months of 18 per 1,000 of the estimand popz.lation.—The Surveyor said the number of deaths during the corresponding month last year was 4G.

div.head: HIGHWAY BUSINESS.
div.p: HIGHWAY BUSINESS.

The minutes of the Highway aRi Sanitary Committee contained the following :—Resolution, "that a sub-com- mittee be formed, consisting of Messrs. Lightburn, Speak- man, Grice, and Farrell, to take into consideration the closing of the road to Weston Point, known as Chadwick'e- lane, and to take evidence relative thereto; and to report to the committee the result of their investigations." It was also resolved that a sub-committee be formed, consisting of Messrs. Lightburn, Speakman, Grice, and Farrell, for the purpose of considering the advisability of the Board com- municating with the London and North-Western R tilway Company with a view to induce them to construct a foot bridge or sub-way at the railway station.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported that during April the receipts amounted to £37 Is 2d, and accounts amounting to £205 9s 3d were passed for payment.

div.head: WATERLOO BRIDGE.
div.p: WATERLOO BRIDGE.

It was resolved that instructions be given to the surveyor to wait upon Mr. Holmes with reference to the prop.sed alterations to Waterloo Bridge. and that he report to the next meeting of the Waterloo Bridge Committee.

div.head: DANGERS OF WESTON POINT.
div.p: THE DANGERS OF WESTON POINT.

Mr. Lightburn said since the construction of the Weston Canal there had been about fifty persons drowned. There was no safe road to Weston Point, and be urged that the committee appointed to deal with the closing of C hadwick's- lana should also consider the advisability of making a road to Weston Point, which would be not only safe for the in- habitants but for traffic.—The Chairman said the committee would no doubt meet Mr. Lightburn's desires.

div.head: INTERNLTIONAL EXHIBITION.
div.p: THE INTERNLTIONAL EXHIBITION.

The secretary to the committee of the Liverpool Inter- national Exhibition wrote to the chairman asking the permission of the Board to erect one or two of the large ex- hibition posters in prominent positi6ns near the Duhlic buildings in Runcorn.—The permission was ieforrually granted.

PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE LIBRA.RY. Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian,wrote t--"I am desired by the Runcorn Free Public Library Committee to submit the fol- lowing report on the need for extension of the Library pre- mises. During the last winter the reading-room has been in- conveniently crowded with readers who have greatly appre- ciated the boon accorded them, and year committee having given the matter a great amount of consideration is of opinion that there is pressing used of extension; and the constant accession of new books to the Library have pro- duced an equally pressing necessity for increased eccom- modation. The committee begs to submit the accompany- ing plan of the extension which, in its opinion, will be feasible, and if carried out will meet the demands of b.lth departments for some time to:come, and urges its favourable consideration."—Mr. Lake moved, as the chairman of the Free Library Committee, that the letter and the accom- panying plan be referred to the Finance Committee, and that such committee report to the Board whether the ac- commodation should be made with estimates and plans at their earliest convenience. He said be could quite bear out what Mr. Jones said. The reading-room especially dur- ing the last winter had been uncomfortably crowded. The reading-room ought to be twice its present size. Tben the Lib- rary space was almost exhausted. Almost all the shelves were occupied, and:when they got this year's new books in there would not be room to turn. Further accommodation should be provided for both reading room and library, and he im- pressed upon the Commissioners the necessity of loosing no time in dealing with the subject. He pointed out that there was in hand the sum of £1,200 which was at present unpro- ductive, and he suggested that part of that sum might be devoted for the purpose required. The alterations would be alterations in the town's property, and therefore he thought the money should come out of the town's funds and not out of the library rate.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the proposition.—Mr. Shaw contended that the Library Committee should bear the cost. —Mr. Imison said the esti- mated coat of the alterations would probably be about £lOO, Borrowed for 30 years, the repayments of principal and interest would be X.as 15s a yeti., so that if the rental of the Library Committee was increased by that amount, they would really have the addition to the building and no cost at all to the ratepayers.—The Chairman said seeing the way the library had grown they ought to look at the matter comprehensively.—The motion was carried.

THE AUDIT. Mr. Shaw said the auditor was about t make his appear- ance, and be asked were the books properly balanced.—The Chairman: Yes —Mr. Shaw: When were they balanced.— The Chairman said the books were balanced either on the 27th or the 28th March.—Mr. Shaw said that was immedi- ately after the close of the year, and he thought it was very satisfactory. Such a thing had not occurred within his recollection as a Commissioner, and it reflected very great credit upon the secretary—(hear, bear)—that the work had been done in the way it had. They ought tl congratu- late themselves that they did not need to be afraid of the auditor.

THE BOARD IN A FIX. Mr. Lightburn said he wished to bring before the Board very sincerely the question of signing cheques. Some mem- bers of the Board woull not under any circumstances sign a cheque, and the cheque-book was handed over to one or two month after month. His idea was that a resolution of the Board was sufficient authority, and bound every mem- ber equally as much as each signer.—Mr.Linaker. said every member who recorded his vote for a cheque being signed L was liable to be charged in a surcharge.—Mr. Lightburn

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

A CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—There is a movement on foot for forming a Conifirvative Club in Widnes. NEW POORS' RATE FOR NORTON.—The Runcorn magis- trates on Monday signed a poor rate of 10d in the 1 to re- alise £284 14s lid for the township of Norton. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH BIBLE CLASS.—The members had their annual tea party on Tuesday evening, when about one hundred persons were present. An enjoyable waning was spent. CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—In aid of the funds to give the scholars their annual summer treat, a concert was given in Holy Trinity Boys' School, on Wednesday night,, before a fair audience. Mr. W. Hankinson presided. A GIRL INJURED AT WIDNES.—Annie Earne, the young daughter of Mr. W. Earne, of Witt-road, had one of her legs broken in two places on Saturday afternoon by falling from a plank which was being moved "see-saw." HOLY TRINITY Y.M.C.A.—The twelfth annual meeting was held on Monday, Mr. J. Jervis in the chair. The Sec- retary's report showed that the association was in a prosper- ous condition. Mr. Henry West was appointed secretary. ACCIDENT AT FRODSHA.M.—On Monday, as a man named Peter Andrews was storing some laths in an outbuilding at Mr. S. Andrews', a portion of the flooring gave way, and be sustained a fractured leg and other injuries. Medical assist- ance was obtained, and the patient is progressing satisfac- torily. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES —The Rev. R. Yeatman en Sunday morning preached an impressive sermon on the subject "Not dead but sleepeth," in which he made special reference to the death of Mrs. Ratcliffe, a former member of the congregation. In the evening the rev, gentleman preached on " Eternal life." "A GLANCE AT THE PEACOCE."—This was the subject of the Rev. R. G. Hughes' address to workingmen and their wives in Milton Congregational Church, Simm's-cross, on Sunday evening. The rev, gentleman's discourse, wnich was directed chiefly against gorgeous dress and showy people in general, was listened to by a large congregation. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The anniversary sermons of this school were held at St. Paul's Chapel on Sunday. The preacher was the Rev. Dr. Nichol- son. On Monday evening the Rev. James Crabtree, of Man- chester, preached the 3ermon. At each service hymns specially selected for the occasion were sung. The collec- tions amounted to about £4l. WIDNES LIBERALS.—The following reply has been re- ceived from Mr. Gladstone in response to a resolution passed unanimouslyAt a public meeting held in Widnes on the 28th April :—" 10, Downing-street. Whitehall, May 4th, 1886. Sir,--I am desired by Mr. Gladstone to thank you for the communication with which you have favoured him on behalf of a Liberal meeting held at Widnes.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, (Signed) G. W. SPENCER- LYTELLTON. E. K. Muspratt, Esq." Lerma{ OF A SCHOONER AT RuNcorar.—ln the presence of a large number of spectators, a new three-masted schoo- ner was on Tuesday launched from the ship-building yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co. The vessel, which is of excep- tionally strong build, was constructed under special survey and classed 13 years Al at Lloyd's. The dimensions are length 103 feet, breadth 24 feet 3 inches, depth 11 feet one inch. The gross tonnage is 159 49'100 ; net registered ton- nage, 145 tons; carrying capacity, 300 tons. As the vessel left the ways she was christened "Despatch " by Miss H. Davies, of Rhyl, neice of the captain, and there were the usual exhibitions of rejoicing. The designer. Mr. John S. Devies, and the builders, Messrs. Brundrit and Co., are to be congratulated upon the completion of so admirable an addition to the Runcorn fleet. The Despatch has been built to the order of several local gentlemen, and Mr. Davies will act as ship's husband. The first voyage will be to Irvine. Instead of giving the men the customary dinner, Messrs. Brundrit will treat the men to a day at the Liverpool Inter- national exhibition.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.—The annual concerts by the band of the training ship Indefatigable in aid of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Sea- men, took place on Tuesday. In the afternoon the concert was given to children and aged people; and by the invita- tion of Mr. Shaw the children from the Union Workhouse at Dutton were present. The latter were afterwards pro- vided with tea at the Duke of Westminster's Cocoa Rooms, the cost of which was defrayed by Dr. McDougall. In the evening they were conveyed to the Workhouse in waggon- ettes, the cost of which was borne by several gentlemen. The audience in the evening was of fairly large proportions, and Mr. P. Speakman occupied the chair. In the course of a brief address, he referred to the good accomplished by the missions in general, and Mr. Shaw, the Runcorn missionary, its particular. The programme consisted of instrumental and vocal music of a sentimental and humourous char- acter. and the youthful performers were frequently recalled. Mr. Smith, the headmaster, and Mr. W. Tapsfield, who ac- companied, are to be congratulated on the success of their training. RUNCORN SCAOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held yesterday under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Present—Messrs. Pritchard, Hazleharst, Lea, Imison, and Rigby (clerk.) Owing to the serious illness of Mr. Bowyer, the senior visitor, Mr. Samuel Inglesfleld was appointed assistant visitor pro tem, at a salary of £1 per week. Mr. George Howard was appointed a permanent visitor at a salary of £lO per annum. The Clerk read a letter from the secretary to the managers of Trinity School with reference to the letter written by Mr. Annett contain- ing expressions which the Board did not consider consistent with their dignity. The managers said Mr. Annett did not consult them in writing the communication, the style of which they did not approee. Mr. Annett had explained that what he wrote was net intended for the Board, but for the school visitor. There were enclosed several cases of complaint for the Board to look into. One complaint was that the neighbourhood of Trinity School had been unneces- sarily posted with bills announcing the opening of Green- way Board Schools. The letter stated that there was no necessity for posting bills near their premises. A second complaint was that Bowyer, the visitor, had made dispar- aging remarks with reference to Trinity School, and had advised a woman to remove her children to the Beard school.-r Mr. Pritchard said the bill poster was entirely re- sponsible for the posting of the bills, The Board knew that Mr. Bowyer, who had been visitor for 11 years, would not make the remarks to narents attributed to him.—The Clerk said Mr. Bowyer had given the charge a flat denial.—There was no other business. MAY DAY AT WIDNES.—May Day was recognised in the. usual fashion at Widnes. The May Day Association offered prizes for the best turn-outs in various classes of horses and vehicles, and the various tradesmen competed. The com- petitors assembled on the vacant ground in Lugsdale-road, and the judging was done by Messrs. William Turton, Burntmill Farm, Hale Bank; John Kenwright, Tarbock, Tarbock ; and Mr. Johnson, Bold Hall, Bold. The result was as follows :—Class 1: Manufacturers' Double Draught Horses: 1 Messrs J Muspratt and Sons chemical manufacturers ; 2 W Smith, ironfounder, Lugsdale.—Class 2: Manufacturers' Single Draught Horses: 1 Widnes Locil Board; 2 London and North-Western Railway, Goods De- partment; 3 Mr Peter Longton, Ditton Brewerv.—Class 3: Manufacturers' Double Cobs: No competition. Mr 'l' Edwardson, mineral water manufacturer, Simm's Cross.— Class 4: Manufacturers' Single Cobs: 1 Widnes Local Board ; 2 Mr Peter Longton ; 3 Mr T Edwardson.—Class 5: Contractors and Cart•Owners' Double Draught Horses: No competition. Mr Thomas Astles.--Class 6: Ditto Single Draught Horses: 1 Mr James Holmes, Anne-street Eist ; 2 Messrs R Evans and Co., coal merchants' 3 Mr J Wade.— Class 7: Ditto Double sobs : No entries.—Class 8 : Ditto Single Cobs: 1 Mrs E Hulme, Widnes' 2 James Hulme, coal merchant.—Class 9 : Tradesmen's Business Tnrnouts (13 hands or over): 1 Mr H Turner, Wellington Hotel; 2 Mr C Hemingway, contractor; 3 Mr W Appleton.—Class 10: Ponies: Mr T Parry, milk dealer; 2 Mr J Parry.— Class 11 : Donkeys:' 1 Mr F Dillon; 2 Mr Barnett Dutton, auctioneer.—The various turnouts gaily bedecked with rib- bons then went in procession through the streets of the town, and attracted some attention. The prizes were in the form of orders upon tradesmen. KAY'S COMPOUND, for Coughs and Colds, is equally service- able for Hems and Cattle. 91d, is lid. and 24 ed.—Advt.

div.head: SHIM CANAL BILL: IMPORTANT OMISSION.
div.p: THE SHIM CANAL BILL: IMPORTANT OMISSION.

Mr. Pritchard asked the law clerk if be was prepared to inform the Board how it was that an important clause was omitted from the Ship Canal Bill after the Parliamentary and Legal Committee had left it in his bands to be in- serted with the other clauses that bad been agreed to by the promoters of the bill.—The Law Clerk said be could add nothing to what he had already stated to the committee.— The Chairman said he should be sorry for this question to be raised publicly. It bad been submitted to a committee of the whole Board, and consideration deferred until further information was obtained.—The Law Clerk said, as they knew, all the negotiations took place in London. He should be in London in a fortnight, and would have an opportunity of getting the exact facts of what took place between Mr. Dyson, of the Ship Canal Company, and his (Mr. Linaker's) Parliamentary agents. This concluded the business.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

This has been a very remarkable week in the House of Commons. Business was resumed on Monday in the presence and with the assistance of something critically near a quorum of members. Mr. Gladstone was net present, and did not reach London till nearly four o'clock on Tuesday. His consequent absence from the ceremony of the open- ing of the Exhibition has been gracefully commen- ted on in Conservative circles, where it is more than hinted that he did not put in an appearance because the cheers which greeted him at the ceremony of last year were varied by some slight hissing. The reason which alike prevented Mr_ Gladstone from taking part in the ceremony of Tuesday and kept, Mrs. Gladstone away from the Queen's drawing- room on Wednesday, was the death of Mrs. Lyttle- ton. Announcement of this cause was publicly made on Monday, and it is difficult to believe it was not within the knowledge of the newspapers which suggest the other reason. But, as we know, Tory animosity to Mr. Gladstone is not bounded by considerations of fact.

The attendance in the House of Common's through- out the week has been unusually small, a circum- stance attended by the accustomed corollary of the rapid disposal of business. On Monday all the Sup- ply placed upon the paper was granted, leaving Mr. Fowler lamenting that he had not added another class or two. On Tuesday the House was counted out, and yesterday it rose a little after four, having advanced many bills a stage. The fact is the ordin- ary course of Parliamentary business is regarded with absolute indifference. All attention is concen- trated on the question of the Government of Ireland Bill. The Speaker must take the chair at the ap- pointed hour. The ordinary business of the House must go forward; but members do not care even to put in an appearance, and those present, with a single exception, are cpntent to look on in silence whilst bills advance and motions are agreed to. The exception is found in Lord Randolph Churchill, who from time to time startles a quiet assembly by going off like an ill-regulated cracker. Thus on Monday he broke the silence of the place, and thus on Wed- nesday he suddenly fell upon Mr. Childers and be- laboured him for a crime the Home Secretary had never committed.

Meanwhile negotiations are going forward with the object of settling the differences between Mr. Chamberlain and his late colleagues in the Cabinet. As I have explained in a former letter, there is no direct communication between Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain. Mr. Chamberlain communicates his views to a member on the Liberal side. This gentleman has confidential communications with Mr. Herbert Gladstone. The Prime Minilter casu- slly becoming acquainted with the case, says what he has to say to his son, who repeats it to the mem- ber who communicates with Mr. Chamberlain. It is a curious way of conducting business. But it answers, and conveniently leaves high contracting parties free from responsilility. The end of it will, I venture to think, be reconciliation, and. we shall have Mr. Chamberlain and his following, which is numerically not large, voting for the second reading of the Bill. Mr. Chamberlain's ultimatum is that a pledge should be given to provide for the repre- sentation of Irish members in the Imperial Parlia- ment. Mr. Gladstone has an open mind on the point, which finds strong opponents in the persons of Sir William Harcourt and Mr. John Morley. But I think both these gentlemen will be found open to acceptance of the compromise. As to the future of the bill itself, it may be safely forecasted. It will pass the second reading by a majority of not less than twenty. It will come to grief upon some point in Committee, and the Go- vernment will quietly accept the rebuff, promising to reintroduce the bill next year. They may do this with a light heart, for surely it is a great achieve- ment that in a single session the House of Commons should be brought to approve the principle of Home Rule in Ireland. That once granted, an Act of Par- ment embodying it is a matter of another session, or at most, two.

The opening of the Col-Indiaries, on Tuesday, was in every respect, save one, a success. The day was fine, the Queen was in a good humour (Sir Wm. Harcourt will never forget the day she opened the new Law Courts), the crowd was enormous, and the pageant most striking. Everybody who is anybody seemed to be present in the brilliant throng that surrounded the dais. Only Mr. Gladstone was ab- sent, excused, as already mentioned, on account of the death of Mrs. Lyttleton, the fair young bride who died the other day within a year of her mar- riage. Doubtless it was the association of the cere- mony with the name of the Prince Consort winch so far worked upon the gracious humour of the Queen , that she read the speech prepared for her. It has , been my fortune for some years to be present when- ever the Queen has taken part in public cere- monies. But never before have I heard her voice. When she opens Parliament, she invariably delegates to the Lord Chancellor the task of readingthe Queen's speech "in Her Majesty's own words." On Tuesday she read every word of the reply to the address the Prince of Wales had recited, and people sitting in the remotest corners of the vast hall tell me they heard every word. The failure alluded to is the ode which Lord Tenny- son contributed. The promiseof the Poet Laureate's December has only once, as far as I remember, risen above the promise of May. At worst his verse will always scan, and runs with brook-like smoothness. But w'mat is to be made of the seventh line of the second verse--
And where'er her flag may fly, Glorying between sea and sky?

The " Standard " came out on Monday without a report of the speeches at the Royal Academy din- ner, an incident regarded in some quarters as a cur- ious omission of editorial arrangement. It was, however, designedly done, and is a course that has been adopted for several years now. According to the old-fashioned and autocratic arrangements of theißoyal Academicians, there is only one paper in England, and that is the " Times." A "Times" re- porter is accordingly invited to the feast of resson and flow of soul which follows upon the removal of the cloth. Consequently the "Times" was at a former epoch the only paper that had an account of the proceedings. When they grew in importance, a modification was made, the "Times" reporter being enjoined to publish his account first in the " Observer " whence other papers take it. When Mr. Mudford assumed direction of the "Standard," he resented this invidious arrangement. A repor- ter should be sent from the "Standard " if he were invited to the dinner; otherwise no report would appear in that paper. The committee of the Academy have maintained their system, and Mr. Mudford has stood by his resolution. The "Stan- dard" reporter is not invited to the dinner, and the "Standard' gives no report of the speeches. I am sorry to say that Mr. Mudford is left alone in this stand against the priggishness of the Royal Aca- demy. If the other London penny papers were to

follow his example, the nonsensical, not to say int pertinent, arrangement would be altered before next May. In the meantime, the greater is Mr. 3fudford's honour in standing alone upon the dignity of the Press. • _ _

An a-musing story of the late Archbishop of Dub- lin is just now going the rounds. Dr. Trench was at a dinner party, and after the ladies had left the room conversation amongst the men became very animated. Contrary to his wont., the Archbishop scarcely spoke. At last, however, he broke silence. " I've found it,"- he said, excitedly, "I've found it." "Found what, my lord," asked several curates, in still greater excitement. "My sense of touch," he said. "For the last six minutes I've been pinching my leg, and I could feel nothing." There was general relief, as it looked as if the poor old hierarch might have had a 'stroke of paralysis. But it was not till the next day the whole truth came out. A clergyman had been sitting next the Archbishop during this after dinner incident, and it was that clergyman's leg, and not his own, that for six consecutive minutes had been pinched. so anxiously and relentlessly by the unsuspecting prelate. The clergyman never flinched nor uttered. a moan. He suffered in silence. Even when the trial of .his fortitude was over, and the Archbishop had, to the unspeakable relief of both, found his own leg, he kept his counsel and his peace. No doubt if Dr. Trench had lived much longer, recogni- tion would have followed this act of conspicuous bravery. There is no Victoria cross possible to any clergy except army chaplains. But I hope Lord Plunkett will remember this parson, and that pro- motion may come where it has certainly been de- served.

The London milliners are in despair. Their trade (like all trades) was depressingly low, but they cer- tainly did not expect the kind of competition to which they have been subjected. The French com- plain of the Germans and the Americans of the Chinese, but at least that was the competition of their fellow creatures. There are things may be borne from a woman or even from a man that is in- sufferable from an insect. It seems that the corals, not content with upsetting geography and making new islands in old oceans, have now, animated by a cruel desire to crush London milliners, taken to making bonnets. I would not believe them capable of it if I had not seen the bonnets. They are like the finest open work straw and in all colours, old gold and beetle green and jetty black. They are to be a rage this season, and are certainly the very latest novelty. As yet, however, Parliament has taken no notice of them, but certainly a question should be asked in the louse. These insects must ke kept in their proper places. They may build as many islands as they like in the Pacific, but the British milliner is not to be trifled with.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JAMES MUSPRATT.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JAMES MUSPRATT.

We regret to have to record the death of Mr. Jas. Muspratt, the founder of the important alkali in-. dustry which in Liverpool, St. Helens, and Newton at one time provided material for a long series of lawsuits, and in Liverpool, St. Helens, and Newton, and finally in Flint, has given employ- ment to many hundreds of men and sustenance to their families. Mr. 31uspratt died on Tuesday, at Seaforth Hall, Seaforth, the comfortable residence which he built for himself many years ago, but which has recently been occupied by his son, Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division at the last election. He had reached the advanced age of ninety-three years, but was in pos- session of his strong and characteristic faculties to the end. He had been in failing health for some months, and his decease was not unexpected. Mr. James Muspratt was born in Dublin on the 12th of August, 1793. His parents were in comfortable cir- cumstances, and educated their son at a good com- mercial school in Dublin. His natural quick- ness and love of learning soon enabled him to carry off prizes for all the sub- jects in which he received instruction. His parents died about the year 1811, and, having been apprenticed to an apothecary and drug mer- chant, he learned chemistry. He commenced a chemical works in Dublin, where he manufactured several chemicals, such as acetic acid, prussiate of potash, &c. • but having conceived the idea that the making of soda from common salt would be pro-. fitable, he came to Liverpool in 1822, and brought the works in Vauxhall-road, and so soon as he had obtained sufficient capital erected plant for the man- ufacture of soda or alkali, which he commenced at a large scale in 1823. At first there was great pre- judice against the use of the so-called artificial. soda, but as it was both stronger and cheaper than the soda made from kelp, the soapmakers began to use it, and in alew years the demand outgrew the sup- ply. To meet this demand Mr. Muspratt erected works in St. Helens, in partnership with Mr. John Gamble; and about the year 1831, at Newton, half- way between Liverpool and Manchester, on the newly-opened railway. .Both in Liverpool and Newton he had to sustain actions for dam- ages and nuisance, in some of which he was successful, but finally had to close the works in. Liverpool and remove the Newton works to Flint and Widnes. During this litigation the condensation of the muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid) was much improved, and by degrees the nuis- ance effectually removed. For many years he re- mained the largest manufacturer, and increased the size of his works very rapidly. The trade is now one of great importance, and, till the development of the ammonia-soda process of late years, a fairly profitable one. The ammonia-soda process itself was worked on a large scale by Mr. Muspratt many years ago, but at that time, owing to defective plant, the loss of ammonia was so great that the older Leblanc method was moie profitable. De- ceased took an active part in the public life of , Liverpool in conjunction with Sir J. Walmsley, Mr. George Holt, the late Mr. William Rathbone, and others, particularly in connection with the Mechan- ics' Institute. He was-always a staunch free trader and supporter of the Anti-corn Law League. An intimate friend of Baron Liebig, he was chosen by that distinguished chemist to put his theories of agriculture into practice by the manufacture of ar- tificial manures, a manufacture which is now of great importance and extent. He lived a compar- tively retired life at his residence. Seaforth Hall, for the last 25 years, as most of his old friends had pas- sed away, and his sons undertook the management of the business. Dr. Sheridan Muspratt died ten years ago, and Mr. Richard Muspratt last year at Flint.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The interment of the remains of the late Mr. Jas. Muspratt, of Seaforth Hall, took place on Friday, at St, Mary's Church, Walton. The funeral was of a private character. The coffin was made of polished. oak, with heavy brass mountings, and it was com- pletely enveloped in floral tributes of respect and. sorrow. It bore the inscription: "James Muspratt. Born August 12th, 1703. Died May 4th, 1886," and. was placed in the family grave at the north-east corner of the churchyard. The service, both in the church and at the grave, was read by the Rev. S. C. Armour. The cortege was as follows :—First carriage, Messrs. Edmond K. Muspratt, James Muspratt, Sydney .Muspratt, and Rev. S. C. Armour; second. (Mrs 3.luspratt's, of the /lollies). Mr. and Mrs Blake, and Mr. and Mrs Harley; third (Mr. Richard Mus- pratt's), Mrs Richard Muspratt, Mrs Edmund K. Muspratt, and Master Muspratt: fourth (Mr. A. B. Forwood's), Messrs. Frederick Muspratt, B. C. Ro- berts, and Gorst ; fifth (Sir W. B. Forwood's), Messrs. Richard Roberts and M. W. Armour, Drs. Lowndes and Bickersteth ; sixth (Mr. J. B. Smith's), Messrs. J. B. Smith, Lister, and Rayner; seventh (Mr. niter's), Messrs. Banister, Dyson, and Dew- ham; eighth (Mr. Sydney Muspratt's), Messrs. Mur- ray, Lea, and Bolton. The funeral arrangements were in charge of Messrs. Bacon, Bold-street.

Say, Brothers, Stockport.—.Advt WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.—The report of this institution for the year 1885 has just been published, from which it appears that the number of students in residence is reported to be 106, viz., 55 seniors an.' 51 juniors. The report gives the result of the Government examination for certifi- cates, held in December, in all 109 certificates hav- ing been obtained against 56 last year. Thirty- three seniors were presented for examination in the elements of agriculture, and all passed—ten in the first-class and the remainder in the second. Six seniors also passed in botany. 11.31. Inspector, Canon IVarburton, assisted by several other,' inspec- tors, paid his annual visit to the college on June 16th. Canon Warburton met the committee on June 22nd. His report was satisfactory. He warmly approved the zeal and vigour of the principal. The staff was strong and satisfactory, and well reported of. The method of teaching and the instruction in cookery and drill were much commended. The students had been examined in inusie by Dr. _ Stainer, as listed by Mr. McNaught, and all passed, twenty of the seniors being classed "excellent," and eight of them obtaining full marks. div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT, MoNDay.—Before the :`,Jay or .(Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, Councillor Greening, and Dr. Gornall. TIM2ITENIZTC4 A WlFE.—Thomas Anderton was charged onsa warrant with using malicious threati towards his wife en the let of May.—Complainant said that she had been married to prisoner 15 years, and dcring that time he bad only, worked about three years. On 0-e day in question he went to his wife, who had been living apart from him, and threatened to throttle her and throw her into the street.— He was ordered to tied two sureties in 25 each, or go to prison for six months in default. ABSE`NTEAS.—WaIter Bevan, charged with absenting him- self from the training of the Warwick Militia during 1885. He was fined 40s and costs, or one month's imprisonmett in default —Michael Grady, charged with being an absentee from the 22nd Regi,r,ent of Foot, stationed at Chester, since

Saturday last, was remanded to await escort. A DRUNKEN ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Attwood, who eaid he came from Craelley, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Scetland-road, on Saturday night, and assault- ing, John Marsh, manager of the -Scotland-road vaults. Prisoner was refused on asking to be served with drink, whereupon he picked up four glasses of beer and threw them at the manager. He was fined 20s and costs, or one , month's imprisonment. THE EXAMINER, SNTURDAT, MAY 8, 1886.

but be had not the least doubt those present were quite as I well informed regarding it as himself. After speaking fur- her on the subject of Ireland, and thanking the electors of the division for the address, Colonel McCotquodale said that he firmly believed that Mr. Gladstone •vas actuated by a sense of duty at the present crisis. (Applause.) At the advanced period of his (Mr. Gladstone's) illustrious life, he , could not have any motive but the good of his country. Now that the subject had been taken up it could not be al- lowed to slumber. (Hear, hear.) The Irish were entitled to attention, and we in England wanted time to attend to English and Scotch business. He fervently trusted that the subject would be carefully and faithfully considered,- that Heaven would guide the counsels of our statesmen, and that while upholding the integrity of the Empire, laws would be passed to secure the peace, prosperity, and happiness of our brethren in Ireland. (Cheers.) The CHAIRMAN then read letters regretting inability to be present from Sir Thomas Brocklebank, Colonel Gamble, JP., Mr. Joseph Evans, J.P., Mr. Sinclair, Mr. Holt, Mr. Pilkington, and others.

Mr. WILLIAM CIIOSFIELD, Liheral candidate for Warring- ton at the last election, rose to propose a resolution. After referring at some length to the long services and great popularity of Colcnel McCorquodale, Mr. Crosfield said it was by such men that the public life of the country was brightened and enriched. (Applause.) They younger men valued Colonel McCorquodale because they found" in him an example of She way in which they might conduct themselves. (Applause,) Colonel McCrequodale, he believed, had throughout his life been identified with questions of public interest, which bad been for the ad- vancement of the people, and as they looked at his long and hon. career they younger men hoped that it might be given to them to do as be had done. (Cheers.) He then proposed "That this meeting records its continued eonfi- &ince in Her Majesty's Government, and ,trusts that the Irish measures introduced by Mr. Gladstone may he found to afford a sound le. for the permanent and satisfactory settlement of Irish difficulties." (Cheers ) Having re- ferred to the influence of the Irish qustion at the recent election, Mr. Crosfielci said they would all unhesitatingly affirm that the time had come for some de- cided action to he taken by the Government. The cendi- firm of Ireland had been the cause of grief and sadnere to to them for many years—the question was always coming to the front ad always requiring settlement of some kind or another—and the time was arrived when it shcruld be finally, so far as anything human bad finality in it, settled. and that our fellow &jeans across tee Irish channel should have a fair chance of developing their resources, and of making themselves great as England had done under the political advantages in which we ourselves lived. (Cheers.) England, in her treatment of the Irish nation, had been sowing the whirlwind, and should be thankful that now statesmen had an opportunity of reaping a peaceful harvest. They had now come to the parting of the ways. They could go on in the way which they would agree with him should be abandoned, or they could diverge from the road in which they were at present walking, and might allow Ireland to govern itself in the way which it thought right, guided to some extent by the wisdom of the Imperial Parliament with safeguards that the country should not entirely run away with itself in its early enthusiasm of self-government. (Cheers) They had confidence in trust- ing these measures with Mr. Gladstone, because he had a thorough sympathy with the Irish nation. The man who had done so much to bring other nations into being was the one that could do most to bring this new nation into life. (Cheers.) Mr. BAMTLINS briefly seconded the motion. The resolution was supported by Mr. Kennedy (Birken- head), who urged the Liberals of that division to again seek the candidature of Colonel McCotquodale, and said if Mr. Gladstone was not able to settle the Irish question no man in the whole of the country was able to settle it. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was carried unanimously amid cheers. The Rev. F. N. Snietsiter moved a vote of thanks to the committee who had charge of the arrangements for the pre- sentation, which was warmly passed, and Mr. B. Harrison (secretary to the committee) responded on behalf of the ' committee.
Colonel MCCORQUODALE proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, which was seco,lded by Mr. P. HALL, and carried.—The CHAIRMAN acknowledged the compliment, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL COUNCIL. DISCUSSION ON TIIE HOME RULE. SCHEME.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL COUNCIL. DISCUSSION ON TIIE HOME RULE. SCHEME.

On Wednesday evening a crowded meeting of the Warrington Liberal Council was held in the Club premises, Bewsey-street, for the purpose of consi- dering the Irish proposals of the Government. The chair was taken by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., and amongst the large number present were Mr. John Crosfield, J.P. (the Liberal candidate for Warring- ton), Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P., the Rev. R. Filcher, B.A. the Rev. E. Moore, Dr. Gornall, J.P., Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., Mr. F. A. Roberts, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mr. J. Walker, Mr. H. J. Fleming, Mr. T. Birchall, &c.

The SECRETARY (Mr. H. Roberts) read letters of apology for non- attendance from Mr. F. Monks, J.P., and the Rev. J. Yonge. Mr. Monks expressed his regret that be could not be present to gives his own views in reference to the two bills now before the country. He could not approve of Home Rule Bill until better protection was given to the loyal minority; and as to the Land Bill he did not think it a sound principle to buy out Irish landowners in order to convert the tenants into landlords. The Rev. J. Yonge, in his letter, cordially supported the proposals of the Govern- ment. and said had he been present he should gladly have supported the strongest possible resolution in favour of Mr. Gladstone's scheme of Home Rule. (Applause.) He was not at all afraid that, if Horne Rule were granted, the Pro- testant minority of Ireland would be unfairly dealt with. The time for religious persecution had gone, and in the Irish national movement the people had led the priests and not the priests the people. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was greeted with loud applause, said it had been thought wise and proper that that council, re- presenting as it did the Liberal party in Warrington, should assemble together and pronounce its opinion upon these great measures introduced in reference to the government of Ireland, and it was in accordance with that wish they as- sembled together that night. In a matter like that it was not at all necessary that they should be unanimous or that the country should be unanimous. (Hear, hear.) About one thing, he dare say they all agreed, and that was that the Liberal party was in the midst of a great crisis, and that they were face to face with a secession greater in number and in- fluence than ever betel the Liberal party before. But when he consielered the conduct of Lord Hartington, Mr. Cham- berlain, Mr. Goschen, Mr. Trevelyan, and some more obscure members of their party, he found noihing to blame. Every- body bad a perfect right to judge for himself as to the wis- dom of any policy that might be recommended, and he con- ceived that those gentlemen were quite within their right in taking the course which they had done. (Hear, hear.) But while they admitted that members of that prominence had left them for the present, it would be a mistake if they forgot that they had a still larger number of statesmen with them of at least equal ability, and that at the bead of those gentlemen was a man: the greatest statesman of our day in Europe. (Loud applause.) When they con- sidered that Mr. Gladstone was surrounded by men like Lord Granville, Lord Spencer (applause) Sir William Harcouit, Mr. Childers, Mr. Campbell Bannerman, and Mr. John Morley—(applause)—and others, they most see that on a question of authority even—and upon his (the chairman's) word he thouglit it would come to that—they were on the stronger side. (Hear. hear.) Now there was a good deal to be said in reference to that question. It was no doubt a very difficult question;. it was one of the most difficult questions that had ever come before the Liberal party to decide about, because they heard so many prophe. cies by people who were prophets, or the sons of prophets— (leughter)—and they had so much opposition of opinion that it made it very difficult indeed for them to decide. It had not been so beiore. The Liberal party had always be- fore been called upon to support some definite object. Some of them might not remember, but they !could have read of it, that in 1823 they had before them the question of the admission of Roman Catholics to the House of Commons, and that was a matter that was very easy to decide about. It. was a matter of justice, and it was dealt with as a matter of justice. In 1832 they had the great question of ieform. The representation of tke country at that time was really no representation at all, and it was easy for them to decide whether or not towns like Manchester, Glasgow, Birming- ham, and other big places should have no representatives, while small places of ten or a dozen inhabitants were to send two uponbers to Parliament. ("Shame.") Then with regard to the question in reference to the Corn Laws, no man with a head on his shoulders really believed that if they made food cheap the csuutry would not be the better for it. It was an easy matter to decide, and so in reference to the extensions of tie fran- chise from 1832 to 185 ; these questions they found no difficulty in deciding. (Applause.) But the present question was rather a difficult question; it was a mysterious had to take a great deal upon trust. Itihehad formed his opinion on authority, and (He question,ar e a ar . eyn he was going to follow the lead of four-fifths of the Liberal party and of the great leader of the party. (Loud applause.) It might appear as though a man ought not to found his political opinions upon anything but his owe sense of what was right and what was just. well he had considered what was right and what was just, and he had come to the conclusion that he should take up his lot in the old ship under the old captain. (Loud applause.) He hoped a reselution would be passed there in support of the measure which Mr. Gladstone had intreduced. He believed himself that the bill was not final in its present shape, but whatever Mr. Gladstone proposed he thought they as mem- bers of the Liberal party ought to support. (Hear, hear.) He bad a strong hope that these measures which Mr. Gladstone proposed would be effectual in securing what they wished, and he hoped sincerely that the result would be that Ireland would be better governed, would be more contented than it has yet been, th:at the feud of centuries would be heeled, and that that emit!, which did exist be- tween the English and Irish races would be appeased, and that they should be dieposad to link with one another in all , those relations of friendliness and fraternity which the ' patriarch of old intended when he said to his young rela- tive, "Let thet o be no strife, I pray thee, between thee aed me, and between my house and thy house." (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. E. WRIGHT moved the following resolution z "That the members of the Warrington Liberal Association hereby

express their hearty sympathy with the Premier in tl-e noble effort he is making to effect a solution of the Irish question and offer him their earnest support in carrying out 1 his scheme, which, though subject to modification in some , minor points, is worthy of his great intellect and sterling I honesty." (Applauss.) With reference to the passage I "though subject to modification in some minor points," I be put it in because he was one who would not lose the bill for tke sake of a trifle. If they got five-sixths of the bill, as they had five-sixths of the votes of Ireland, they would have five-sixths of it rather than none. Having re- ferred to the vile malpractices by which the union was brought about, and to the merciless exactions of the Irish landlords, Mr. Wright said there was one thing in connec- tion with the bill, and that was that so surely as "Eastern Emperor" had won the Chester cup that day so surely would the bill of Mr. Gladstone pass. (Laughter and applause.) He also argued that the present policy of the Government was placed in a direct manner before the constituencies at the general election. In appealing to them to pase the reso- lution, be did so not because he was an Irishman or Catholic, it was not because he was a Protestant or belonged to any creed, but it was because he believed in the prin- ciple ennunciated thousands of years ego—" Do as you would like to be done by." (Applause.) It was also be- cause many years ago he took to heart the words of Mr. Gladstone, who said that the deep underlying principles of the Liberal party were trust in the people, tempered by prudence in contradiction to the creed ot Toryism, which t was distrust in the people, tempered by fear. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. DIINBOBBIN seconded the proposal. He did so, he said, because the Irish people had suffered tyranny for something like 600 years, and the time had4now come when they should do something for Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Home Rule was necessary to meet the wants of Ireland, and to bring the Irieh people to that state of quietude that was wanted. (Hear, hear.) ' Mr. H. Wetrrarier supported the proposal. He was glad, I he said, to be there on that occasion, an occasion which ought to have come six or seven years ago- He was a Home Ruler six or seven years ago, when there were very few of them. A Home Ruler then was an outcast in poli- tics. To-day the Irishmen were shcceseful, for tp a certain extent they were having more than they asked for, and more than seemed palatable to a great many of the Liberal party. The present Home Rule measure, he thought, could certainly be amended, and with regard to the Land Bill he was very much in favour of Mr. Chamberlain's views. He could not see why the landlords should have £50,000,000, or a quarter of X:50,000,000. (Hear, hear, and Oh, oh.) ' He was opposed to the parchasing of the land, but if it was to be purchased he would rather take the view of Mr. Monks. that the State should be tbe purchaser. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitham also argued that there were two classes of owners of land in Ireland. One ef those classes had never pur- chased their land nor !rorked for it, while the other had purchased their land with their savings, with money which Lad been gained legitimately. He really believed that if the former party were put to it they could not produce their title deeds. (Hear, bear, and laughter.) He thought from what he saw in the current "Freeman " that the re- ligious question was being brought a little too much for- ward by the Nationalists. This should be put on one side, and let them have religious freedom in Ireland as in Eng- land. (Hear, hear.) Religious matters were a great ob- I sticle in the way of this Irish question, but be hoped education would do a great deal to remove them. (Ap- plause.)

- Mr. E. A. BOBERST said he had been very pleased to hear Mr. Wright's speech, and he would willingly accept the resolution except for one part of it. He objected to the words "subject to modification in some minor points" be- ing inserted. He wanted to give Mr. Gladetone and his Governmeet a perfectly free hand. (Applause.) He thought very little himself of the opposition to the bills. (Hear, hear.) Unless Mr. Wright would consent to leave out the part of his resolution referred to he (Mr. Roberts) would rather ask them to support a resolution similar to that which was carried at the meeting of the National Reform Union, viz. :—" That this meeting of the Council of the Warrington Liberal Association desires to express its unabated con- fidence in Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, and to place upon record its ophaion that their proposals for the future government of Ireland form an excellent basis for the set- tlement of the Irieh difficulty, and are calculated to promote the welfare and contentment of the Irish people, and estab- lish thereby on a firm and more solid foundation the union between Great Britain and Ireland." (Applause.) He (Mr. Roberts) wanted the small minority to join the great majority, and he asked the seceders to come to them again. He was tired of waiting on the Whigs. (Hear, hear.) If the Whigs would not come with them they must stop be- hind. (Applause.) He could not agree with those who looked upon Mr. Chamberlain as the leader of the Radical party. Be did not compare Mr. Gladstone to Mr. Chamber- lain in the same breath, and he did not believe they could be compared as statesmen in the same week. (Laughter and hear, hear.) Mr. Jones CROSFIELD, who had a very cordial reception, said he thought that as they had elected him to be the Liberal candidate for Warrington, they would like to hear what he thought about that Bill. (Hear, hear.) They were aware he had been from home for three weeks. He .had been on a visit to one of the lovelisst places on earth— the island of Madeira, and he had come back to old England as ignorant of what had been going on in the country as if he had been in a balloon. There were no newspapers where he had been; there was no telegraph, and as no steamer ca4led they were in an utter state of ignorance. The Queen might have been shot, and England might have been sunk but they would not have been any the wiser. (Laughter.) He must confess, however, that he did enjoy the quiet rest and communion with nature, because in these days one sometimes got worried and hurried with news- papers and telegrams, and it was a very pleasant relief to him. The day he sailed was the 9th of April, and fortu- nately they got newspapers at Plymouth with Mr. Glad- stone's grand speech in it. (Hear, hear.) They might believe he was thankful to get it; it was a delightful thing to read on board tne steamer, and he read that magnificent speech with the greatest interest and pleasure. and when he had read it he came to the conclusion that if be went to Parliament he would support that bill. (Loud applause.) He believed in Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) He thought he was the finest statesman England ever produced—(ap- plause)—and he thought that that measure was a master- piece of statesmanship and of intellect. (Applause.) The fact was, Mr. Gladstone was constructing a new constitu- tion. Talk about dissolving the Union! It was perfect nonsense ; it would cement the Union. (Applause.) If there was to be a Union between England and Ireland there must be good feeling between the two nations. (Hear, bear.) There was not the slightest doubt in his mind that the effect of that mea- sure would be to draw England and Ireland more closely together than they had ever been before and they should see peace, contentment, and prosperity rule through- out the land. (Applause.) He was exceedingly sorry that members of their party, men that were highly respected— for he had the highest eettem for Lord Partington and he ' respected Mr. Chamberlain—did not see their way to sup- port this measure, but they could not help that. Every Liberal had a right to hie own opinion, and he did not be- lieve now that Mr. Chamberlain would vete aeainst the measure, and he believed it would be very difficult for Lord Hartington to vote against it. (" Oh.") He saw that the papers that day said Lord Hartington was wavering in his opinion, and there was no mistake about it—the great bulk of the English people were for the measure. Let Mr. Glad- appeal to the country and he would carry it by thousands. I (Loud applause.) Mr. Monks in his letter mentioned the province of Ulster, but as he (Mr. Crosfield) understood the measure Mr. Gladstone was going to have two orders, the ' one to be formed of the present Irish peers in the House of Lords and members to be elected by people living in houses worth £25 a year by which he crould secure in the Irish Parliament a good and strong representation of the Protestant element in the country. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Crosfield) could not see what more could possibly be done than that. He did not: see why they need alarm themselves about the people in Ulster. He thought the measure was fair in every way, and he should support it. (Aphlause.) Having been away, as he told them, and not having seen the newspapers, he. had not had the opportu- nity of reading Mr. Gladstone'e second speech on the Land Bill,and therefore he was not able to tell them that night what he thought about it. But he did not think there was any great hurry about that,, be- cause it would be a considerable time before they got to the Land Bill, and it was a question whether the Laud Bill would be pressed by Mr. Gladstone. There was no doubt whatever that the Land Bill was very distasteful to a good many Liberals, and he confessed that at present he did not like the thoughts of it. (Hear, hear.) But be was not going to express an opinion about it. He believed in the wisdom and the justice of Mr. Gladstone, and he did not think he would propose anything to the House of Commons that he (Mr. Crosfield) could not heartily support. (Hear, later.) He had tnerefore great pleasura in seconding Mr. Roberts' resolution, and he hoped Mr. Weight would consent to with- draw his resolution in favour of the one proposed by Mr. :Roberts. (Loud applause.) Mr. S. BARLOW supported Mr. Roberts' amendment. He believed such a bill as the present one had never before been brought before the House of Commons in the whole,of their exietence, and he believed ha reference to Ireland that Irish men would support it to a man. He did not think that it would in the slightest degree tend to disintegrate the Em- pire, and he would recommend to one leader of their party not to write letters saving that certain gentlemen were try- ing to stifle discussion.. That was Mr. Chamberlain', who had done a great deal of harm on that question. (Rear, hear.) He (Mr. %flow> was a Presbyterian, and although he believed in Presbyterianism he did not bslieve in the political opinions of the Presbyterians in the North of Ire- land. Mr. Barlow also argued against Mr. Whithant's view as to the Land Bill, and said that no. matter how certain persons originally got possession of Irish land they had handed it down to ther successors, whose rights had always been recognised. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. L. EXPLAINED.—The following is told of a well-known diner- out whose love of oysters is notorious. At a dinner party one evening oysters were duly served to him; but, when he got the fourth, he sent his plate away. The hostess, by whom he sat, observing this, expressed her concern, adding, "I assure you, they are natives 1" "I don't doubt it," he replied ; "but that last one I ate was a settler !" PERMANENT RELIEF SOCIETY FOR WARRINGTON. On Tuesday afternoon the adjourned meeting of the subscribers to the Relief Fund and others wa held in the Council Chamber at the Warringtons Town Hall, to consider the subject of forming a per- manent relief society. , The Mayor (Alderman Har- rison) occupied the chair, .and there were also present the Revs. S. Wilkinson, R. Pilcher' J Drummond, E. C. E. Carleton, and G. Anton J. Messrs. R. Davies, If. Whitham, A. Mackie, J'. Smethurst, and a number of ladies.—The Mayor, be- fore proceeding with the business of the afternopn said that he had received several letters from gentle- men who were not able to attend. Major Litton wrote that as he did not think it was advisable to have such a fund, he should be glad if his name were taken off the committee. Mr. Monks, Mr. Broadbent, the Rev. Father Fishwick, the Rev. , Father Sumner, and Mr. John White wrote saying they were not able to attend; and Mr. R. Kendrick wrote explaining the absence of his sister.—Mr. 1 Robert Davies said that, as it appeared to him, the , first question before the meeting was whether or I not a charitable committee should be established for Warrington, and if established, what the limits of such committee should be. If established the position of the committee would always be a diffi- cult one. It would have on the one hand to satisfy the wishes of those kind-hearted but incon- siderate people who seemed to desire to see every hungry person fed and every ill-clad per- son clothed at the expense of the charitable, what- ever the merits of the case might be. On the other hand they had to avoid increasing pauperism, to arrest the tendency of those limp and helpless crea- tures who were always ready to throw themselves without an effort of their own upon some one else, and to take the utmost care not to usurp in any way the duties and responsibilities of the Guardians of the Poor by relieving cases of chronic and irreme- dial destitution. He found, that there was some difference of opinion, judging by the letters the chairman had read and what he had heard in the town, but the great majority of those he had con- I suited thought that a permanent committee should be started. After reading the reports of various societies he also had come to a conclusion in favour of a permanent committee. (Hear, hear.) When he mentioned the fact that Mr. Bleckly, whose practical experience in such matters was very great, and who was not likely to be led away by mere sentiment, was a handsome subscriber to one of the societies he had mentioned, they might feel quite sure that they were justified in trying the experiment. With a view to arriving at a decision he had drawn up a number of resolutions to submit for the approval of the meeting.—The resolutions, which Mr. Davies had had printed, were then discussed. They were : "The Warrington Charity Committee. 1. That a committee be formed under the name of the War- rington Charity Committee,. 2. That the committee consist of an equal number of ladies and gentlemen (so far as may be), and that the following ladies and gentlemen, viz. : The Mayor (Alderman „Har- rison), the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, S. Wilkinson,A Father Summer, R. Pilcher, J. Yonge, J. Drummond, Messrs. F. Monks, R. Davies, 11. Whi .Smethurst, John White, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Litton, tham, 5, Miss Clara Harvey, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Fox, Mrs. William Dutton, Miss Kendrick, Mrs. Reynolds, Miss Dutton, Mrs. White, Mrs. Wilkinson, and Mrs. Allton, do form the first committee, with power to fill up vacancies, and to keep up and (if they think fit) add to their number. 3. That the composition and. objects of the committee be at all times unsec- tanan. 4. That the committee be not expected to inquireinto cases of vagrancy or ordinary street begging. 5. That one or more matrons be engaged, and a room or rooms taken for the purpose of offices, sewing classes, or other female industries as a .beginning. 6. That all cases of distress, whether arising from death, sickness, want of work, or other .causes, be in the first instance, as far as practicable, Investigated by the person recommending the same, if any, and where application shall be made by the poor persons themselves, or in cases otherwise brought to the knowledge of the committee, then by the matron or by some member of the committee. 7. That the committee do, as far as possible, work in unison with the other charitable organizations of

PRESENTATION TO COLONEL McCORQUODALE.

On Thursday evening, the Liberals of tile Newton Division paid a well-earned tribute of respect t their popular leader, Colonel George .McCorquodale, J.P., as a mark of their appreciation of his gallant fight against Sir Richard Assheton Cross, a Tory Cabinet Minister, and one who was acks;towledged as the best and strongest candidate they could pro- duce as their champion in the political contest of last December. The testimonial took the form of a splendidly illuminated address, and the announce- ment of its forthcoming presentation a short time ago aroused the utmost enthusiasm among all shades of the Liberal party. The gathering was held in the large hall of the Vilduct Institute, Earlestown, and this was a crowded and most enthusiastic audience. The Viaduct Institute Brass Band kindly volunteered their services for the occasion, and met Colonel McCorquodale and party in Colonel McCorquodale's carriage at Cross-lane. They played in front of the carriage along Cross-lane, Bridge- street, and Earle-street to the hall. The entrance of the Colonel and party was the signal for enthusi- astic cheers. The chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Pilking,ton, J.P., Chairman of the Executive of the Liberal Council of Newton Division, who was sup- ported by a large number of gentlemen and ladies. Among those present were Colonel George McCor- quodale, J.P., Mrs. McCorquodale, Miss McCorquo- dale, Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, J.P., Mr. Norman McCorquodale, Mr: Harold McCorquodale, Mr. W. T. S. Blacklock, Mrs. Blacklock, Rev. H. Sherlock, Mrs. Sherlock, Miss Hamilton, Miss Nairne, Mrs. Broadbridge, Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., late Liberal can- didate for Warrington; the Rev. F. N. Shimmin. (Earlestown), Rev. W. C. Tayler, Messrs. F. A. R. Neill (Bold), W. Mitchell (Golborne), P. Hall (Ear- lestown), Kelsall (Rainhill), G W. Rawlins (Rain- hill), M. Birkhead, P. M. Campbell, and others. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said that that was not only a political meeting, because he saw friends present who were not altogether on the same side of politics as themselves. Still it was a Liberal meeting— (applause)—censisting of the Liberals of the district, to H present to one of their number a testimonial in recognition of the great services he had done for the Liberal cause in that division. (Applause) It was also a meeting at which those present, whatever might be their politics, had assembled to show esteem and respect to a man. (Applause.) Colonel McCorquodale—(ap- plause)—was the unanimous choice of the Liberal "300 ' when they required a candidate to contest the division at the last election, and subsequent events proved the wisdom of •the choice, for throughout England there was scarcely a more popular candidate than the Colonel. (Applause.) During the contest the candidate set an example to all by his exertions, for he was not working for himself alone, but for the Liberal cause, and for the Liberals of that division. (Applause.) Commenting on the Tory tenden- denci:s of that part of Lancashire, and the strong opponent Colonel McCorquodale met in the person of Sir Richard Cross, the chairman drew satisfaction from the result of the poll, showing that, consider- ing many adverse circumstances, the Liberal candidate ' had achieved a moral victory. If anything could increase his respect for Colonel McCorquodale, which woald be a difficult thing to do, it would be the manner in which he , (the colonel) took his beating. It was thought desirable that some testimonial of esteem should be made to Colonel ' McCorquodale, and a subscription, which was made as re- presentative as possible, was set on foot, which had its out- come in that meeting. He wished they could say they were presenting it to their member—(applause)—or to their future candidate. (Renewed applause.) They made the ;presentation in remembrance of a bard-fought battle, with I all the enthusiasm it was possible to feel, but above all they gave it as a testimony of their esteem to Colonel McCor- quodale as a friend. (Applause.) He then formally made I the presentation and read the address. It was as follows :

"To Colonel McCorquedale, J,P., D.L.—Sir,---We, the ! Liberal electors of the Newton Division of Lancashire, de- sire to record our high appreciation of your earnestnes!, I energy, and devotion as our candidate in the first contest ! for the representation of this constituency in Parliament. Your opponent, at that time Home secretary, was the ! strongest possible Conservative candidate, and we wish to ' express our great admiration for the gallantry with which ! you fought the battle. The closeness of the contest bears ' the strongest testimony to the high esteem in which you are held by the electors, who value not only your long and honourable services to Liberalism, but also your many and generous efforts for the moral and social improvement of the people. In thanking you most heartily in the name of our party for your past labours in the Liberal cause, we trust as one of our leaders you may long be spared to aid us in furthering that cause in the Newton Division.—Signed on behalf of the electors. JOSEPH EVANS, president; CHAS. PILICINGTON, chairman of the Executive." '1 he address is the work of Mr. Richards, of Nuttall-et., Liverpool. The etvle adopted by the artist was pure Gothic of the 13th century, except the large capitals which are filled with very fine work of early English or the 12th century. The heraldic portion of the illumination harmon- ises well with the fine border. On the left are the arms of Colonel AlcCorquodale ; on the right those of the Duchy of Lancaster. The arms of, Liverpool on a rest of almost microscopic work fill the space under the signatures. Colonel MCCORQUODALE, on rising to respond, was re- ceived with prolonged cheers. He observed that it was with feelingi of no ordinary character that he rose to acknow- ledge the kind expressions concerning himself used by the chairman, and so kindly received by those present. (Ap- plause.) He wished he could deserve everything that had been said concerning him. (A voice : "A good deal moor, owd mon," laughter, and cheers.) Speaking of the contest in which he was engaged, he said he spent a thoroughly happy time at that period, and as to the bard work he was said to have gone through, he came out quite as well, if not better, as he was at the commencement. (Applause.) He proceeded to quote the points of his address to the electors preceding the contest, and in employing the opinions be then expressed, and the measures he thought would be for the benefit and advantage of his fellow men, asked why none of them had been brought forward. Speaking of the points mentioned in his address to the electors, be said he would ever have respect and consideration for members of every religions , denomination, and it was an erroneous impression to sup- I pose that he and his friends wished 80 pull down the Church of England. They would always be as firmly at- tached to education, coupled with religions instruction, but they wished to have an alteration in regard to the payment of school fees to poor people. He believed county boards would be a great benefit, and they would give the People a greater control over the issue and renewal of licences. The House of Lords was by no means perfect, and he had no doubt it would be altered by and by. (Applause.) In regard to the land question they needed alterations in regard to the laws of primogeniture and entail. These sub- jects were those considered at the time of the election, and he asked how was if that the vlrious schemes bad not been brought before Parliament? The answer was the one en- grossing subject which prevented legislation on every other subject—that of Ireland. That subject would have to be grepnled with before we had legislation for the Scotch and the English; legislation to carry out the various schemes that were in abeyance, and they hoped that the time would come before long. Ireland was a very interesting subject,
