div.head: DISORDERLY PARISHIONERS' MEET-
div.p: DISORDERLY PARISHIONERS' MEET-
ING AT WIDNES.
DISGRACEFUL SCENE.

For some time past a scandal of a grave nature has been circulated with reference to a Church dignitary of the parish of Widnes, and it was anticipated that there would be an outburst of pent up feeling at the vestry meeting held a few days ego. The proceedings, however, passed of£ in a quiet manner under the presidency of the Vicar. A. rumour was then set afloat that a public meeting would be held to discuss the matter, and at the beginning of the week a small handbill was distributed inviting tiles parishioners of St. Mary's Church to attend a public meeting at Malice's Temperance Hall, Simms Cross. It was an- nounced that "several gentlemen" would take part in the proceediege, bat for what purpose they were called together was not stated. When our representative arrived at the place of meeting on Thursday ,evening the room was tilled, and a most extraordinary scene was taking place. Ranged on one side of the platform were Mr. Foley, the lay reader of St. Mary's Church, and Messrs. W. J. Rankin, Samuel Pelin, W. Rogerson, Jos‘ph Ford, John Ford, and several others ; whilst ranged on the other side were Messrs. J. B. Imison, F. Neil (vicar's warden), L. liilcross (people's warden), F. Cave. H. A. Wharton, Beat- tie, J. Williams, H. Brooks, W. Dvverryhouse, C. Watson, W. Lowe, and P. Hunt, members of the Parish Church, and the greatest uproar prevailed. It appears that Mr. Foley'e party had poseession of the platform, with Mr. Ran Lin as chairman. Upon the latter rising to open the proceedings it was pretested that the meeting had a right to decide who should preside over them, and Mr. L. Kilcross moved, and Mr. Neill seconded, a motion that Mr. J. B. Raison occupy the chair. This was cirried by a laree majority, and Mr. Imison accompanied by Mr. Kilcrose, walked to the steps letding to the platform. Those in possession resisted their advance. There was a rush of Mr. I:nison's supporters, and the plat- form was stormed, the violence of the struggle being testi- fied to by the smashed handrail of the steps, which lay on the floor.—Amid cries of "Chair, chair," hisses, and groans, Mr. Foley shouted that there was a chairman already ap- pointed. "They" had paid for theiroom, and the room was theirs. Striking the table very violently with his bands, he ordered Mr. Imison from the platform, but Mr. Imison re- Insect to go. (Cheers and groans.)—During a lull in the disturbance, Mr. Foley shouted that if they would allow them say what they had V. say they should be satisfied. —Mr. Imison was about to make further remarks, when Mr. Foley screamed. "Sit down !" Mr. Imison's reply was lost in the howl that arose from the throats of Mr. Folev's ad- herents on the platform and in the audience. Mr. Imison, Me. Feley, and Mr. Rankin were to be seen having an ex- cited altercation together, but the shouting, hooting, and other noises that were given utterance to drowned every word, and the scene was like a pantomime. Those on the platform were ranged like opposing armies, whose only weapon of offence and defence was the tongue, and aided by their followers below they almost howled themselves hoarse. The excitement led to gesticulations, and the application of force appeared imminent. Leaning over the rail of the platform and di- recting his voice tee tbe reporters, Mr. Foley juet succeeded In making heard the threat that the Bishop of the diocese should hear of this "obstruction." Mr. Imison made an in- audible reply, and Mr. Foley laughed in his face. Mr. Imi- son, Mr. Rankin, and Mr. Foley in turn attempted to address the Meeting, and were in turn literally" yelled" down. A man ascended the platferm with a jug of water and a glass, and offered a glass of water to Mr. Cave, but one of Mr. Foley's supporters snatched it from his lips and ran off the platform with it, and the uproar increased. At length Mr. Foley and his supporters capitulated, and took seats near the platform, one of them observing that if he bad his way he would chuck them (Mr. Irnison's party) out. Mr. Imi- son aeain attempted to speak, but Mr. Ford went close to him, and, waving his arms, shouted "Bow, bow; bow, bow." Mr. Foley took up a position on the platform again, and called upon Inspector Wood and Sergeants Robin- son and Strickland to eject Mr. Imison, but the officers made no sign. After further altercations had passed, Mr. Harrison said that the use of that room was granted not for a ne2etieg of that description but for the purpose of pre- eenting a testimonial to Mr. Foley.—Mr. Imison (Nadine out the handbill) : We take this bill as the business of the meeting. (Cheers.)--:-Mr. Foley : Order, order. You ought to know better. Mr. Imison. (Disturbance.)—A Parish- ioner: So ought you.—Mr. Imison : We have accepted an invitation to attend a meeting of parishioners. That meeting has appointed the chairman—(cheers and hooting) —which position I intend to occupy to-night. (Cheers.)— Remarks followed as to who engaged and who would ply for the room.—Mr. Foley (very excitedly and pointing his stick at Mr. Imison) said: We ask you respectfully te re- tire. You are Radicals and they who pull down the Church and wish to destroy it. (Great uproar.)—Mr. Imison said his was a most embarrassing position. He was asked to preside over a meeting called by some individual unknown. (Mr. Joseph Ford: " Bah, bah, bah, bah.") He thought be was only expressing the feelings --(hooting)—of the majority when he said he came there reluctantly, but it wee thought desirable to attend to en- deavour to find out who had had the astounding audacity to call the meeting together—(applause)—without so mlich as censulting the Vicar—(applause)—who it was well- known had the good of the parish at heart, and was sever slow to lend a helping band to any good object. (Applause.) The notice left them in blissful ignorance—(a. Voice: out of that," and disturbance)—as to the bu.sinese sine ehe ject of the meeting. (A Voice: " Put on ti, n specs.") Imison added that they had come there after taking the advice of the Church Council, and then called unon the convener of the meeting to state the business..—Mr. Foley and several of his supporters were then standing near toe doorway, and upon hearing this Mr. Foley came forward and said, "Do you reque,t me to addree.e a rowdy meeting." Mr. Foley then left the room amid a storm of booting.—Mr. Imison now called upon the " several gentlemen who are expected to take part in the proceedings " to state the business, but there was Co re- sponse. Mr. Rankin shouted "all our statements will go by letter." Mr. Imison went on to justify his appointment to the chair, and Mr. Reseal' shouted " Conic down out of that." The Chairman called upon Mr. F. Neil to address the meeting. Mr. Neil protested against anyone other than the vicar or the wardens calling a meeting of the parishioners—Mr. L. Killcross characterised the calling of the meeting as impertinent, and upheld the appointment of Mr. Imison to the chair.—Mr. Cave said that in viow of the gross piece of insubordination committed by Mr. Foley, he moved (disturbance) that the vicar of Widnes, the Rev. J. Wright-Vi illiams, be asked to at once dispense with the services of Mr. Foley." (Cheers.)—Mr. Beattie seconded the proposition and made some severe remarks upon Mr. Foley, which were loudly cheered.—The proposition was carried with loud cheers, only three women and one man holding up their hands against it.—Mr. Craw- ford. made a speech in which ho remarked that during his 21) years' residence in Widnes be had never seen. such unseemly behaviour at a meetine. Mr. Chadwick appealed to every person in that Toom whether Mr. Foley had not had a fair opportunity to speak, and whetter be h.ad not then a fair opportunity Of address- ing them if he wished to .come forward. (Loud cries of "yes.") He had no feeling against Mr. Foley, but he taught they lead shown Mr. Foley that 99 par Cent of the parishioners of Widres did not endorse his proceedings and the sooner Mr. . Foley 's services ceased the better would the parishioners be pleased. (Cheere.)— After further discussion a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman.—Mr. J, Reap, on behalf of the trustees of

the Malins Temperance Hall, wished it to be understood tion with the legal proceedings in question so far as they that they were entirely ignorant of the object of the meet- had the power to do.—Mr. A. WOODS seconded the proposal, ing, and were led to belteve that it was for the purpose of which was agreed to. presenting a testimonial to Mr. Foley.—After singing a por- RE•APPOINTMENTS. tion of the National Anthem and giving three cheers for Mr. Dr. Sephton was re-appointed medical officer for the en- Imison, the poceedings terminated, suing year, and Mr. Bawling nuisance impector. This was all the business.

'On each evening an excellent band of about 20 performers, whose very varuable aid was gratuitously given,was present, and played selections under the able leadership of Mr. W. S. Woods. "Tins FLOWER QUEEN."—A somewhat novel but certainly very pleasing entertainment was given in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday even- ing in connection with the Middle Class School, The Mount, Warrington. There was a crowded at- tendance. The entertainment consisted of a render- ing of a cantata, composed by Mr. George F. Root, and entitled" The Flower Queen, the Coronation of the Rose." The performers were pupils of the above- named school, assisted by Miss Slater. In this piece each of the young artistes, all of whom were prettily and tastefully attired, are supposed to represent flowers of one kind or another, and the plot begins with a meeting of the flowers in a secluded dell in the forest to choose their queen. A person discontented with the world seeks in the same place retirement from its cares and disap- pointments. The flowers tell of love and duty, and the recluse, learning that to fill well the station al- lotted by Providence is to be happy, resolves to turn again to usefulness and contentment among her fellow creatures, The stage was beautifully dis- played with flowers and plants, and altogether the arrangements were most admirable. As the re- cluse, Miss Slater had an important part to fill, but she filled it very successfully, and the solos, duets, choruses, &c., were rendered by the pupils in a manner which betokened careful training and much aptness on the part of the youthful vocal- ists. The soloists, in addition to Miss Slater, were Misses A. Dewhurst, May Grainger, May Clare, Florence Royston, and Clara Moores, and a recita- tion was given by Miss H. Whitham. Some of the choruses and part songs were charming in their effect, and were evidently highly appreciated by the audience. The accompaniments were excel- lently played by Mr. W. Woods.

GAME TRESPASS. —At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Mon- day, before Messrs. J. C. Gamble and W. Pilkington, John Thomas Peak and Herbert Coughtrev, Young men residing at :utton, were summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Bold, in the occupation of John Rowcock, farmer, Moat House Farm. They were farther charged with using a dog to take game, ,Aithout a license, at the same time.—Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted, and Mr. R. W. H. Thomas defended.—Mr. Swift stated that en the previous Tuesday afternoon the defendants were driving in a trap along the road leading from the Chanel House, Burtonw4d, to Sutton through Bold, and had a dog with them. In a clover root field they saw two hares feeding, and they stopped the trap. The defendants then waved the dog into the field after the hares, and one of the hares was chased across two fields. On seeing a keeper approach the defendants drove away.—Each defendant was fined 108 and costs.

SINGULAR DEATH OF A PUBLIOAN.—On Friday Mr. William Bromilow, 67 years of age, landlord of the Clock Face Inn, Bold, died under somewhat singular circum- stances. On the 28th ult. he went to Warrington and called at a public-house in Rylands-street, kept by lieorge Wright, where he had some beer. He left without saying weere he was going, but some time afterwards a man named J9hn Davis, of Bridge-street, foung him insensible and bleeding from his ears in an adjoining entry. Dr. Fox was sent for, and eventually Brom'low was taken home in a cab, but death ensued as stated. On Monday morning an inquee was held by Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the coroner, at the Clock Face Inn, on the body of the deceased. Dr. Fox, of Warrington, who attended the deceased from the time of the accident until death ensued, said in his opinion death had ensued from fracture of the skull, but he had no suspicion of foul play, as he had evidently fallen On the side of his head.—lne jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

A fine of 40s and costs was imposed. CHARGE AGAINST A PENKETH PUBLICAN. John Johnson, occupier of the licensed premises, the Ferry Inn, Penketh, was summoned for permit- ting drunkenness on his premises on Good -Friday. Mr. Swift, solicitor (St. Helens), defended.—Supt. Weir said that the proceedings were taken in con- sequence of evidence that came out before Mr. Brig- house, coroner, at an inquiry held relative to the death of a man named John Garnett, of Penketh, who was drowned in the river Mersey on Good Friday. It appeared that on the afternoon of that day Garnett was, with others, in the house of the defendant, and was served with some beer. He left and went with other men for a sail, and, it was alleged, he was at that time drunk. When on the river the boat capsized and Garnett was drowned. The result of the inquiry was such that in the pub- lic interest he felt it his duty to summon the de- fendant.—John Boscoe, journeyman butcher, Pen- keth, said that on Good Friday he saw the deceased man Garnett drink a glass of beer at the Ferry Inn. iHe afterwards went for a sail with Garnett and others. Witness swore that lie only saw Garnett I have one glass of beer, and that lie (Garnett) did I not seem to be the worse for drink. He did not see any whisky in the boat. In reply to Mr. Swift, witness said that Garnett did not assist in the man- agement of the boat, but sat still. The boat cap- sized, because the keel caught the bottom. There was no moving about, or disorderly conduct on the boat.—Thomas Johnson, postman, Penketh, said that he saw Garnett on the afternoon in question. He considered him to be rather fresh. Witness would not call him drunk.—George Randall, Penketh, said that he also saw Garnett, and considered that he was drunk, because he could not walk straight.— Mr. Swift was about to speak for the defence, when the magistrates announced that they had de- cided to dismiss the case. ALLEGED OFFENCE AT RIXTON.

WHICH SHALL IT BE? Sir,—The time has arrived when the electors of Great Britain must give plain answers to plain questions. The electors of Ireland at the last general election gave such evidence of unenimity on the Home Rule question that could not possibly have been foreseen ten years ago, and to-day we are called upon to dtcide which shall it be— Home Rule or coercion. It is of no use to repeat the his- tory of the past eighty years. Mr. Gladstone in introduc- ing U e measure intended to establish Home Rule in Ireland laid bare all the wrongs and grievances Ireland had suf- fered at the hands of her rulers. Coercion has done its worst, and what is the result ? Ireland is to-day more hos- tile to England than at any period in its history. Another .Ireland is growing across the Atlantic, money and sympathy are being sent without grudge, and a fixed determination exists that the sons of Ireland shall no longer have emigra- tion held out to them as the only means whereby happiness can be attained. No doubt can exist in the mind of anyone at all acquainted with Irish history that the breaking up of , the Irish parliament was a great crime. English money ' and English influence contributed largely to bring about the present deplorable state of things, and the sooner we set about paying the ransom the better. It is a most remarkable thing, that lock were we may outside the measure which now " holds the field," we fin-el no way out of the dilemma. "Integrity of the empire," " protests against disintegration," unanimous votes in favour of preserving the unity of the United Kingdom, all this we see, but not one word of advice is given as to how Ireland shall be pacified. Lord balisbury at the close of his short term as care- taker, and after sending the possessor of all the "dormant talent" the Tories could boast of to Ireland. was fain to confess at Newport that the suggestion of Mr. Parnell would have to be acted upon, and he would most certainly have brought in a Home Rule measure had not the blockheads in his Cabinet resisted authority and argument. Even after all this, and as a forlorn hope within twenty-four hours of dissolution, Mr. Smith was despatched to freland with in- structions to find cut a cure for the "veiled reb,llion " of Lord Beaconsfield; and what was the result of all this splendid statesmanship? a ride for a fall: the charger to be the weather beaten Rosinante, Ceercion. I, for one, am proud to thine that coercion from today is dead, whatever the future of Ireland may be, or however her eons may conduct themselves, at least it will not be said that she suffers in consequence of the wrong-doings of an alien race. The dual measure, as introduced by Mr. Gladstone, may fairly cause men to pause and ponder. It would be no sat- isfaction to find Liberals trooping at the heels of Mr. Glad- stone, prepared to support and vote for any and every mea- sure, in the happy-go-lucky style in which the measures of Lord Beaconsfield were supported by Tories. The essence of Liberalism is diversity of opinion, and when this is not married to open and vaunting opposition works well for the country. Home Rule must be granted; it is but a loftier term for what both Liberals and Tories have hitherto ex- pressed their willingness to grant. Under no conditions that can at present be imagined can the Parliament at Westminster be made to do the legislative work of the na- tion. Congestion is fast setting in; what laws are passed to: the welfare of tke United Kingdom are passed in a slipshod fashion, and are needing constant revision. Why, then, should we as Enelishmen be found fighting vainly for the shadow termed "Integrity of the United Kingdom," while at the same time we are letting slip every opportu- nity for drawing together the English speaking races, , and every chance that may occur for drawing together, people, not of the same race, but whom policy would teach it is their interest to be enited ? Federation by force will never come about; natonal pride will always prevent this. Federation through self-interest may, if it is fairly shown that England has no dread of au- tonomy, neither in her colonies nor vet in Ireland. Justice to Ireland, sp-rdy and sure, must be the cry of the electors ere many weeks have passed over our heads. CIIFFORD DIX.

William Perrin was summoned for being on licensed premises at Rixton, the Red Lion, after closing time on the night of Saturday, May Ist. He was seen leaving the house, where, however, he was not supplied with anything. Defendant admitted being in the yard of the public-house, but denied going into the house.—The case was dismissed. A SHAM TRAVELLER.

Elizabeth Kirk, a married woman, was summoned for falsely representing herself to be a traveller, and for by that means obtaining a glass of beer from John Johnson, of the Ferry Inn, Penketh, on the afternoon of Good Friday. A policeman in plain clothes saw the defendant with a glass of beer, which she tried to hide. She afterwards admitted that she told the landlord that she came from Latchford, whereas she lived in Dale-street, !Little Sankey, a distance of about two miles from the public-house in question.—The Bench imposed a tine of lOs and costs.

Houghton, Grange, Humphries, Kilshall, A. Woods, Owen, Heaton, Pennington, Swinton, Gibson, C. Broadbent, and W. Long (ex- officio); Mr. S. Sutton (clerk), Mr. W. HOUGHTON, seconded by Mr. LONG, the Rev. G. F. Roberts was elected vice-chairman. DAY OF MEETING. It was agreed, on the motion of the Rev. G. F. Roberts, that the day and time of meeting continue as previously, viz., balf-past ten o'clock in the morning of the first Friday in each month.

PENKETH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. OwEet. seconded by Mr. A. WOODS, that the Penketh Parochial Committee be constituted as formerly, and that the committee be em- powered to suggest any alteration in the membership they might think advisable. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. SEPHTON reported that there had been during the past month 31 births and 18 deaths. Toe death-rate from all causes was equal to 16-6 per 1,000, as compared with 15 in the corresponding month of last year. The doctor re- ported that the Authority's district was in good sanitary condition for a rural district, and remarkable for its long- evity, the united ages of four out of the five deaths in the Rixton district during the month amounting to 318, or an average of 70 years for each person. Lord Winmarleigh, two cottages at Rixton, to be supplied from well ; the Right Hon. Lord Winmarleigh, two farm houses and outbuildings, Rixton Moss, to be sripplied from well ; Mrs. Ashbrook, new house at Orford, to be supplied from well. The building certificates issued to the Right Hon. Lord Winmarleigh and Mrs. Ashbrook to be endorsed "that tlee certificate for habitation will not be issutd until the analysis of the drinking water is approved by this Authority."—The report was adopted. If they were to become liable to proceedings of that kind they might as well be muzzled as the dogs were in London, because they could be of 14 0 use to the public. If there was an action ICE hoped it would have the good effect to lead to a clear state- ment as o what Authorities of that kind could do and say and what they could not. He assumed that there would be only one opinion that they .should stand by their clerk.— Mr. J. C. SUTTON said the action was simply based on what was partially reported in one newspaper, the other two newspapers correctly dealing with the subject. It was not what the officer said, but what the newsbp.oanonedr irnephoornteodurhim o protect taeyc theirMr Lc rr k d a G, thought t h their tr were m privileged s n (t Hh eeiatr d, ile,eoaur;) He also asked how far they were sion in that room.—Mr. J. C. SUTTON said he was sorry to siy that as far as h i e understood the law n this country on the point, it was a perfect bagatelle, It was utterly impos- sible to tell what would he the result of an action of that kind. The judges themselves were constantly differing as to the state of the law. But his own opinion was that both an officei and a member acting in the fair discharge of his duty without personal feeling was protected by the laws of this country, but it did not protect him from being put to considerable expense in defending an action. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. OWEN moved that the Authority recoup the clerk and Mr. Gibson for any expense they might be put to in connec•

MANCHESTER HAY AND STRAW, FRIDAY.—flay. 51c1 to 61c1; clover. 60 to 71c1; wheat stlaw, 41 to 4d; oat straw, 4d to 4il r srone of 4b. GLASGOW PIG IRON, FRIDAY. Business at 38s ad cash. Closing ; Sellers 38s 4d cash, and 38s bld one month; buyers id less. Market idle. CORK 13uTTE•s, FRIDAY. Ordinary: Firsts, 87*; se- conds. ; thig cia, 53s ;,f ow the, 47*; fit ths. —s. In the market, 1.100 firkins, 104 mild, and 7 kegs. LONDON PRODUCE. PREDA.Y.—Sugar market remains dull; beetroot quoted 13s lid May-June. Ccffee generally steady Tea: 193 packages Indian advertised for sale to-day. Ric* in- attive Cotton market very quiet. Jute extremely dull. Tal- low, Y.O , 32s on the spot. Turpentine, 2's 9d to 265. Petro- leum, sid to 6d. Rape oil. 19s 9d to 20s Od ; linseed oil, 19J 4;cl to 19s Ad. on the spot WAKEFIELD CORN, FRIDAY.—Under the influencs of brilliant weather the wheat trade remains quiet but steady, at full prices; Engli,h is again in very small supply and dearer to buy. These is little or no demand for barley. Egyptian beans rather easier Maize steady. Oats firmer. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—There is not much doing in any departm-nt, and the grater activity in Liverpool causes no respopse here. Spinners hold very firmly to lull quota- tions, but they do not get much inquiry. Cloth callers are not making headway. t orne inquiry for Eastern goods is still to the fore but buyers' limits are not tempting to makers. LivERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY.—Beef quiet, but with. o t change. Pork s eddy in value, but not specially active. Rather better inquiry in Bacon for boneless meats for the Continent; fancy cuts firmer, but not quotably higher, In Hams Vng cuts are the turn dearer and short cuts steady. Spec'al brands of borax-cured Shoulders scarce and wrnted. Cheese quietly steady. Butter inactive, and prices nominal. WARRINGTON CORN MARKET, WEDNESDAY.— At to-day's market we had a good average attendance. Wheat and oats clearer to buy. Flour advanced 6d. to 9d. per load. PRESCOT. 1 THE CATTLE FAIR, on Tuesday, was prstty well attended, There was a good stock of heifers and dairy Cows, most of which changed hands. New RATES.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Thee day, the magistrates signed the following rates for tne ensuing year :—Prescot poor rata is 24 in the 4 Rainbill poor rate 2e in the X, lighting rate 3d in the X, KnowsleY poor rate is Od in the X. THI3 WHISTON WAYWARDEN.—In accordance witb node* given at the last Prescet Petty Sessions, Mr. Henry Cross, clerk to the Highway Board, applied to the magistrates, on Tuesday (I'4essrs. Willis and Gibbon) for the appointment. ,of Mr. James Sumner as waywarden for the township 01 Whiston.—The magistrates granted the application. CHURCH OF ENGLAND BAND OF HOPE.—On Monday a meeting of the above was held in the school-room, Hough" ton-street. There was a moderate attendance. A presenta- tion afterwards took place to Mr. James Case, late superin" tendent of the boys' 6unday school, which post he has held for some years. Rev. F. R. Lee made the preaentitien' which took the form of a very handsome timepiece and an address. Air. Lee made some appropriate remarks, to which Mr. Case suitably replied. The meeting closed in the usual- way.

Torn FLOWFR QUEEN."—In connection with the Pre? cot Church of England Band of Hope an amateur oPeratle performance of " The Flower Queen" and Red Riding Hood's Rescue" was given in the Assembly Room, OP Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. The ele. cutauts in this charming performance were 30 children, un- der the management of Miss G. E. Myers, the accornpair ist being Miss G. Prescott. The most prominent part" in " The Flower Queen" were taken by Misses Kate Prescott, Myers, S. J. Hamby, M. Harrison, E. z4orman, E. J. John- son, L. Myers, M. Prescott, M. A. Ellard, A. Jones, Edwards, M. E. Taylor, and E. Evans ; and in " Red Rid- ing Hood's Rescue " Misses I, Myers, Myers, W. /Ishii croft, S. J. Hornby, E. Norman, and Masters P. Reusba.',, and C. Bryan. At the conclusion the Rev. F. R. Lee, I" the absence of HT, vicar, cordially thanked the performer' and friends for the very pleasant evening they PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.—Tbe Ike m' bad monthly Ineetuli afford.ed• of the Prescot Highway Board for the ensuing year was her' on Tuesday atternoon, when there were preti-ent—Captall, Willis (who was elected to preside). Messrs. E. Tyrerd• Newton, H. Cross (clerk), and W. Goldsworth (surveyor.)--* Appointment of Chairman and Vice-chairman : On the motion of Mr. Tyr..r. seconded by Captain Willis, Mr. W. Evans, J.P., was re-elected chairman for the ensuing Moir' inonths.—Mr. Tyrer proposed Mr. Lowe as vice-chairo.lan for the ensuing year.—Captain Willis seconded the rnotioc, which was adopted.—Surveyor's Expenditure The Sur,: veyor's expenditure for the three weeks ending April 29. t" was as follows :—Bold £l3 4s 4d, Knowsley £9'3s 21, }taloa; bill £l6 us 10d, Whiston £5 15s 81, team labour gl 17s sd, new materials £2O 7s Bd, incidentals 3s 3d, tut 3 £75 3s 41.—The Rainhill Telephones: The Surveyor re- ported that he had heard nothing further with regard to the erection of telephones at Rainhill than what had Leen re reported.—There was no other business.

The race for the Chester Cup was decided on Wedneel3l, when the Duke of Beaufort's Eastern Emperor won, Mr.,cl,e,. Rothachild's Beaver being second, Lord Bradford's Hamo, third. THE QUEEN'S BARER.—The working bakery which iS being constructed for Messrs. Kirkland Bros. is fast sr proaching completion. All the processes of making a°l baking the noted Vienna bread will be shown. In front the bakery an Oriental caf6 is being constructed, and 0.4 ' whole building when completed and in working order ty" be one of the most attractive and interesting exhibits the ground. We are informed that Messrs. Kirkland 1301 have been appointed bread makers to the Queen and 801-3 household during the stay of her Majesty and suite 1° Liverpool. EXTRAORDINARY IMPEISONKENT. About miclnigl3 si;ort time ago a signalman named Clarke, stationed in tbe Raven-street box, St. Helens Station, heard someone shoot. ing and groaning in the direction of the canal. He gO: information at the station and foreman-porter Forshaw to ascertain the cause. An investigation led him to a soli" office attached to a mason's shed in the yard of Mr. Melling, stone flqg merchant. He tried the door but was fast. He then mounted the roof, and on flashing bis lamp down the chimney, which rose about four feet, he dis- covered a labouring man " stuck fast." Not being able 10 reach the man, Forshaw, with commendable promptud„e! proceeded to pull down the brickwork, and continued to so until he reached the armpits of the man, who was the released. It appears that the man had been working f°,r Mr. Melling for about two days, and bad evidently, ivbi`6l under the influence of drink, gone to the yard to find a PIO' in which to sleep. The door being fast, he conceived tql novel idea of getting down the'chimney, which is about 1" inches square, and on arriving at the " bend " be could got neither up nor down. He remained in this singular Pr.!; dicament for two hours, and whsn discovered was covert' with soot and wassomewhat exhausted.
The cutter Ida was run down by the steamship Mar- tell°, off Falmouth, on Thursday night. One man was drowned.

Lord and Lady Salisbury arrived at Windsor on Friday evening, on a visit to Her Majesty, and were included in the Royal dinner party. On Thursday night a most destructive fire broke out at Messrs. Hurtley's flour mills, Hull. The damage is estima- ted at many thousands, but is fully covered by insurance. The fire at the Derby theatre resulted in two deaths, viz , those ot Mr. J. W. Adams, native of Bradford, a comedian. and a member of Mr. Edward Terry's company, and a stage carpenter named Loxlev.

The "Gazette" of last evening publishes a Royal procla- mation appointing and commanding Wednesday, the 12th inst., as a special day to be observed as a bank holiday throughout the city of Liverpool. SHOCKING StuctoE.--A prisoner under remand from one of the metropolitan police courts committed suicide in Hol- loway Gaol on Friday morning. He was lodged in a cell in the top gallery ; on his way to the exercise ground he jumped over and fell on the pavement beneath, a distance of 40 feet, and died immediately. DISPUTES IN THE CorroN TIIADE.—The Executive of the Weavers' Associations in North and North-East Lancashire is at present dealing with several fresh wages disputes which have arisen in the Burnley district. A num- ber of hands, too, in the Blackburn district have come out on strike, and there appears no prospect of a settle- ment.

• THE IRISH QUESTION. It was arranged 0)1 Thursday that Lord Hartington should on Monday next move the rejection of the Home Rule Bill. It is said that Mr. Chamberlain has informed the Premier that be will support the second reading if the Irish representation at Westminster is retained. The Presi- dent of the Baptist Union (the Rev. C. Williams) has writ- ten a letter expressing the hope that the Premier will suc- ceed in his Irish scheme ; and the President of the Congregational Union (the Rev. H. White) says he is disposed to follow the lead of Lord Spencer and Mr. Glad- stone.
THE EASTERN CRISIS. RECALL OF MINISTERS.

The Greek Minist.lr of Marine has ordered the gun boat Salaminia to proceed at once to Constantinople t) bring away M. Condouriotis, the Greek Minister to Turkey. This order was given after the arrival of the Turkish gunboat Ha nie at the Pirreas on Thursday evening. A conference of the representatives of England, Austria, Russia, Germany, Italy, and Turkey was held at Athens on Thursday evening at the Italian Legation, at which it was decided that each Minister should separately address a note to the Greek Government notifying his departure. Sir Horace Rurnbold will go to Sada Bay and thence to Malta. The Ottoman Minister will return to Constan- tinople. The Greek troops at Vole, have been ordered to Larissa. Many soldiers have telegraphed to their parents, announc- ing their departure for the front, and asking their blessing. The men of the garrison received marching orders with cheers.

div.head: BLOCKADE OF GREEK FORTS.
div.p: BLOCKADE OF GREEK FORTS.

ATHENS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—lnstructions to blockade the Greek ports have been given to the allied squadron. The Greek Government have ordered the Peloponnesian army to proceed to Thessaly. Two battalions of the Athens garrison left for the frontier to-day, amidst the greatest en- thusiasm.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 o'clock.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The Marquis of Ripon said the Ad- miralty would give all practical facilities to naval volun• teers to learn gun boat drill.—Replying to Lord Sidmoutb, the Marquis of Ripon said a report on tbe explosion of the gun on board her Majesty's ship Collingworth, on Tues- day, had beon received at the Admiralty, and it had been determined to strengthen the guns of that class alre-rdy mounted.—The Commons amendments to the Lords amend- ments to the Poor Relief (Ireland) Bill were considered and agreed to. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at 4 o'clock. THE CHARTER HOUSE.—Sir R. WEBSTER moved the second reading of the Charter House Bill. Its object was by disposing of some land to provide means for carrying out the original intentions of the founder.—Mr. WALTER JAMES said the bill was most objectionable, and would sweep away some'of the old and ancient buildings which ought to be preserved.—After a long discussion, Mr. B. HOPE moved the adjournment of the debate to give the governors time to consider the objections raised to the bill.—The motion for adjourning the debate was rejected by 198 to 99, and the bill was then withdrawn.

Tim GREBE Crarsts.-:—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir M. Beach, said the reply of Greece to the note of yesterday had been received and was unsatisfactory, and British, German, Austrian. and Italian Ministers had left Athens. Further information would soon be received. THE HOME Rims BILL.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir M. Beach said on Monday be would state the arrange. ment for continuing the debate on the Bill for improving the Government of Ireland.

THE ESTIMATES.—A COUNT OUT.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Esti- mates, Mr. Hutton moved a motion, the object of which was that the people of this country should be in a position to take advantage of the treaty which was called the Postal Union, in order that anomalies which now existed might be removed to the advantage of the commercial community of Great Britain.—Mr. H. FOWLER said at present the foreign and colonial postage was carried on at a loss of £395,000 per annum, and if they further reduced the Indian postage a greater loss would be occasioned. He objected to increase the already heavy burdens on the British taxpayer. The proposal of Mr. Hutton was negatived without a divi- sion.—Mr. THEODORE FRY called attention to the present hours of polling at School Board elections in cities and boroughs, and urged that the present hours should be ex- tended from eight a.m. to 8 p.m. in order to give facilities for working classes registering their votes.—Sir J. Fergu- son, Mr. W. Saunders, Mr. Picton Cook, Mr. F. S. Powell, Mr. Carvell Williams, Mr. E. Russell, Mr. L. Fry, and Dr. Foster warmly supported the extension of the hours.— Sir L. PLAYFAIR said he bad no doubt the strong opinion so generally expressed in favour of keeping the poll open for twelve hours would induce the Privy Council at once to consent to a prolongation of present hours. His own eng• gestion was that the object would be met by keeping the poll open in populous places for twelve hours and in smaller places from twelve to eight.—Sir M. BEAcn ex- pressed approval of this suggestion, and the subject dropped. Mr. C. BENTINCIC urged that increased facilities should be given for posting letters at railway stations.—Mr. FOWLER was replying when the House was counted, ..nd only 39 members being present the House adjourned at five minutes past seven.
The Bank rate of discount has been raised from 2 to 3 per cent.
A sailor incarcerated in Lewes Naval Prison escaped on Thursday morning by scaling the walls. He got clear away.

A guard named Green, in the South-Eastern Company's service, fell on the line near High= on Thursday, and was cut to pieces by a train. George Harries, a patient of Carmarthen Lunatic Asy- lum, eluded his keepers and hung himself on a tree. He had a delusion that if he could kill someone he would be well again.

A bricklayer named Baker is in custody at Carlisle on suspicion of -being the fourth man concerned in the Netherby Hall burglary and the subsequent attempts to murder three pol The International Exhibition of Industry, Science, and Art, which occupies a large building specially crected in the West Meadows, Edinburgh, was on Thursday formally *opened by Prince Edward of Wales,who had overnight been the guest of Lord Lothian at Newbattle, Dalkeith.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT EABLESTOWN.-011 Tuesday fore- noon Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Royal Hotel, Cross-lane, Earlestown, touchiuw the death of Michael Kelly, 60 years of age, residing in Houghton-SL, and who for nearly 40 years was employed as a carter by Mr. Joseph Pennington, contractor, dzc. According to the evidence the deceased had suffered from bronchitis for some time past and had been off his work. On Thursday last week he felt a little better and went out of the house for a walk. He went to Pennington's building yard and he was seen standing in the yard near to the boiler house by a man named Thomas Hyde. A few minutes afterwards it was found that he had fallen down the " firehole," and was insen- sible. Be did not appear to have sustained any serious injury after he had recovered consciousness, and he walked to his home. Dr. Patterson was, however, sent for, and an exam- ination revealed the fact that the deceased had fractured bis collar bone. He lingered until Sunday night when he died. —The jury returned a verdict of. " Accidental death,"

PROSPECTUS. This Company has been formed to acquire. continue, and extend the business of Mr. John Milling, trading as John Milling and Partners, of Leeds, Warehousemen, General Drapers, and House Furnishers. The business is well and favourably known throughout the North cf England, and has been successfully carried on for many years past by the founder, who is the vendor. It is name of its kind, there being no other general drapery estab- lishment in the town at all approaching it in magnitude, or having so wide a connection in the eurrounding districts. It is in the very heart or the borough. being located close to the tramway system, railway stations, markets, places of amusement, &c. Indeed, it would be impossible to select a better situation for any business, where a vast population and the utmo.t publicity are of paramount importance. • In consequence of advaneead years and enfeebled health the proprietor is no longer able to give the constant attention which is necessary to an undertaking of its dimensions ; and he has, therefore, determined to form it into a Joint Stock Company. with a view of relieving himself of some of the re- sponsibilities. The Company, in securing the services of Mr. Milling as a Director, will have the beeefit of his matured experience and assistance in the future conduct of its affairs, and as far as practicable the p 'resent staff of managers and assistants will be retained. The Managing Director, Mr. Colquhoun, has a thorough knowledga of the concern in all its branches, haying been for upwards of twelve years in the employment of the firm, for the greater part of the time taking an active part in the management. At the first General Meeting of the Company the Sharehol- ders will be requested to elect two auditional Directors, or more if considered desirable. The Company will acquire the following property, the real estate being taken at the valuation recently made by the well. known architect and surveyor, Mr. O. S. Nelson, of Leeds, Viz . : (a.) The excellent freehold premises in which the business of the firm is now conducted, covering an area of 1,962 square yards, being situated in the centre of the town, and in one of the best position of Leeds. The warehouse and shops are admirably adapted to, and were specially built for, the purposes for which they are now in use. (8) The st, ek-intrade. tog,ther with the trade fixtures and household furniture, at the valuation made at the ordinary stock tsking of the firm on the let of Idarcti last, from which date all business done will be for the benefit of the Company. A small portion of the premises in the rear of the main building, not required for the use of the firm, is let to good tenants, and produces a rental of 1240 per annum. The Company does not tske over the book debts of the 11 ; hut the debts owed to or by the latter, prior to the let of March, will be received and paid through the counting-house of the Company, so that, whilst the fiancial arrangements will not be interrupted, the Company will incur no risk in respect of them. The only agreement is one dated 13th of April, 1885, between John Milling, as vendor, of the one part, and William Sykes. as trustee for the Company, of the other part; a cony whereof may be seen on application at the registered office of the Comnany. Reference to any agreement entered into in the ordinary course of the business of the old firm must be considered as waived. No charge is made for the valuable goodwill of the business. as Mr. lit thing and his family are taking a very large interest in the concern, nor will any promotion money be Paid by the Company, all expenses up till the date of allotment being de- frayed by the vendor. The Directors, other than the Managing Director, have agreed to take no remuneration for their services until the Shareholders have received a dividend of at least 18 per cent. in each year. The present opportunity is one that rarely occurs, and affords to those who desire a steady and permanent investmeet a pros- pect of handseme dividends without speculative risks Apaleatton for shares must be en the form accompanying the Prospectus. and forwarded to the hankers, with the neces- sary deposit. If no allotment be made the deposit will be re- turned in full. The shares will be allotted in the order of priority of applica- tion. Prospectuses and fee ins of application can be obtained of the bankers, secretary, or of any stockbroker.
